title: Does the inverse distance ladder rule out late-time solutions to the Hubble tension? A model-independent test using DES-Dovekie supernovae and DESI DR2 BAO

paper.title: Does the inverse distance ladder rule out late-time solutions to the Hubble tension? A model-independent test using DES-Dovekie supernovae and DESI DR2 BAO
paper.abstract: Abstract It has been argued that the inverse distance ladder disfavours late-time solutions to the Hubble tension. We test this with a cosmographic expansion where H H is a fourth-order polynomial in 1 − a 1-a . We combine the uncalibrated DES-Dovekie SNIa with DESI DR2 BAO, assuming a standard sound horizon r d = 147.05 ± 0.30 r_{\rm d}=147.05\pm 0.30 Mpc. Using only DES SNIa yields H 0 = 76.25 ± 2.87 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=76.25\pm 2.87\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , which is 3.1 ​ σ 3.1\sigma above the CMB-calibrated Λ \Lambda CDM prediction but consistent with SH0ES ( 1.0 ​ σ 1.0\sigma ). Adding the legacy SNIa decreases H 0 H_{0} to 67.98 ± 0.69 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 67.98\pm 0.69\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , 4.7 ​ σ 4.7\sigma below SH0ES. The 8.27 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 8.27\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} drop in H 0 H_{0} upon including the legacy SNIa cannot be attributed to expected sample variance: under a fiducial Λ ​ CDM \Lambda\text{CDM} model, only 1.24 % 1.24\% of 10 4 10^{4} mock realisations exhibit such a large H 0 H_{0} shift due to the changed redshift sampling. This points to a systematic tension between DES and legacy SNIa datasets. We next add local H 0 H_{0} anchors (the bright siren, SNII, TRGB + SBF) and test a parametrisation where the Λ \Lambda CDM H ⁡ ( z ) H(z) is enhanced by Δ H ( z ) = A exp ( − z / z 1 ) \Delta H(z)=A\exp(-z/z_{1}) . We recover H 0 = 70.00 − 0.98 + 4.78 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=70.00^{+4.78}_{-0.98}\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} and z 1 < 0.086 z_{1}<0.086 at 1 ​ σ 1\sigma confidence using DES SNIa, but H 0 = 67.66 ± 1.01 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=67.66\pm 1.01\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} and z 1 z_{1} is unconstrained using DES + legacy. Late-time solutions are thus viable with the homogeneous DES catalogue, but not with the legacy SNIa as published. Allowing them to be arbitrarily recalibrated relative to the main DES sample yields an inferred offset of Δ ​ M legacy = 0.0646 ± 0.0391 \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}=0.0646\pm 0.0391 mag, raising the predicted H 0 H_{0} to 71.03 ± 1.99 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 71.03\pm 1.99\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} . Ongoing SNIa surveys like DEBASS will provide a homogeneous sample of SNIa down to redshifts accessible via the distance ladder, assessing the validity of the current legacy samples and hence the feasibility of late-time solutions to the Hubble tension.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: One of the most challenging problems in modern cosmology is the tension between different estimates of the present expansion rate H 0 H_{0} . This Hubble tension describes the discrepancy between the expansion rate of the Universe inferred through local distance measurements ( Breuval et al., 2024 , e.g. H 0 SH0ES = 73.17 ± 0.86 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}^{\mathrm{SH0ES}}=73.17\pm 0.86\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} from SH0ES;) and the predicted expansion rate based on calibrating the parameters of the Lambda cold dark matter ( Λ \Lambda CDM) standard cosmological paradigm ( Efstathiou, Sutherland and Maddox, 1990 ; Ostriker and Steinhardt, 1995 ) using the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB), which gives a far lower value ( SPT-3G Collaboration, 2026 , e.g. SPT-3G + ACT DR6 + Planck obtained that H 0 SPA = 67.19 ± 0.38 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}^{\mathrm{SPA}}=67.19\pm 0.38\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} ;) . These results are in 6.4 ​ σ 6.4\sigma tension with each other. An even higher tension has recently been claimed by the Local Distance Network based on combining several popular local determinations and taking into account their covariance ( H0DN Collaboration, 2026 ) . However, this does not properly model selection effects or distance priors ( Desmond et al., 2026 ; Stiskalek et al., 2026 ) . The three possible explanations for the tension are unaccounted-for systematics in the distance ladder, statistical inadequacy of the inferences ( Becker et al., 2015 ; Feeney et al., 2018 ; Desmond et al., 2026 ; Percival, 2026 ; Stiskalek et al., 2026 ; Stiskalek and Desmond, 2026 , e.g.) , and new physics beyond the standard Λ \Lambda CDM model (e.g. Di Valentino et al., 2025 , and references therein) . New physics could primarily affect the Universe prior to recombination or have little impact until more recent epochs, leading to a distinction between early-time and late-time solutions. A useful expansion probe is provided by supernovae (SNe) of Type Ia (SNIa). These thermonuclear explosions occur when a carbon–oxygen white dwarf in a binary system reaches a mass close to 1.2 ​ M ⊙ 1.2\,M_{\odot} , as predicted by models like the dynamically driven double-degenerate double-detonation ( D 6 ) \left(\mathrm{D}^{6}\right) scenario ( Shen et al., 2018b ; Shen et al., 2018a ; Bauer et al., 2021 ) . Since SNIa occur at nearly the same mass, they are good standardisable candles, i.e., the peak absolute magnitude M B M_{B} in the B B band can be estimated independently of the redshift z z ( Phillips, 1993 ; Tripp, 1998 ; Phillips et al., 1999 ) . Due to the known H 0 H_{0} – M B M_{B} degeneracy ( Cai and Wang, 2026 ; Wang and Wang, 2026 ) , SNIa require an absolute calibration to measure H 0 H_{0} . Since SNIa are very luminous ( M B ≈ − 19.3 M_{B}\approx-19.3 ), they can be detected out to z ≈ 2 z\approx 2 ( Scolnic et al., 2022 ) . However, it is difficult to access all of this redshift range using just one survey. Modern SNIa catalogues like Pantheon+ ( Scolnic et al., 2022 ) , Union3 ( Rubin et al., 2025 ) , and Unite ( Camilleri et al., 2026 ) typically combine different surveys. This may create problems due to the use of different filters, selection functions, and relative calibration offsets ( Betoule et al., 2014 ; Scolnic et al., 2014 ; Scolnic et al., 2015 ; Efstathiou, 2025 ) . A homogeneous catalogue with only one survey and one selection function would be far preferable for cosmological inference. This is provided by the Dark Energy Survey ( DES Collaboration, 2016 , DES;) through its Dovekie catalogue ( Popovic et al., 2026 ) . This single-instrument dataset with a single filter system is typically complemented by legacy SNIa from older surveys to improve the leverage on the shape of the expansion history at z ≲ 0.2 z\la 0.2 , where there are very few SNIa in DES ( DES Collaboration, 2024 , though it has SNIa down to z = 0.073 z=0.073 ;) . However, including the legacy SNIa risks the aforementioned problems with combining surveys, and assessing this legacy sample relative to the DES sample is a main aim of this paper. Our baseline analysis involves only SNIa in the DES data, which we label simply DES. We also consider an extension including the legacy SNIa (DES + legacy), which corresponds to what other authors typically mean by “DES” ( DESI Collaboration, 2025 , e.g.) . This distinguishes our work from similar studies ( Popovic and Sullivan, 2026 , most notably) , which generally do not distinguish between legacy and DES SNIa. Our main motivation is the presently open discussion on whether the legacy SNIa have been correctly recalibrated onto the DES photometric filter system, something which cannot be directly verified through further observations given the transient nature of SNIa ( Efstathiou, 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Ormondroyd et al., 2026 ) . Since the legacy SNIa lie in z ∈ [ 0.025 , 0.087 ] z\in[0.025,0.087] , they provide a critical lever on the value of H 0 H_{0} , making it crucial that they be unbiased. This motivates further analyses where we calculate the possible offset between the legacy SNIa and the main DES sample. This is also a crucial issue for the evidence for evolving dark energy, which is largely driven by the legacy SNIa; allowing an offset provides a better fit to the data in a Bayesian sense than allowing a time-variation in the equation of state of dark energy ( Ormondroyd et al., 2026 ) . In Section 4.5 , we explore the extent to which the legacy SNIa affect the evidence for evolving dark energy. There are two main routes to determine the absolute SNIa magnitude M SNIa M_{\rm SNIa} . The first route is through the cosmic distance ladder, usually with three rungs. The first rung involves geometry to calibrate distance indicators like Cepheid variable stars ( Leavitt and Pickering, 1912 ; Riess et al., 2022 ; Breuval et al., 2024 ) , the tip of the red giant branch ( Lee et al., 1993 ; Madore and Freedman, 1995 ; Freedman et al., 2019 ; Hoyt et al., 2024 , TRGB;) , or the J-region Asymptotic Giant Branch ( Madore and Freedman, 2020 ; Lee et al., 2025 , JAGB;) . The second rung is where the M B M_{B} calibration happens using SNIa host galaxies near enough to contain a first rung indicator. The third rung contains SNIa in the Hubble flow at z ≳ 0.023 z\ga 0.023 , where peculiar velocities are not important in Λ \Lambda CDM, allowing a determination of H 0 H_{0} from the slope of the Hubble diagram. Using this approach, the SH0ES collaboration derived a value of M B = − 19.253 ± 0.027 M_{B}=-19.253\pm 0.027 ( Riess et al., 2022 ; Scolnic et al., 2022 ) . The second route to M SNIa M_{\rm SNIa} is through the inverse distance ladder (IDL). This involves anchoring M SNIa M_{\rm SNIa} using our understanding of the early Universe to set the baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) comoving sound horizon r d r_{\rm d} at the end of the baryon drag epoch ( Hu and Sugiyama, 1996 ; Eisenstein and Hu, 1998 , z d ≈ 1060 z_{\rm d}\approx 1060 ;) and then propagating this to intermediate redshifts using the BAO evident from galaxy clustering, which nowadays is typically obtained from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Data Release 2 ( DESI Collaboration, 2025 , DR2;) . One common assumption which we follow is to adopt the Planck constraint of r d = 147.05 ± 0.30 r_{\rm d}=147.05\pm 0.30 comoving Mpc (cMpc) from Planck Collaboration VI 2020 (hereafter 100 ). This explicitly adopts Λ \Lambda CDM at early times, so the IDL approach implicitly assumes that the Hubble tension, if due to new physics, must be solved at late times. Under this assumption, M SNIa ≈ − 19.30 M_{\rm SNIa}\approx-19.30 to − 19.40 -19.40 ( Camilleri et al., 2025 ; Popovic and Sullivan, 2026 ) , which is significantly lower than suggested by the local distance ladder. This is because a lower H 0 H_{0} value requires SNIa to be more distant at given z z , which for given apparent magnitude requires the SNIa to be brighter. The discrepancy with the locally determined M B M_{B} leads to the usual conclusion that a successful solution to the Hubble tension requires a smaller r d r_{\rm d} , which is possible only through new pre-recombination physics ( Cai and Wang, 2026 ; Sabogal et al., 2026 ; Tiwari et al., 2026 ) . Although the expansion history is nowadays mainly probed through the distance–redshift relation, it is possible to bypass distances altogether by instead focusing on the lookback time. The elapsed time between any two redshifts can be found using the cosmic chronometer (CC) technique, which involves comparing massive passive elliptical galaxies at those redshifts to determine the relative age ( Jimenez and Loeb, 2002 ; Moresco et al., 2012 ; Moresco, 2015 ; Moresco et al., 2016 ; Moresco et al., 2022 ; Moresco, 2024 ) . Since we can relate distance and lookback time using the speed of light c c , we can use CC datasets to calibrate M B M_{B} without assuming any value for r d r_{\rm d} , thereby obtaining an estimate for H 0 H_{0} ( Cogato et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . Early-time solutions to the Hubble tension seek to resolve it by decreasing r d r_{\rm d} , which requires modifying the redshift dependence of the sound horizon and/or the redshift of recombination ( Mirpoorian et al., 2025 ) . Since BAO measurements are most sensitive to the product H 0 ​ r d H_{0}r_{\rm d} , reducing r d r_{\rm d} allows for an increased H 0 H_{0} . However, these solutions face at least seven problems ( Vagnozzi, 2023 ) . One of these is that they would imply a significantly reduced age of the Universe ( Vagnozzi et al., 2022 ) . This prediction is in significant tension with the observed ages of the oldest Galactic stars and globular clusters ( Montalbán et al., 2021 ; Valcin et al., 2020 ; Valcin et al., 2021 ; Cimatti and Moresco, 2023 ; Souza et al., 2024 ; Valcin et al., 2025 ; Valcin et al., 2026 ; Banik et al., 2026b ) . These features cannot be explained through a simple change to r d r_{\rm d} . Moreover, currently known early-time solutions struggle with Big Bang nucleosynthesis (BBN) due to their need for a generically higher baryon density to match the CMB anisotropies, which affects primordial light element abundances ( Giovanetti, 2026 ; Launders et al., 2026 ; Poulin et al., 2026 ) . More generally, the success of Λ \Lambda CDM in fitting the CMB anisotropies by now limits the scope for substantial modifications prior to recombination ( Calabrese et al., 2025 ; SPT-3G Collaboration, 2026 , 100 ;) , including in models where electron density fluctuations cause inhomogeneous recombination ( Lynch et al., 2026 ) . Late-time solutions to the Hubble tension avoid these problems by assuming standard pre-recombination physics, but such models have their own problems at z ≲ 1 z\la 1 ( Krishnan et al., 2021a ) . In particular, Bansal and Huterer (2026) find that a model modifying only the late-time expansion history cannot simultaneously fit H 0 SH0ES H_{0}^{\mathrm{SH0ES}} , the DESI BAO data, and relative SNIa distances. A fit is possible only if M SNIa M_{\mathrm{SNIa}} takes a sharp step at very low redshift ( z ≲ 0.01 z\la 0.01 ) or the distance-duality relation is broken. Both escapes are trivial since they decouple the calibrated SNIa from the remaining data. Importantly, their analysis rests on the Pantheon+ catalogue. A step in M B M_{B} at low redshift is degenerate with precisely the relative calibration offsets between surveys described above, given the difficulty of covering a very wide redshift range using the same survey. Their most successful late-time magnitude step model has a transition in the redshift range where a heterogeneous compilation is least able to separate new physics from filter-related changes to the zero point. This motivates the test we present here. We note that astrophysically it is difficult to understand why SNIa might abruptly change in intrinsic brightness, with terrestrial data placing strong constraints on models with a sharp change in G G in the geologically recent past ( Banik, Desmond and Samaras, 2025 ) . Such models also face difficulties with the mass–radius relation of red dwarf stars due to their long thermal timescales ( Sakstein and Desmond, 2026 ) . Our main goal is to assess if the IDL can accommodate a late-time solution to the Hubble tension, i.e., if the assumption of standard pre-recombination physics is compatible with the high H 0 H_{0} required to match various local constraints ( Di Valentino et al., 2025 ; H0DN Collaboration, 2026 ) . The observational data we use for this purpose are described in Section 2 . We then explain the IDL, our Bayesian model comparison of late-time solutions to the Hubble tension, and consistency tests (Section 3 ). We go on to present our results (Section 4 ) and discuss their implications (Section 5 ). We conclude in Section 6 . In Appendix A , we present the Alcock–Paczynski (AP) consistency test between DESI DR2 BAO and DES-Dovekie SNIa. Appendix B reports how the inferred cosmological parameters depend on the polynomial order. Appendix C contains all the posteriors from our analyses. In Appendix D , we use Λ \Lambda CDM mocks to better understand how our analysis is affected by the limited DES coverage at low redshift.

sections.heading: 2.1 DES-Dovekie SNIa
sections.text: The DES-Dovekie compilation of SNe provides 1820 spectroscopically and photometrically classified events with their full statistical plus systematic covariance ( Popovic et al., 2026 ) . The intrinsic scatter contribution to this covariance is calibrated so that Λ \Lambda CDM yields an acceptable fit to the Hubble diagram. This is because we currently lack sufficiently large samples of SNIa with redshift-independent distances from which the intrinsic scatter can be inferred, as is usually done with other indicators like Cepheids. The total SNIa uncertainties are therefore scaled to a reference cosmology, which means that an acceptable χ 2 \chi^{2} under Λ \Lambda CDM in SNIa-dominated analyses like ours does not by itself demonstrate that Λ \Lambda CDM is an adequate description of the data. We consider two SN samples, which we label DES and DES + legacy throughout this paper. Our baseline is the DES sample, which uses the 1623 DES SNe alone ( IDSURVEY = 10 \mathrm{IDSURVEY}=10 ), leading to a redshift range of z ∈ [ 0.073 , 1.14 ] z\in[0.073,1.14] – though in practice there is limited constraining power at z ≲ 0.2 z\la 0.2 ( DES Collaboration, 2024 , see figures 3 and 4 of) . We select the SNe with magnitude uncertainty σ μ < 1 \sigma_{\mu}<1 , removing 82 SNe as these are likely contaminants (e.g. other types of SN) given they are down-weighted by the Bayesian Estimation Applied to Multiple Species (BEAMS) analysis ( Kunz et al., 2007 ) . They carry ≈ 10 − 5 \approx 10^{-5} of the total statistical weight, so removing them does not significantly change the results. The DES + legacy sample adds an external low-redshift anchor from legacy surveys, which contribute a further 197 spectroscopically confirmed SNIa with z ∈ [ 0.025 , 0.087 ] z\in[0.025,0.087] , lowering the redshift floor from z ≈ 0.073 → 0.025 z\approx 0.073\to 0.025 . It is important to stress that both DES and legacy SNIa are uncalibrated as there is no independent determination of their absolute magnitude in the DES filters. We denote this absolute magnitude M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} rather than M B M_{B} to differentiate it from the rest-frame Johnson B B -band in which the SH0ES M B M_{B} is defined. The reported distance modulus μ ⁡ ( z ) = m ⁡ ( z ) − M DES \mu(z)=m(z)-M_{\mathrm{DES}} assumes a fiducial M DES = − 19.327 M_{\mathrm{DES}}=-19.327 , but this can be arbitrarily varied. We infer M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} jointly with the other parameters, which implicitly imposes a calibration via the IDL. The predicted μ ≡ 25 + 5 ​ log 10 ​ D L / Mpc \mu\equiv 25+5\log_{10}D_{\rm L}/\mathrm{Mpc} , with the luminosity distance D L D_{\rm L} found as follows: D L \displaystyle D_{\rm L} = \displaystyle= ( 1 + z hel ) ​ D M ​ ( z HD ) , \displaystyle\left(1+z_{\mathrm{hel}}\right)D_{\rm M}\left(z_{\mathrm{HD}}\right), (1) D M ​ ( z ) \displaystyle D_{\rm M}\left(z\right) = \displaystyle= c ​ ∫ 0 z d ​ z ~ H ⁡ ( z ~ ) , \displaystyle c\int_{0}^{z}\frac{\mathrm{d}\tilde{z}}{H(\tilde{z})}\,, (2) where D M D_{\rm M} is the comoving distance, z hel z_{\mathrm{hel}} is the heliocentric redshift of each SNIa, and z HD z_{\mathrm{HD}} is its “Hubble diagram” redshift obtained after corrections for peculiar velocities. To study possible differences between the main DES sample and the legacy SNIa, we also consider adding a systematic offset of Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\rm legacy} to the absolute magnitude of the legacy SNIa. This measures possible systematics when correcting the legacy SNIa for survey completeness effects or converting the observed legacy magnitudes to what would have been measured in the DES filters – despite the lack of direct measurements in those filters. We label this as DES + legacy ( Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\rm legacy} ) and explain it further in Section 3.5 .

sections.heading: 2.2 DESI DR2 BAO
sections.text: The BAO is a statistical standard ruler arising from matter fluctuations in the primordial Universe ( Eisenstein and Hu, 1998 ) . We consider the latest DESI data release ( DESI Collaboration, 2025 , DESI DR2;) . They report six measurements of D M / r d D_{\rm M}/r_{\rm d} , six of D H / r d D_{\rm H}/r_{\rm d} at the same redshifts, and one of D V / r d D_{\rm V}/r_{\rm d} at a lower redshift: D H ​ ( z ) \displaystyle D_{\rm H}\left(z\right) = \displaystyle= c H ⁡ ( z ) , \displaystyle\frac{c}{H\left(z\right)}\,, (3) D V ​ ( z ) \displaystyle D_{\rm V}\left(z\right) = \displaystyle= [ z ​ D M 2 ​ ( z ) ​ D H ​ ( z ) ] 1 / 3 , \displaystyle\left[zD^{2}_{\rm M}\left(z\right)D_{\rm H}\left(z\right)\right]^{1/3}, (4) r d \displaystyle r_{\rm d} = \displaystyle= ∫ z d ∞ c s ​ ( z ~ ) H ⁡ ( z ~ ) ​ 𝑑 z ~ , \displaystyle\int_{z_{\rm d}}^{\infty}\frac{c_{\mathrm{s}}\left(\tilde{z}\right)}{H\left(\tilde{z}\right)}\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{z}\,, (5) where c s c_{\mathrm{s}} is the sound speed in the baryon–photon plasma. We use the full DESI covariance matrix, which has a block-diagonal form because measurements at different redshifts use different galaxies, making them independent.

sections.heading: 2.3 CC
sections.text: We use 15 CC measurements to constrain the expansion history without assumptions about M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} or r d r_{\rm d} ( Moresco et al., 2012 ; Moresco, 2015 ; Moresco et al., 2016 ) . CC measurements constrain the Hubble–Lemaitre parameter via the following relation H ⁡ ( z ) = − z ˙ 1 + z , \displaystyle H(z)~=~-\frac{\dot{z}}{1+z}\,, (6) where an overdot denotes a time derivative. z ˙ \dot{z} is measured through the differential age evolution of early-type galaxies ( Jimenez and Loeb, 2002 ) . We use the full covariance reported in Moresco et al. (2020) . The errors quoted in CC compilations like Moresco et al. (2022) omit the stellar-population modelling systematic. We find that this is crucial as it can significantly change the cosmological parameter posteriors. In particular, the error on r d r_{\rm d} roughly doubles when considering the full covariance rather than only the diagonal terms. Since the covariance with other CC measurements is not known, we do not use the other 18 of the 33 available CC measurements ( Moresco et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . We use the CC data for an extended analysis in which a direct comparison between differential age H ⁡ ( z ) H(z) measurements and D H / r d D_{\rm H}/r_{\rm d} BAO measurements can independently calibrate r d r_{\rm d} (Section 4.3 ). This affords an IDL independent of the CMB.

sections.heading: 3.1 Model setup
sections.text: The cosmic expansion history a ⁡ ( t ) a(t) can be approximated as a Taylor series around the present epoch, where a a is the cosmic scale factor normalised to unity today and t t is the time since the Big Bang. The use of a Taylor series minimises assumptions about the expansion history, making the results model-independent. The series expansion is commonly based on redshift, but since we consider data out to z = 2.33 z=2.33 , we instead expand in the lookback scale factor a ~ = 1 − a \widetilde{a}=1-a , limiting the range to 0–1. We therefore use the following series expansion: E ⁡ ( a ~ ) = 1 + ∑ k = 1 k max C k ​ a ~ k , a ~ ≡ z 1 + z = 1 − a , \displaystyle E\left(\widetilde{a}\right)~=~1+\sum_{k=1}^{k_{\max}}C_{k}\,\widetilde{a}^{k}\,,\qquad\widetilde{a}~\equiv~\frac{z}{1+z}~=~1-a, (7) where E ⁡ ( a ~ ) ≡ H ⁡ ( a ~ ) / H 0 E(\widetilde{a})\equiv H(\widetilde{a})/H_{0} is the normalised expansion rate and k max k_{\max} is the order of the polynomial with coefficients C k C_{k} . Using the lookback scale factor a ~ \widetilde{a} instead of z z leads to a narrower range because a ~ < 1 ​ ∀ z \widetilde{a}<1\forall z . This is important here because DESI reaches out to z = 2.33 z=2.33 , which is too large for a convergent Taylor series since it converges only for | z | < 1 \lvert z\rvert<1 ( Cattoën and Visser, 2007 ) . This means that expanding in powers of z z and fitting the model with data at z > 1 z>1 is not a cosmographic expansion but rather a polynomial fit, which is clearly model-dependent (e.g. with fixed asymptotic behaviour). In this case, the parameters H 0 , q 0 , j 0 , … H_{0},q_{0},j_{0},\dots do not represent the standard cosmographic parameters but rather are parameters of the polynomial model. This problem does not arise in our setup because a ~ ≤ 0.70 \widetilde{a}\leq 0.70 . Since the z ≪ 1 z\ll 1 correspondence is a ~ = z − z 2 + 𝒪 ⁡ ( z 3 ) \widetilde{a}=z-z^{2}+\mathcal{O}(z^{3}) , the deceleration parameter can be found from q 0 = C 1 − 1 q_{0}=C_{1}-1 . Figure 1: Illustration of our prior on the shape of the expansion history E ⁡ ( a ~ ) ≡ H ⁡ ( a ~ ) / H 0 E(\widetilde{a})\equiv H(\widetilde{a})/H_{0} (Eq. 7 ). The thick orange line shows flat Λ \Lambda CDM with Ω m = 0.3175 \Omega_{\rm m}=0.3175 , which has negligible errors for the purpose of this plot ( SPT-3G Collaboration, 2026 ) . The dashed blue line shows the best quartic fit to the Λ \Lambda CDM prediction. The dotted black line at E = 1 + 3.5 ​ a ~ E=1+3.5\widetilde{a} approximately connects the fixed point at a ~ = 0 \widetilde{a}=0 to the Λ \Lambda CDM prediction at a ~ = 0.7 \widetilde{a}=0.7 . The solid black line at twice this level ( 2 + 7 ​ a ~ 2+7\widetilde{a} ) shows our prior upper limit on E E , above which the grey shading indicates the excluded region. We also require E ≥ 0 E\geq 0 to enforce an expanding universe. Our limits apply only to the range 0 ≤ a ~ ≤ 0.70 0\leq\widetilde{a}\leq 0.70 as we do not use data outside this range. For the AP test in Appendix A , we further restrict to 0 ≤ a ~ ≤ 0.53 0\leq\widetilde{a}\leq 0.53 for the same reason. We adopt a uniform prior on E E at k max k_{\max} control points in a ~ \widetilde{a} and then check that the unique polynomial through these points with E = 1 E=1 today remains within the above bounds. A crucial aspect for a cosmographic analysis is the prior on the polynomial coefficients C k C_{k} , but it is difficult to estimate an appropriate prior range. Instead of directly bounding each C k C_{k} separately, we set a prior on the shape of the expansion history by requiring the following: 0 ≤ E ⁡ ( a ~ ) ≤ 2 + 7 ​ a ~ , 0 ≤ a ~ ≤ a ~ max , \displaystyle 0~\leq~E(\widetilde{a})~\leq~2+7\,\widetilde{a},\qquad 0\leq\widetilde{a}\leq\widetilde{a}_{\max}\,, (8) where a ~ max = 0.70 \widetilde{a}_{\max}=0.70 is around the largest lookback scale factor considered by the data (the DESI DR2 BAO point at z = 2.33 z=2.33 ). The lower limit imposes an expanding universe. The upper limit is twice our Λ \Lambda CDM-inspired linear model of 1 + 3.5 ​ a ~ 1+3.5\widetilde{a} , which approximately joins the two ends of the flat Λ \Lambda CDM E ⁡ ( a ~ ) E(\widetilde{a}) relation over this range with the SPA parameters (Figure 1 ). This means the upper limit lies between ≈ 2 × \approx 2\times and 3.3 × 3.3\times the Λ \Lambda CDM expansion rate at every a ~ \widetilde{a} in this range. The broad allowed range of E E permits any plausible late-time departure from Λ \Lambda CDM. We sample our E E prior (Eq. 8 ) using a uniform prior on E E over the allowed range (0 to 2 + 7 ​ a ~ 2+7\widetilde{a} ) at each of k max k_{\max} control points, which we place at the Chebyshev–Lobatto nodes a ~ j = a ~ max ​ [ 1 − cos ⁡ ( j ​ π / k max ) ] / 2 \widetilde{a}_{j}=\widetilde{a}_{\max}\left[1-\cos\left(j\pi/k_{\max}\right)\right]/2 , where j = 1 ​ … ​ k max j=1\ldots k_{\max} . Given also that E ≡ 1 E\equiv 1 today, this defines a unique polynomial of order k max k_{\max} through a fixed linear transformation dependent only on k max k_{\max} . We then reject the polynomial if it goes outside our prior limits anywhere in the interval 0 ≤ a ~ ≤ a ~ max 0\leq\widetilde{a}\leq\widetilde{a}_{\max} . This gives a joint prior that is uniform in the C k C_{k} over the region allowed by Eq. 8 , although the marginal prior on each C k C_{k} is not uniform (Section 4.8 ). We show in Section 4.8 that this condition does not truncate our posteriors, which give relatively narrow ranges across which the priors are essentially flat. Table 1 shows the prior on every parameter considered in this paper. The best-fitting parameters can be found using the least-squares approach, where χ 2 \chi^{2} is assumed to vary quadratically with the model parameters near its minimum, corresponding to a locally Gaussian approximation to the likelihood. This approach does not require us to explicitly set prior ranges. However, we do not use least squares for our baseline results because it is preferable to relax the Gaussian assumption. We therefore sample the posterior with the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) as implemented in numpyro ( Hoffman and Gelman, 2014 ; Bingham et al., 2019 ; Phan et al., 2019 ) . We ensure convergence with the Gelman-Rubin diagnostic R − 1 < 0.02 R-1<0.02 ( Gelman and Rubin, 1992 ; Brooks and Gelman, 1998 ) . Results obtained in this way are similar to those using least squares, further demonstrating that our priors are broad enough (Section 4.8 ). Since we consider a large number of analysis variants, we use least squares for many of our variants to reduce the computational cost compared to NUTS, given the numerically similar results. We also fit the flat Λ \Lambda CDM model for comparison. This involves replacing the cosmographic expansion of Eq. 7 with the following: H ⁡ ( z ) = H 0 ​ Ω m ​ ( 1 + z ) 3 + ( 1 − Ω m ) , \displaystyle H\left(z\right)~=~H_{0}\sqrt{\Omega_{\rm m}\left(1+z\right)^{3}+\left(1-\Omega_{\rm m}\right)}\,, (9) where Ω m \Omega_{\rm m} is the matter density parameter. All other aspects of the analysis remain unchanged, but the free parameters are now Ω m \Omega_{\rm m} , H 0 H_{0} , M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} , and r d r_{\rm d} . The deceleration parameter is the derived quantity q 0 = 3 2 ​ Ω m − 1 q_{0}=\tfrac{3}{2}\Omega_{\rm m}-1 . Eq. 9 has much less flexibility in the shape of H ⁡ ( z ) H(z) , allowing us to check how conclusions like the predicted H 0 H_{0} and any calibration offset in the legacy SNIa (Section 3.5 ) depend on the extra flexibility afforded by our model-agnostic cosmographic fit (Eq. 7 ). If there is a departure from flat Λ \Lambda CDM behaviour at low redshift, Eq. 9 is too restrictive, leading to a divergence between results assuming it and results with a more flexible parametrisation. The cosmographic expansion in Eq. 7 or the flat Λ \Lambda CDM version (Eq. 9 ) is the only description of the background in our analysis. It enters every likelihood: the CC directly through H ⁡ ( z ) H(z) , the SNIa through the luminosity distance D L D_{\rm L} (Eq. 1 ), and the BAO through D M D_{\rm M} , D H D_{\rm H} , and D V D_{\rm V} , which are the integrals and ratios of the same H ⁡ ( z ) H(z) . The C k C_{k} coefficients (or Ω m \Omega_{\mathrm{m}} for Λ \Lambda CDM), M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} , and r d r_{\rm d} are sampled jointly, so the three types of observation are coupled through a common expansion history and cannot drift apart. Since we consider both luminosity distances to SNIa and angular diameter distances for the BAO, our results assume the Etherington distance-duality relation D L = ( 1 + z ) ​ D M D_{\rm L}=(1+z)D_{\rm M} ( Etherington, 1933 ) . Throughout the paper, our baseline truncates Eq. 7 at k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 , the order with the highest Bayesian evidence for DES. We test how the results depend on this choice by repeating the analysis for k max = 2 k_{\max}=2 –6 and computing the Bayesian evidence Z ⁡ ( k max ) Z(k_{\max}) of each order. We use the nested sampling algorithm dynesty ( Skilling, 2004 ; Skilling, 2006 ; Speagle, 2020 ; Koposov et al., 2024 ) with random slice sampling, 1000 live points and a stopping criterion of Δ ​ ln ⁡ Z ^ = 0.1 \Delta\ln\hat{Z}=0.1 , under the same prior on the expansion history as the rest of this paper. Assigning every order the same prior probability, the weighted posterior probability of order k max k_{\max} is as follows: w ⁡ ( k max ) = Z ⁡ ( k max ) ∑ k = 2 6 Z ⁡ ( k ) . \displaystyle w\left(k_{\max}\right)~=~\frac{Z\left(k_{\max}\right)}{\displaystyle\sum_{k=2}^{6}Z\left(k\right)}\,. (10) We present the results using different k max k_{\max} as a robustness test of our baseline in Section 4.8 , where we then average the results for different k max k_{\max} using the above weights to get the Bayesian model average (BMA; see Appendix B ). The basic idea behind the IDL is to calibrate datasets assuming the validity of Λ \Lambda CDM prior to recombination. In our setup, the total χ 2 \chi^{2} is therefore χ total 2 = χ SNIa 2 + χ BAO 2 + { χ CMB 2 (configuration A), χ CC 2 (configuration B), \displaystyle\chi^{2}_{\rm total}~=~\chi^{2}_{\rm{SNIa}}+\chi^{2}_{\rm BAO}+\begin{cases}\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{CMB}}&\text{(configuration A),}\\ \chi^{2}_{\rm CC}&\text{(configuration B),}\end{cases} (11) where χ SNIa 2 \chi^{2}_{\rm{SNIa}} is the contribution of SNIa from DES (possibly supplemented by the legacy SNIa), χ BAO 2 \chi^{2}_{\rm BAO} is the contribution of DESI DR2 BAO measurements, χ CMB 2 \chi^{2}_{\mathrm{CMB}} is the CMB constraint imposed via a Gaussian prior of r d = 147.05 ± 0.30 r_{\rm d}=147.05\pm 0.30 cMpc ( 100 ) , and χ CC 2 \chi^{2}_{\rm CC} is the CC contribution. We use either the CMB constraint on r d r_{\rm d} assuming Λ \Lambda CDM prior to recombination, or we use CC and impose only a broad uninformative prior on r d r_{\rm d} . We break the well-known H 0 H_{0} – M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} degeneracy in the SNIa by requiring consistency with BAO, but the BAO data itself suffers from a D M , H , V D_{\rm M,H,V} – r d r_{\rm d} degeneracy. This is because the observables are the BAO angular scale and redshift depth, which measure distances relative to r d r_{\rm d} . We obtain an independent calibration of r d r_{\rm d} using two different approaches: 1. Baseline (configuration A): Assuming standard pre-recombination physics, which requires r d = 147.05 ± 0.30 r_{\rm d}=147.05\pm 0.30 cMpc ( 100 , TT, TE, EE + low-E modes in the CMB;) ; or 2. Extension (configuration B): Comparing CC measurements of H ⁡ ( z ) H(z) to BAO measurements of D H / r d D_{\rm H}/r_{\rm d} , with a wide uniform r d r_{\rm d} prior covering 120–175 cMpc. This approach does not assume Λ \Lambda CDM prior to recombination, instead relying on stellar physics. Our baseline assumes Λ \Lambda CDM behaviour at high redshift. The extension relaxes this assumption, limiting potential systematic error while also reducing the statistical constraining power of the analysis. The extended case can still be used as a robustness check of the baseline assumption. Importantly, the former’s ability to constrain r d r_{\rm d} independently of the CMB allows it to test whether early-time solutions to the Hubble tension can be accommodated without considering their impact on the CMB. Since these models have no new physics after recombination, BAO datasets tightly constrain H 0 ​ r d H_{0}r_{\rm d} , leading to a low predicted r d r_{\rm d} . We can compare this to the r d r_{\rm d} inferred by our extension analysis. This calibration also sets absolute BAO distances, which can be used to calibrate M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} via the Etherington relation.

sections.heading: 3.2 Redshift-floor sweep
sections.text: To check if our results are driven by SNIa at especially low redshifts, we conduct a sweep of the redshift floor z floor z_{\mathrm{floor}} below which SNIa are neglected, recalibrating the IDL each time. Some studies report a descending trend in H 0 H_{0} with the redshift of the data used to measure it ( Krishnan et al., 2020 ; Krishnan et al., 2021b ; Lopez-Hernandez and De-Santiago, 2025 ; Jia et al., 2025 ; Jia et al., 2026 ) . Unlike those studies which infer H 0 H_{0} from data in a narrow redshift range centred on z z and thereby obtain a curve of H 0 ​ ( z ) H_{0}(z) , our approach uses a redshift floor, so we denote the results as H 0 ​ ( z floor ) H_{0}(z_{\mathrm{floor}}) . A clear trend in H 0 ​ ( z floor ) H_{0}(z_{\mathrm{floor}}) which becomes asymptotically flat would indicate that the lowest redshift SNIa carry the cosmological parameters away from the more robust result from higher redshift SNIa. On the other hand, a flat trend in H 0 ​ ( z floor ) H_{0}(z_{\mathrm{floor}}) at the low-redshift end would indicate that different SNIa subsets prefer much the same present expansion rate, though error bars should widen at high z floor z_{\mathrm{floor}} as more data is excluded.

sections.heading: 3.3.1 Alternative models
sections.text: To assess if the data prefers a late-time solution to the Hubble tension over Λ \Lambda CDM, we consider the following phenomenological expansion history ( Nájera, Banik, Desmond and Kalaitzidis, 2026 ) : H ⁡ ( z ) = H 0 , Λ ​ CDM ​ Ω m ​ ( 1 + z ) 3 + ( 1 − Ω m ) + Δ ​ H ​ ( z , A , z 1 ) , \displaystyle H\left(z\right)~=~H_{0,\Lambda\mathrm{CDM}}\sqrt{\Omega_{\rm m}\left(1+z\right)^{3}+\left(1-\Omega_{\rm m}\right)}+\Delta H\left(z;A,z_{1}\right), Δ H ( z ; A , z 1 ) = A exp ( − z / z 1 ) , \displaystyle\Delta H(z;A,z_{1})~=~A\exp\left(-z/z_{1}\right), (12) where A A is the amplitude and z 1 z_{1} is the redshift scale of Δ ​ H \Delta H , an extra contribution to H ⁡ ( z ) H(z) . A solution to the Hubble tension should have A ≈ 6 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 A\approx 6\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , while we expect z 1 ≲ 0.2 z_{1}\la 0.2 ( Nájera et al., 2026 ) . This exp model represents a flexible late-time solution to the Hubble tension in which H 0 = H 0 , Λ ​ CDM + A H_{0}=H_{0,\Lambda\mathrm{CDM}}+A . We adopt A ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( − 10 , 10 ) ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 A\sim\mathcal{U}(-10,10)\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} (Table 1 ). This range comfortably covers the A ≈ 6 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 A\approx 6\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} needed to solve the Hubble tension, and it is symmetric about zero, so it does not favour a positive A A a priori. We also consider the Chevallier-Polarski-Linder ( Chevallier and Polarski, 2001 ; Linder, 2003 ; Linder, 2008 , CPL;) model in which the dark energy equation of state is linear in a a ( w = w 0 + w a ​ a ~ w=w_{0}+w_{a}\widetilde{a} ), so the expansion history is as follows: H ⁡ ( z ) \displaystyle H\left(z\right) = \displaystyle= H 0 ​ Ω m ​ ( 1 + z ) 3 + ( 1 − Ω m ) ​ f ​ ( z ) , \displaystyle H_{0}\sqrt{\Omega_{\rm m}\left(1+z\right)^{3}+\left(1-\Omega_{\rm m}\right)f(z)}\,, (13) f ⁡ ( z ) \displaystyle f\left(z\right) = \displaystyle= ( 1 + z ) 3 ​ ( 1 + w 0 + w a ) ​ exp ⁡ ( − 3 ​ w a ​ a ~ ) . \displaystyle\left(1+z\right)^{3\left(1+w_{0}+w_{a}\right)}\exp\left(-3w_{a}\widetilde{a}\right). (14) We can recover Λ \Lambda CDM behaviour by setting w 0 = − 1 w_{0}=-1 and w a = 0 w_{a}=0 , in which case w = − 1 w=-1 and f ⁡ ( z ) = 1 ​ ∀ z f(z)=1\forall z , indicating a constant dark energy contribution. The Bayesian evidence of model ℳ i \mathcal{M}_{i} is defined as follows: Z ⁡ ( ℳ i ) ≡ ∫ ⁡ d ​ θ ​ π ​ ( θ | ℳ i ) ​ ℒ ​ ( D | θ , ℳ i ) , \displaystyle Z\left(\mathcal{M}_{i}\right)~\equiv~\int\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\theta\,\pi\left(\theta|\mathcal{M}_{i}\right)\mathcal{L}\left(D|\theta,\mathcal{M}_{i}\right), (15) where π \pi is the prior and ℒ \mathcal{L} is the likelihood of the data D D if the vector of model parameters is θ \theta . We compare the exp and CPL models to Λ \Lambda CDM through the Bayes factor B 10 ≡ Z ⁡ ( ℳ 1 ) Z ⁡ ( ℳ 0 ) , \displaystyle B_{10}~\equiv~\frac{Z\left(\mathcal{M}_{1}\right)}{Z\left(\mathcal{M}_{0}\right)}\,, (16) where ℳ 0 \mathcal{M}_{0} is Λ \Lambda CDM and ℳ 1 \mathcal{M}_{1} is an alternative, which in our case is either the exp model (Eq. 12 ) or the CPL model (Eq. 14 ). Both models are phenomenological, with the exp model aimed at the Hubble tension ( Nájera et al., 2026 ) and the CPL model aimed at the preference of DESI DR2 BAO for evolving dark energy ( DESI Collaboration, 2025 ) . The Bayesian evidence automatically applies an Occam penalty for the two extra parameters that these models have compared to Λ \Lambda CDM. Since the exp and CPL models have the same number of free parameters as each other, Bayesian evidence differences between them are not directly related to the number of free parameters. Even so, the size of the Occam penalty depends on how much of the prior range the data exclude, and therefore on the adopted prior ranges (given in Table 1 ). To compare these models on an equal footing, we must use the same dataset in all cases. We use the SNIa, BAO, and CC data described in Section 2 , possibly supplemented by local anchors on H 0 H_{0} . As described below, we supplement these with additional constraints from the early Universe. χ total 2 = χ SNIa 2 + χ BAO 2 + χ CMB 2 + χ BBN 2 + χ CC 2 ​ ( + χ anchor 2 ) , \displaystyle\chi^{2}_{\mathrm{total}}~=~\chi^{2}_{\rm SNIa}+\chi^{2}_{\rm BAO}+\chi^{2}_{\rm{CMB}}+\chi^{2}_{\rm{BBN}}+\chi^{2}_{\rm CC}\,\left(+\chi^{2}_{\rm anchor}\right), (17) with the anchor term entering only where stated (Section 3.3.3 ). Since we are interested in a model comparison, we need the Bayesian evidence, so for this analysis we cannot use NUTS. We therefore use the nested sampling algorithm dynesty ( Skilling, 2004 ; Skilling, 2006 ; Feroz et al., 2009 ; Speagle, 2020 ; Koposov et al., 2024 ) with random slice sampling, 800 live points and a stopping criterion of Δ ​ ln ⁡ Z ^ = 0.01 \Delta\ln\hat{Z}=0.01 , where Z ^ \hat{Z} denotes the approximate remaining Bayesian evidence.

sections.heading: 3.3.2 Compressed CMB likelihood
3.3.3 Local H 0 H_{0} anchors
sections.text: To assess the feasibility of a late-time solution to the Hubble tension, we consider the case with and without anchors on H 0 H_{0} from the standard distance ladder. We use either the SH0ES constraint of H 0 = 73.17 ± 0.86 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=73.17\pm 0.86\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} from the traditional Cepheid–SNIa route ( Leavitt and Pickering, 1912 ; Breuval et al., 2024 ) , or we use three anchors which are independent of Cepheid and SNIa absolute magnitudes, thereby making them independent of some of the main contributors to the Hubble tension. We assume all three are independent of each other because they come from non-overlapping datasets, as follows: 1. The TRGB ( Lee, Freedman and Madore, 1993 ; Madore and Freedman, 1995 ) is used to calibrate distances to galaxies with measured surface brightness fluctuations ( Tonry and Schneider, 1988 , SBF;) . Our adopted TRGB + SBF value is H 0 = 73.8 ± 0.7 ​ ( stat ) ± 2.3 ​ ( sys ) ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=73.8\pm 0.7\,({\rm stat})\pm 2.3\,({\rm sys})\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} ( Jensen et al., 2025 ) . We combine statistical and systematic errors in quadrature to obtain a single uncertainty of 2.4 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 2.4\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} . 2. The GW170817 standard siren ( Abbott et al., 2017 ; Virgo & LIGO Collaborations, 2017 ) is used to obtain a luminosity distance. This is combined with a peculiar velocity correction and the very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) constraint on the inclination to obtain an estimated H 0 = 68.3 − 4.5 + 4.6 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=68.3^{+4.6}_{-4.5}\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} ( Mukherjee et al., 2021 ) , as listed in table 2 of Alfradique et al. (2026) . We adopt the larger uncertainty of 4.6 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 4.6\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} to be conservative. We do not use the headline result of Alfradique et al. (2026) as this also combines the single bright siren with 17 dark sirens, which would significantly complicate our analysis while only slightly improving the constraining power. 3. Type II SNe (SNII) with the expanding photosphere method ( Vogl et al., 2025 , EPM;) . Their study gives an estimated H 0 = 74.9 ± 2.7 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=74.9\pm 2.7\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} if we assume the statistical and systematic errors are comparable, which the authors indicate is a reasonable conservative assumption. We stress that adding SH0ES and legacy SNIa to the same analysis risks overlapping data. This is the reason why we lead with the non-SH0ES anchors, which we can use even if we also include the legacy SNIa. However, if the latter are excluded, there is negligible overlap between the SNIa used by DES and by SH0ES ( Riess et al., 2022 ) . There is an important caveat that we must take into account for the exp model. Measurements of H 0 H_{0} from the above anchors compute it by fitting the luminosity distances with their second-order kinematic expansion in z z , assuming that q 0 = − 0.55 q_{0}=-0.55 and the jerk parameter j 0 = 1 j_{0}=1 , allowing us to fit even a single data point. This approach is similar to that used in the literature, since probes at very low redshift usually lack enough data to constrain higher order cosmographic parameters. H 0 H_{0} can then be obtained only by extrapolating from the redshift of the data down to z → 0 z\to 0 . The consequence is that if z 1 ≲ z max z_{1}\la z_{\mathrm{max}} , the maximum redshift of the data considered, then the exp model H 0 H_{0} does not correspond to that measured from the Taylor series. For these cases, we therefore do not compare the model H 0 H_{0} directly with the published H 0 H_{0} anchor. We instead calculate the exp model distance moduli at the redshifts of the real data and fit them with the same kinematic expansion, giving each object equal weight, from which we can read off H 0 H_{0} ( Nájera et al., 2026 , similarly to section 4.1.1 of) . This calculates the value of H 0 H_{0} that would have been reported by observers from distance measurements to anchors with the same redshift distribution as the real data, if the universe followed the phenomenological exp cosmology. The same quantity decides whether a model solves the Hubble tension. Since SH0ES measure H 0 H_{0} from SNIa at z = 0.023 z=0.023 –0.15, a model whose excess expansion rate is concentrated below z ≈ 0.05 z\approx 0.05 predicts a lower SH0ES measurement than its H ⁡ ( 0 ) H(0) , because the observers fit a smooth Hubble law across a window in which most of the excess has already decayed. We therefore quote, alongside H ⁡ ( 0 ) H(0) , the value H 0 win H_{0}^{\rm win} that the SH0ES analysis would infer from each exp posterior (Table 4 ). Throughout, H ⁡ ( 0 ) H(0) remains the expansion rate today, while H 0 win H_{0}^{\rm win} decides whether a model reproduces the SH0ES measurement.

sections.heading: 3.4 Alcock–Paczynski consistency
sections.text: We subject the IDL to the AP consistency test ( Alcock and Paczynski, 1979 ) . This is based on the AP ratio F AP ≡ D M / D H F_{\mathrm{AP}}\equiv D_{\rm M}/D_{\rm H} (Appendix A ). Using SNIa alone and assuming smoothness of the distance–redshift relation combined with the Etherington relation, we predict F AP F_{\mathrm{AP}} at three redshifts where particularly precise BAO measurements of F AP F_{\mathrm{AP}} are available from DESI DR2. Taking the ratio causes r d r_{\rm d} to cancel out, so the AP test is independent of the absolute calibration of the BAO sound horizon. It is therefore also independent of the SNIa absolute magnitude – and thus H 0 H_{0} . The AP test instead probes the shape of the reconstructed distance–redshift relation, or equivalently of our cosmographic E ⁡ ( 1 − a ) E(1-a) expansion.

sections.heading: 3.5 Systematics with the legacy SNIa
sections.text: The DES-Dovekie compilation ( Popovic et al., 2026 ) combines the homogeneous, single-instrument DES catalogue of SNe ( z ∈ [ 0.073 , 1.14 ] z\in[0.073,1.14] ) with an external low-redshift anchor assembled from several legacy surveys ( z ∈ [ 0.025 , 0.087 ] z\in[0.025,0.087] ). The legacy SNIa come almost entirely from the Foundation sample (117 SNIa) or from the Center for Astrophysics CfA3 and CfA4 samples (72), with a further 8 from the Carnegie Supernova Project (CSP-I). We denote the CfA and CSP samples together as CfA/CSP. As noted in Section 2 , the homogeneous DES sample has practically no SNIa at z ≲ 0.1 z\la 0.1 , but all 197 legacy SNIa lie here. This makes the legacy SNIa an important lever on the z → 0 z\to 0 region, where BAO data is scant (though see table 1 of Banik and Kalaitzidis, 2025 , and references therein) . We therefore test whether the legacy SNIa follow the same distance–redshift relation as DES. We conduct another analysis to test what this means for H 0 H_{0} . We stress that the redshift distributions of the legacy SNIa and the main DES sample have very little overlap ( DES Collaboration, 2024 , see figure 3 of) . This means our test relies on a downward extrapolation of the DES sample, not a comparison of SNIa apparent magnitudes at the same redshift between the two subsamples. The legacy SNIa span z ∈ [ 0.025 , 0.087 ] z\in[0.025,0.087] while DES begins at z = 0.073 z=0.073 , so only 2 DES SNe and 10 legacy SNIa lie in the overlap region. Given the large number of legacy SNIa with modest error bars, the uncertainty in Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} is dominated by extrapolation uncertainty, i.e., how much freedom the DES reference has below its own floor. The main uncertainty in Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} is thus not from the legacy SNIa themselves – at least if we take their uncertainties at face value. Our test for systematics in the legacy SNIa is designed to require no absolute calibration. We proceed in three steps: 1. We fit the shape of the DES Hubble diagram (using only DES SNIa) with a rigid fourth-order polynomial as the baseline model (Eq. 7 ), the same expansion additionally constrained by the DESI result for F AP ≡ D M / D H F_{\rm AP}\equiv D_{\rm M}/D_{\rm H} (which is independent of r d r_{\rm d} ; see Section 3.4 ), rigid Λ \Lambda CDM with free Ω m \Omega_{\rm m} (Eq. 9 ), and rigid Λ \Lambda CDM likewise constrained by F AP F_{\rm AP} . 2. We extrapolate the fitted relation below the DES floor ( z = 0.073 z=0.073 ) down to the redshifts of the legacy SNIa, allowing us to calculate the residuals r i ≡ m legacy , i − m pred ​ ( z i ) r_{i}\equiv m_{{\rm legacy},i}-m_{\rm pred}(z_{i}) between observed legacy SNIa and our extrapolated predictions. 3. We take Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} to be the weighted mean of the r i r_{i} under the full statistical + systematic covariance of the compilation, including the legacy–DES cross-covariance. It is important to highlight why this approach is calibration-free, since this property is what makes Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} comparable across the four parametrisations. Rescaling H → λ ​ H H\to\lambda H maps D M → D M / λ D_{\rm M}\to D_{\rm M}/\lambda and hence m → m − 5 ​ log 10 ​ λ m\to m-5\log_{10}\lambda , so that ( H 0 → λ H 0 , M → M + 5 log 10 λ ) (H_{0}\to\lambda H_{0},\,M\to M+5\log_{10}\lambda) is an exact flat direction of the fit. We therefore fix H 0 = 70 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=70\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} and let M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} float freely. Every predicted apparent magnitude is invariant along this direction, making the fitted M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} meaningless by construction. This means that no absolute scale enters Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} , making it independent of the sound horizon and the local distance ladder. In particular, Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} inherits no part of the calibration chain that later produces H 0 H_{0} . To constrain H 0 H_{0} , we cannot simply add the Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} obtained above to the legacy SNIa because H 0 H_{0} and Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} are correlated. We therefore conduct a separate analysis where we sample Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} alongside the other parameters. The constraints we apply are SNIa + BAO + 100 r d r_{\rm d} . We consider the cosmographic expansion as well as Λ \Lambda CDM. For comparison, we also report results for the two cases that do not have Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} as a model parameter: excluding the legacy SNIa altogether, or including them at face value ( Δ ​ M legacy = 0 \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}=0 ). These results highlight the role of the legacy SNIa in H 0 H_{0} determinations via the IDL.

sections.heading: 4.1 The observed distance–redshift relation
sections.text: To gain a first impression of whether the Hubble tension might plausibly be solved at late times, we can consider the ratio between observed distances from SNIa and BAO and those predicted in the flat Λ \Lambda CDM cosmology that best fits the CMB ( SPT-3G Collaboration, 2026 , the SPA cosmology;) . The results are shown in Figure 2 , which plots DESI DR2 BAO measurements of D V / r d D_{\mathrm{V}}/r_{\rm d} and binned D L D_{\rm L} from SNIa, using uniform bins in ln ⁡ z \ln z . The SNIa are calibrated according to the best-fit value of M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} , which has very little uncertainty due to the need for consistency with the BAO. This is evident in the excellent agreement between SNIa and BAO measurements in the regime where they overlap ( z = 0.3 z=0.3 –1). In particular, the DES SNIa have a weighted mean ratio of D L D_{\rm L} relative to the SPA prediction of 0.981 ± 0.003 0.981\pm 0.003 , while the corresponding result for DESI DR2 BAO measurements of D V / r d D_{\rm V}/r_{\rm d} is 0.987 ± 0.003 0.987\pm 0.003 . This agreement is inevitable in the IDL approach since it is how we calibrate M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} . However, it does not guarantee consistency over the wide redshift range where there is an overlap between SNIa and BAO. We revisit this issue in Section 3.4 using the AP test, which does not rely on an assumed r d r_{\rm d} . The solid lines show our fourth-order cosmographic expansion (Eq. 7 ). At each redshift, the shaded band shows the 1 ​ σ 1\sigma uncertainty using Gaussian equivalent percentiles (i.e., the 15.87–84.13% range). Figure 2: Observed distances divided by the flat Λ \Lambda CDM prediction with the SPA parameters ( SPT-3G Collaboration, 2026 , H 0 = 67.19 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=67.19\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} and Ω m = 0.3175 \Omega_{\rm m}=0.3175 ;) and r d = 147.05 r_{\rm d}=147.05 cMpc ( 100 ) . We neglect the small uncertainties in these parameters and in M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} , which is fixed at the best fit of each analysis. Faint grey (magenta) points show individual DES (legacy) SNIa at their Hubble diagram redshift. Circles show inverse variance-weighted mean SNIa luminosity distances relative to SPA using the full DES-Dovekie covariance for DES (black), legacy at face value (red), and legacy recalibrated by the jointly inferred Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} (blue; Section 3.5 ), which lowers them by ≈ 3 % \approx 3\% . The SNIa are binned uniformly ln ⁡ z \ln z bins. Magenta squares show DESI DR2 D V / r d D_{\mathrm{V}}/r_{\rm d} , combining D M D_{\rm M} and D H D_{\rm H} using their published covariance. Lines in the same colour as the data show the best-fitting k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 cosmography (Eq. 7 ) up to z = 2.33 z=2.33 , with 1 ​ σ 1\sigma Gaussian-equivalent bands. Results are extrapolated below the lowest SNIa of each sample, as marked by the lines becoming dotted and a short gap in the band. The green band is H 0 SPA / H 0 SH0ES H_{0}^{\mathrm{SPA}}/H_{0}^{\mathrm{SH0ES}} , the level that a late-time solution to the Hubble tension must reach as z → 0 z\to 0 . As we move towards lower redshift, Figure 2 shows that there is a drastic difference depending on whether we use only SNIa from the homogeneous DES-Dovekie catalogue, also include the legacy SNIa normally included in this catalogue at face value, or include them after recalibrating them by the best-fitting value of Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\rm legacy} in our analysis where this is inferred jointly with the other parameters (Section 3.5 ). The legacy SNIa cover the crucial range of z = 0.025 z=0.025 –0.087, but they sit systematically above where we would expect them to sit based on the DES SNIa. Recalibrating the legacy SNIa naturally reduces this discrepancy using an offset of Δ ​ M legacy = + 0.065 \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}=+0.065 mag. Since H 0 H_{0} is inversely related to the distance scale in the z → 0 z\to 0 limit, these differences can be expected to significantly affect our conclusions regarding the IDL prediction for H 0 H_{0} . To highlight this, we add a green horizontal band at H 0 SPA / H 0 SH0ES = 0.918 ± 0.012 H_{0}^{\mathrm{SPA}}/H_{0}^{\mathrm{SH0ES}}=0.918\pm 0.012 , which is the level that must be reached as z → 0 z\to 0 in order to solve the Hubble tension. Our results suggest that this is quite likely if we only consider the homogeneous DES catalogue, marginally possible if we include the legacy SNIa after recalibrating them to line up with the extrapolated relation constrained by BAO + DES, and not possible if we take the legacy SNIa at face value. The rest of this study elaborates this basic picture without much altering it.

sections.heading: 4.2 Reconstructed expansion history
sections.text: We now turn to the expansion history a ˙ ​ ( z ) = H ​ ( z ) / ( 1 + z ) \dot{a}(z)=H(z)/(1+z) inferred by fitting our cosmographic expansion (Eq. 7 ) to the datasets mentioned in Section 2 . The median result for each analysis is shown in Figure 3 , with the shaded bands showing the 1 ​ σ 1\sigma range using Gaussian equivalent percentiles. We use a solid line to illustrate the range covered by the underlying SNIa dataset, while the dotted line shows the z → 0 z\to 0 extrapolation. The orange line without uncertainty shows the Λ \Lambda CDM prediction based on the H 0 H_{0} and Ω m \Omega_{\mathrm{m}} required to fit the latest CMB observations ( SPT-3G Collaboration, 2026 ) . The reconstructed a ˙ \dot{a} is higher than this expectation at z ≈ 0.4 z\approx 0.4 . This discrepancy narrows towards lower redshift – possibly even reversing sign. At the very lowest redshifts probed by the SNIa, a ˙ \dot{a} rises sharply towards lower z z . This rise is most pronounced with DES alone and least pronounced with DES + legacy. Allowing recalibration of the legacy SNIa returns an intermediate result (Section 3.5 ). Figure 3: The median reconstructed a ˙ ​ ( z ) \dot{a}(z) in our cosmographic expansion with k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 (Eq. 7 ) constrained using SNIa from DES only (solid black line), DES + legacy (solid red line), or DES + legacy allowing the legacy SNIa to be recalibrated by Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} (dashed blue line at an intermediate level). The shaded bands show the 1 ​ σ 1\sigma uncertainty using Gaussian equivalent percentiles. The dotted lines in the same colour show the extrapolation below the lowest redshift SNIa in each case, which we mark with a small gap in the error band. The solid orange line without uncertainty shows the flat Λ \Lambda CDM prediction using parameters that best fit the CMB ( SPT-3G Collaboration, 2026 ) . The inset shows the z < 0.2 z<0.2 region in more detail. The inset to Figure 3 shows the z < 0.2 z<0.2 regime in greater detail. It is clear that if the legacy SNIa are taken at face value and assumed to be free of systematics, then the Hubble tension will be very difficult to solve at late times. But if the legacy SNIa are excluded or we assume that systematics with them can be rectified using a single recalibration parameter, then a late-time solution becomes much more plausible and may even be preferred. We note that since we do not apply a full CMB comparison and only consider r d r_{\rm d} , the a ˙ \dot{a} reconstructions shown here likely need to be reduced by a few percent to preserve the comoving distance to recombination, which is related to the precisely measured angular scale of the CMB anisotropies. Roughly speaking, one can think of this as constraining c ​ ∫ ⁡ 𝑑 z / H c\int\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}z/H up to very high redshift, so a higher a ˙ \dot{a} at some redshifts must be compensated by a lower a ˙ \dot{a} elsewhere. Given the integral is barely affected by the z ≲ 0.1 z\la 0.1 regime crucial to the Hubble tension, a compensating reduction in the overall normalisation designed to preserve the comoving distance to recombination would not qualitatively change our conclusions. A more detailed comparison with the CMB is not possible in our cosmographic approach because it cannot be extrapolated to very high redshift where E → ∞ E\to\infty , but this is possible in the exp and CPL models considered in Section 3.3.1 .

sections.heading: 4.3 Cosmological parameters
sections.text: Figure 4: The joint inference on H 0 H_{0} and q 0 q_{0} from our k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 cosmographic expansion using SNIa from DES (black), DES + legacy (red), and DES + legacy with free Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} (blue). In all cases, the darker shading shows the 1 ​ σ 1\sigma region and the lighter shading shows the 2 ​ σ 2\sigma region. The orange star shows the Λ \Lambda CDM expectation based on the latest CMB observations ( SPT-3G Collaboration, 2026 ) . The vertical green band shows H 0 SH0ES H_{0}^{\mathrm{SH0ES}} ( Breuval et al., 2024 ) . Our results in Figure 3 show moderate deviations from the SPA cosmology at z ≲ 0.8 z\la 0.8 , even though we adopt a Planck prior of r d = 147.05 ± 0.30 r_{\rm d}=147.05\pm 0.30 cMpc and BAO data show at most modest deviations from Λ \Lambda CDM predictions calibrated using the CMB ( Banik et al., 2026c ) . These predictions are evidently accurate at high redshift, so any deviations at low redshift should be apparent in both the Hubble and deceleration parameters. We therefore use Figure 4 to show the joint posterior of H 0 H_{0} and q 0 = C 1 − 1 q_{0}=C_{1}-1 . The black contours show that without the legacy SNIa, the parameters are indeed significantly different to the Λ \Lambda CDM expectation, which we show using an orange star ( SPT-3G Collaboration, 2026 , neglecting the very small uncertainties;) . Remarkably, the predicted H 0 H_{0} with our DES-only cosmographic IDL is very much in line with the H 0 H_{0} anchors mentioned in Section 3.3 , even slightly exceeding the central value of H 0 SH0ES H_{0}^{\mathrm{SH0ES}} ( Breuval et al., 2024 ) . The high H 0 H_{0} is related to a very negative inferred q 0 q_{0} , which implies the expansion rate accelerates more than expected at late times. Adding the legacy SNIa tightens the constraints considerably, but it also shifts both H 0 H_{0} and q 0 q_{0} very close to the CMB-calibrated Λ \Lambda CDM prediction (Figure 4 ). The 2 ​ σ 2\sigma constraints with and without the legacy SNIa barely overlap in the ( H 0 , q 0 ) (H_{0},q_{0}) plane, which is unusual given the latter is strictly a subset of the former. This suggests that the estimated DES filter system apparent magnitudes of the legacy SNIa might have unrecognised systematics. If we allow for this possibility using our analysis with free Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} (Section 4.7 ), we get intermediate results. Our main results are presented in Table 2 , which we split into different sections to indicate if we are using configuration A or B (Eq. 11 ), whether the legacy SNIa are included, and whether we parametrise the expansion history using our fourth-order cosmographic expansion (Eq. 7 ) or flat Λ \Lambda CDM (Eq. 9 ). Our baseline (cosmographic configuration A) result is that the predicted H 0 = 76.25 ± 2.87 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=76.25\pm 2.87\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} for DES. This is only 1.03 ​ σ 1.03\sigma above SH0ES ( Breuval et al., 2024 ) , but it lies 3.13 ​ σ 3.13\sigma above the latest CMB-constrained flat Λ \Lambda CDM prediction ( SPT-3G Collaboration, 2026 ) . This falls to 2.22 ​ σ 2.22\sigma once we calibrate the significance on mock data, which reveal an upward bias in our estimator (Section 4.8 ). Since we do not use constraints from the standard distance ladder, our IDL result is not a reformulation of the classic Hubble tension, although it can be considered a rediscovery of it using the IDL. Importantly, the tension with SPA depends on our choice of k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 , since a Bayesian model average (BMA) over k max = 2 k_{\max}=2 –6 weighted by the Bayesian evidence yields a larger uncertainty on H 0 H_{0} , which means that DES alone does not determine H 0 H_{0} precisely enough to rediscover the Hubble tension (Section 4.8 ). We stress that the larger uncertainty in the BMA compared to a fixed choice of k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 is partly due to SNIa from the homogeneous DES catalogue having a redshift floor of 0.073 and lacking effective coverage at z ≲ 0.2 z\la 0.2 (with barely any SNIa at z < 0.1 z<0.1 ), requiring us to extrapolate the behaviour here — which is then dependent on the assumed k max k_{\max} . We can reduce this extrapolation error if we extend the low-redshift coverage by adding the legacy SNIa, in which case the predicted H 0 H_{0} using our cosmographic IDL drops to 67.98 ± 0.69 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 67.98\pm 0.69\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} . This is only 1.00 ​ σ 1.00\sigma above H 0 SPA H_{0}^{\mathrm{SPA}} ( SPT-3G Collaboration, 2026 ) , but lies 4.69 ​ σ 4.69\sigma below SH0ES ( Breuval et al., 2024 ) . Adding the legacy SNIa therefore completely changes the result. To reduce sensitivity to the assumption of Λ \Lambda CDM prior to recombination, we can drop the Planck prior on r d r_{\rm d} and set the absolute scale of the expansion history using CC datasets. This is our configuration B, which yields H 0 = 75.7 ± 5.3 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=75.7\pm 5.3\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} for DES and 67.6 ± 3.6 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 67.6\pm 3.6\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} for DES + legacy. The inferred r d r_{\rm d} lies within 0.10 ​ σ 0.10\sigma ( 0.16 ​ σ 0.16\sigma ) of the standard Planck value for DES (DES + legacy). A clearer picture will emerge with further improvements to CC measurements, especially at low redshift where leverage from DES remains limited ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Our constraints rely on an absolute calibration of DES SNIa, for which we use DESI DR2 BAO calibrated assuming a standard r d r_{\rm d} . In all cases, the results in Table 2 are consistent with an absolute SNIa calibration of M DES ≈ − 19.38 M_{\mathrm{DES}}\approx-19.38 , with a narrow range of − 19.380 ± 0.012 -19.380\pm 0.012 for DES alone to − 19.378 ± 0.012 -19.378\pm 0.012 for DES + legacy. These results are in 4.30 ​ σ 4.30\sigma and 4.23 ​ σ 4.23\sigma tension, respectively, with the SH0ES Cepheid-based result of M B = − 19.253 ± 0.027 M_{B}=-19.253\pm 0.027 ( Riess et al., 2022 ) . The result would differ slightly if we had instead used the slightly higher and more precise H 0 H_{0} measurement from Breuval et al. (2024) , but those authors do not directly publish a value for M B M_{B} . We note that when using the traditional Cepheid–SNIa route to H 0 H_{0} as an anchor on some of our models, we adopt the Breuval et al. (2024) constraint because it improves upon Riess et al. (2022) by adding the Small Magellanic Cloud as a fourth geometric anchor to reduce uncertainties, but otherwise the two studies use the same formalism. Figure 2 shows that our result for M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} is largely set by BAO data at z = 0.51 z=0.51 –0.93 combined with the Planck prior on r d r_{\rm d} , so M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} is not dependent on how we extrapolate below the DES floor. This explains why M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} and its uncertainty are barely affected by inclusion of the legacy SNIa, even though these significantly extend the coverage towards lower redshift. Configuration A (SNIa + BAO + Planck r d r_{\rm d} ) pins the sound horizon to the 100 prior ( r d = 147.05 ± 0.30 r_{\rm d}=147.05\pm 0.30 cMpc). Configuration B (SNIa + BAO + CC) replaces the r d r_{\rm d} prior with CC datasets, so r d r_{\rm d} is derived without CMB input. In the first block for each configuration, we obtain the deceleration parameter q 0 = C 1 − 1 q_{0}=C_{1}-1 in our cosmographic IDL analysis with k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 (Eq. 7 ). The second block of each configuration repeats the IDL assuming flat Λ \Lambda CDM (Eq. 9 ), for which we obtain q 0 = 3 2 ​ Ω m − 1 q_{0}=\tfrac{3}{2}\Omega_{\rm m}-1 . The final column shows the reduced χ 2 \chi^{2} using the posterior mean value of each parameter. We quote the posterior mean and standard deviation, except for markedly non-Gaussian posteriors (mode and mean differing by more than 0.3 ​ σ 0.3\sigma , or the two sides of the 68% highest posterior density interval differing by more than 0.3 ​ σ 0.3\sigma ), for which we quote the mode and that interval. The large discrepancy between our clear result for M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} and the SH0ES result for M B M_{B} could arise due to the use of different photometric filter systems. Unlike the SH0ES result based on an absolute calibration of SNIa close enough to have a Cepheid distance, SNIa in DES are too distant for this approach. It is therefore difficult to directly test whether M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} might plausibly be − 19.4 -19.4 , as required by our analysis if standard physics applies prior to recombination (configuration A). In configuration B where this assumption is relaxed and we replace the Planck prior on r d r_{\rm d} with cosmology-independent CC constraints, the preferred value of M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} remains very close to − 19.4 -19.4 , but the uncertainty is considerably larger, reducing the discrepancy with the SH0ES result to ≈ 1.1 ​ σ \approx 1.1\sigma – 1.2 ​ σ 1.2\sigma . As a further check that the M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} constraint does not depend on our particular cosmographic expansion (Eq. 7 ), we repeat our IDL analysis using instead the flat Λ \Lambda CDM form of the expansion history (Eq. 9 ). This is shown in Table 2 as the second block of results for each configuration. The M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} calibration remains unchanged, sitting at − 19.377 ± 0.012 -19.377\pm 0.012 ( − 19.379 ± 0.012 -19.379\pm 0.012 ) for DES (DES + legacy) in configuration A. The equivalent result for configuration B is − 19.40 ± 0.12 -19.40\pm 0.12 ( − 19.40 ± 0.13 -19.40\pm 0.13 ) for DES (DES + legacy). This matches the calibration of our cosmographic IDL to within 0.02 mag. The offset from the SH0ES M B M_{B} therefore remains much the same: it is 4.20 ​ σ 4.20\sigma ( 4.26 ​ σ 4.26\sigma ) for configuration A with DES (DES + legacy). The equivalent result for configuration B is 1.20 ​ σ 1.20\sigma ( 1.11 ​ σ 1.11\sigma ) for DES (DES + legacy). The lower tension is due to wider error bars, since CC datasets have a constraining power that is presently far weaker than the CMB under the assumption of flat Λ \Lambda CDM prior to recombination, an assumption that is not required for CC. The quality of fit to the data remains the same regardless of whether we use flat Λ \Lambda CDM or our cosmographic expansion, with reduced χ 2 = 0.92 \chi^{2}=0.92 –0.94. We note that since we have N data = 1555 N_{\mathrm{data}}=1555 (1752) data points without (with) the legacy SNIa and the number of model parameters is negligible in comparison, we expect the reduced χ 2 \chi^{2} to approximately follow a Gaussian distribution centred on 1 with dispersion 0.036 (0.034) in these cases. The reduced χ 2 \chi^{2} drops from 0.94 to 0.92 upon excluding the legacy SNIa in all analysis variants, indicating a slightly better fit quality without the legacy SNIa. In our analyses with the tight Planck prior on r d r_{\rm d} (configuration A), the posterior remains the same as the prior because there is no information to shift the absolute scale of H ⁡ ( z ) H(z) from uncalibrated SNIa or from BAO data that inherit their absolute calibration from r d r_{\rm d} . To relax the assumption of standard physics prior to recombination, we can relax the Planck prior on r d r_{\rm d} and constrain it with CC. This alternative route (configuration B) yields r d = 148.48 ± 8.39 r_{\rm d}=148.48\pm 8.39 ( 148.51 ± 8.68 148.51\pm 8.68 ) cMpc in flat Λ \Lambda CDM with SNIa from DES (DES + legacy). These results are within 0.2 ​ σ 0.2\sigma of the model-dependent Planck value of r d r_{\rm d} . We note that our results without this prior are not as precise as in Guo et al. (2025) , who used a somewhat different approach and a larger number of CC measurements, combined as here with uncalibrated BAO and SNIa. Interestingly, their predicted H 0 = 68.4 − 0.8 + 1.0 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=68.4^{+1.0}_{-0.8}\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} lies 3.6 ​ σ 3.6\sigma below the central SH0ES value.

sections.heading: 4.4 Redshift-floor sweep
sections.text: Figure 5: The solid lines show the recovered H 0 H_{0} ( top ) and q 0 q_{0} ( bottom ) in our k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 cosmographic IDL constrained by DES-Dovekie SNIa + DESI DR2 BAO + Planck r d r_{\rm d} , shown as a function of the redshift floor z floor z_{\rm floor} below which SNIa are excluded and the sample re-fitted. In both panels, we present results with DES (black), DES + legacy (red), and DES + legacy with free recalibration of the legacy SNIa by Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\rm legacy} (blue; Eq. 22 ). The dashed vertical lines show the lower limit of each dataset without truncation. The upper limits of z = 0.087 z=0.087 for the legacy SNIa and z = 1.14 z=1.14 for DES are not shown here. At redshift floors which reject all legacy SNIa, we show results only for DES. In the top panel, the horizontal dotted lines with 1 ​ σ 1\sigma error bands show H 0 SH0ES H_{0}^{\mathrm{SH0ES}} ( Breuval et al., 2024 ) and H 0 SPA H_{0}^{\mathrm{SPA}} ( SPT-3G Collaboration, 2026 ) , as indicated. In the bottom panel, the horizontal dotted orange line shows q 0 SPA q_{0}^{\rm SPA} . To check if our results are particularly sensitive to SNIa at the low-redshift end, we truncate the SNIa to only those with z > z floor z>z_{\mathrm{floor}} . The top panel of Figure 5 shows how the predicted H 0 H_{0} depends on z floor z_{\mathrm{floor}} . The black line shows no obvious trend with only DES SNIa – all results are ≈ 2.5 ​ σ \approx 2.5\sigma – 3.5 ​ σ 3.5\sigma above H 0 SPA H_{0}^{\mathrm{SPA}} until we get to high z floor z_{\mathrm{floor}} , when the error bars become large due to the small number of SNIa. The predicted H 0 H_{0} is always above the SH0ES value ( Breuval et al., 2024 ) , but the level of tension is below 2 ​ σ 2\sigma except at z floor = 0.15 z_{\mathrm{floor}}=0.15 , where it is 2.1 ​ σ 2.1\sigma . Importantly, the tension with SH0ES is only 1.03 ​ σ 1.03\sigma when we consider DES without any redshift floor (or equivalently z floor < 0.073 z_{\mathrm{floor}}<0.073 ). Thus, the high predicted H 0 H_{0} in our baseline analysis (without any redshift floor) agrees reasonably well with local H 0 H_{0} anchors, which are generally in good agreement with SH0ES ( Di Valentino et al., 2025 ; H0DN Collaboration, 2026 ) . The bottom panel of Figure 5 shows that the high H 0 H_{0} is associated with a very low deceleration parameter of q 0 ≈ − 3 q_{0}\approx-3 . This is expected since the expansion history needs to be similar to that in the Planck cosmology at high redshift, so we can get elevated H 0 H_{0} only with extra acceleration at late times. Similarly to the results for H 0 H_{0} , the black line shows no obvious trend in q 0 q_{0} with z floor z_{\mathrm{floor}} when considering only the homogeneous DES catalogue. These results change substantially upon including the legacy SNIa at low redshift, as shown by the red curve in each panel of Figure 5 . As we start to include legacy SNIa by decreasing z floor z_{\mathrm{floor}} , the predicted H 0 H_{0} drops sharply until it becomes consistent with H 0 SPA H_{0}^{\mathrm{SPA}} . This behaviour is mirrored for q 0 q_{0} , which is far below the SPA value of 3 2 ​ Ω m − 1 = − 0.52 \tfrac{3}{2}\Omega_{\rm m}-1=-0.52 at high z floor z_{\mathrm{floor}} , but rises sharply towards and ultimately becomes consistent with it as z floor → 0 z_{\mathrm{floor}}\to 0 . Adding the legacy SNIa considerably reduces the formal uncertainties, so the predicted H 0 H_{0} at the lowest z floor z_{\mathrm{floor}} values lies well below SH0ES and other local H 0 H_{0} anchors. This tension is clearly driven by the legacy SNIa. We note that when we set z floor = 0.073 z_{\mathrm{floor}}=0.073 in our DES + legacy analysis to include all DES SNIa while minimising the number of legacy SNIa, we end up including 10 legacy SNIa. Adding this handful of legacy SNIa should have a negligible impact on the results, but in fact it decreases H 0 H_{0} by 4.45 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 4.45\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , which is 1.6 × 1.6\times the uncertainty prior to adding the legacy SNIa. This suggests a direct tension between DES and the legacy SNIa in the narrow redshift range where they overlap. While we do of course expect the addition of more data – especially at low redshift – to tighten the constraints, such large parameter shifts are not expected on the basis of the stable DES-only results. This is apparent from repeating our redshift-floor sweep test on the 10 4 10^{4} mock datasets presented in Appendix D , which we generate assuming correctness of the published BAO and SNIa covariance matrices and analyse similarly to the real data. Despite the scatter between the H 0 ​ ( z floor ) H_{0}(z_{\mathrm{floor}}) curves and a gradual upwards drift due to our cosmographic expansion not being exact, it is difficult to find a mock realisation of Λ \Lambda CDM where the behaviour resembles that of the real data (Figure 16 ). The sharp feature in the DES + legacy result for H 0 ​ ( z floor ) H_{0}(z_{\mathrm{floor}}) at precisely the redshift where the catalogue transitions from legacy SNIa to DES suggests a systematic affecting the legacy SNIa rather than a genuine transition at low redshift. The DES-only result for H 0 ​ ( z floor ) H_{0}(z_{\mathrm{floor}}) is fairly smooth out to z floor = 0.3 z_{\mathrm{floor}}=0.3 , so the sharp feature at z ≈ 0.08 z\approx 0.08 in the DES + legacy case is not expected either in Λ \Lambda CDM mocks or from analysis of the homogeneous DES catalogue.
