All results shown here are relative to the Λ \Lambda CDM control. For clarity, we omit the numerical uncertainty on ln ⁡ B 10 \ln B_{10} of ± 0.19 \pm 0.19 . To make the results with the two z 1 z_{1} priors more comparable, we show the mean and standard deviation of A A and H 0 = H 0 , Λ ​ CDM + A H_{0}=H_{0,\Lambda\mathrm{CDM}}+A . H 0 win H_{0}^{\rm win} is the H 0 H_{0} that SH0ES would infer if the Universe followed each posterior, i.e. the kinematic fit of Section 3.3.3 applied over the redshifts of the SH0ES Hubble-flow SNIa ( z = 0.023 z=0.023 –0.149). Table 4 shows the impact of changing the z 1 z_{1} prior from 𝒰 ⁡ ( z 1 ) → 𝒰 ⁡ ( ln ⁡ z 1 ) \mathcal{U}(z_{1})\to\mathcal{U}(\ln z_{1}) . We begin with the case without a local H 0 H_{0} anchor, so the inferred H 0 H_{0} can be considered a genuine prediction of the IDL approach constrained by SNIa + BAO + CC + CMB + BBN. With SNIa from DES alone, A A remains very consistent with zero for both priors, though the uncertainty rises from 2 to 5 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 5\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} when going from the uniform prior to the log-uniform prior. These changes directly affect the predicted H 0 H_{0} , which is 68.83 ± 2.02 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 68.83\pm 2.02\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} with the uniform prior and 68.93 ± 5.02 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 68.93\pm 5.02\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} with the log-uniform prior. While these results are more in line with A = 0 A=0 and H 0 = H 0 SPA H_{0}=H_{0}^{\mathrm{SPA}} , they cannot exclude the possibility that A ≈ 6 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 A\approx 6\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} and H 0 = H 0 SH0ES H_{0}=H_{0}^{\mathrm{SH0ES}} – especially with the log-uniform prior. The picture remains similar upon including the legacy SNIa with free Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} , which again shows no preference for A > 0 A>0 . The Bayesian evidences are also not appreciably different from that of Λ \Lambda CDM. The results are quite different with DES + legacy regardless of the prior choice. We infer A < 0 A<0 with either z 1 z_{1} prior. In particular, A = − 2.17 ± 1.65 ​ ( − 4.20 ± 2.89 ) ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 A=-2.17\pm 1.65(-4.20\pm 2.89)\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} with the uniform prior on z 1 z_{1} ( ln ⁡ z 1 \ln z_{1} ). Although the Bayesian evidence no longer disfavours the exp model and actually prefers it with the log-uniform prior, this reflects a preference for A < 0 A<0 , which is strongly incompatible with the A ≈ + 6 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 A\approx+6\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} required to solve the Hubble tension. This is evident in that the inferred H 0 H_{0} is 66.21 ± 1.70 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 66.21\pm 1.70\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} with the uniform z 1 z_{1} prior, which is lower than the 67.94 ± 0.24 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 67.94\pm 0.24\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} we obtain for flat Λ \Lambda CDM from the same data. With the log-uniform prior on z 1 z_{1} , the inferred H 0 H_{0} drops to just 63.92 ± 2.92 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 63.92\pm 2.92\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} . In both cases, the results are considerably below the SH0ES measurement. We note that a sharp reduction in predicted H 0 H_{0} upon including the legacy SNIa is also evident from our sweep of the redshift floor using a model-independent cosmographic expansion (Figure 5 ). We are able to recover this feature in the context of our exp model due to it allowing a sharp feature in the expansion history at z ≲ z 1 z\la z_{1} . Despite the preference for A < 0 A<0 , we are still not able to meaningfully constrain z 1 z_{1} with DES + legacy if we adopt a uniform prior. With a log-uniform prior, we obtain z 1 < 0.019 z_{1}<0.019 at the 1 ​ σ 1\sigma C.L., which is considerably tighter than the z 1 < 0.070 z_{1}<0.070 given by the prior alone (Table 4 ). This shows that while z 1 z_{1} remains essentially unconstrained with the uniform prior, the log prior suggests a rather low z 1 z_{1} . Since A A is still plausibly consistent with zero, we suggest that there is no clear preference for the exp model when we include the legacy SNIa at face value. Once we impose a local H 0 H_{0} anchor, the inferred H 0 H_{0} is no longer a prediction, so the important quantity is now the Bayesian evidence. We find that using a log-uniform prior on z 1 z_{1} increases ln ⁡ B 10 \ln B_{10} in nearly all cases, typically by about 0.7. The increases exceed the numerical uncertainty of ± 0.19 \pm 0.19 , often by a considerable amount. The only decrease occurs if we combine the SH0ES anchor with DES + legacy allowing a free Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} , in which case ln ⁡ B 10 \ln B_{10} decreases by just 0.06. The systematic increase in the Bayesian evidence in the remaining cases is caused by a log-uniform prior increasing the prior weight on low values of z 1 z_{1} , which are preferred even for a uniform prior. As a result, the DES-only case with SNIa-independent anchors shifts from ln ⁡ B 10 = + 1.54 \ln B_{10}=+1.54 to + 2.53 +2.53 , which is now a clear preference for the exp model. This is related to a corresponding rise in H 0 H_{0} from 72.53 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 72.53\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} to 74.23 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 74.23\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} . The Bayesian evidence for the DES-only case with the strong SH0ES anchor strengthens from + 10.61 +10.61 to + 11.26 +11.26 , while A A rises from 8.00 ± 1.46 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 8.00\pm 1.46\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} to 8.25 ± 1.32 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 8.25\pm 1.32\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} . In the DES + legacy case with the SH0ES anchor, changing from a uniform prior to a log-uniform prior reduces H 0 H_{0} from 68.84 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 68.84\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} to 68.28 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 68.28\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , demonstrating that even the tight SH0ES anchor cannot pull the legacy-dominated fit up to H 0 SH0ES H_{0}^{\mathrm{SH0ES}} regardless of the z 1 z_{1} prior. Our overall conclusions regarding the exp model do not change much depending on whether we use a uniform prior on z 1 z_{1} or on ln ⁡ z 1 \ln z_{1} . A late-time solution with A ≈ 6 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 A\approx 6\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} is preferred only when we impose a local H 0 H_{0} anchor and do not consider the legacy SNIa, though there is a weak preference if we include them allowing recalibration. Without any local H 0 H_{0} anchor, the data are consistent with a late-time solution to the Hubble tension, but do not prefer the high required A A . With the strong SH0ES anchor and SNIa only from DES, we infer that A ≈ 8 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 A\approx 8\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} and z 1 ≈ 0.03 z_{1}\approx 0.03 with either z 1 z_{1} prior. We stress, however, that our prior on A A bounds both values. Since most of the SH0ES Hubble-flow SNIa lie at z > z 1 z>z_{1} , the distances they measure respond mainly to the integrated excess ∫ Δ ​ H ​ 𝑑 z = A ​ z 1 \int\Delta H\,\mathrm{d}z=Az_{1} rather than to A A and z 1 z_{1} separately. The likelihood therefore has a ridge along which A A rises as z 1 z_{1} falls, with A ​ z 1 = 0.29 − 0.08 + 0.12 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 Az_{1}=0.29^{+0.12}_{-0.08}\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} . The upper edge of our prior at A = 10 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 A=10\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} truncates this ridge, and 31% of the posterior mass lies at A > 9 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 A>9\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} (36% with the log-uniform prior on z 1 z_{1} ). A wider prior would thus raise A A and lower z 1 z_{1} . It would also change ln ⁡ B 10 \ln B_{10} , both through the larger prior volume, which lowers it by ln ⁡ 2 \ln 2 for each doubling of the range of A A , and through the additional likelihood along the ridge, which raises it.

sections.heading: 4.6 AP consistency test
sections.text: Most of our results are heavily influenced by the tight Planck prior on r d r_{\rm d} . As discussed in Section 3.4 , the AP test avoids this dependence by using the AP ratio F AP ≡ D M / D H F_{\mathrm{AP}}\equiv D_{\rm M}/D_{\rm H} . In Appendix A , we apply the AP test to check whether the shape of the expansion history is consistent between SNIa and BAO at three redshifts where particularly tight BAO results are available and there is good SNIa coverage. We find consistency for both DES and DES + legacy, with the p p -value (likelihood of a higher χ 2 \chi^{2} ) being 9.7% and 10.5%, respectively. There is a mild ≈ 2 ​ σ \approx 2\sigma deficit in both cases at z = 0.510 z=0.510 , while at z = 0.934 z=0.934 , there is a mild excess of 2.0 ​ σ 2.0\sigma for DES and 1.8 ​ σ 1.8\sigma for DES + legacy. However, there is excellent agreement at z = 0.706 z=0.706 . The acceptable p p -values indicate that fitting our cosmographic expansion to SNIa predicts F AP F_{\mathrm{AP}} values that are in line with BAO measurements regardless of r d r_{\rm d} , justifying our approach of combining SNIa and BAO datasets assuming the Etherington relation. However, there is some tension between the DESI DR2 BAO measurements at z = 0.706 z=0.706 and previous BAO results at a similar redshift ( Banik et al., 2026c , section 3.6 of) . It will therefore be important to revisit these results with future BAO measurements.

sections.heading: 4.7 Systematics with the legacy SNIa
sections.text: Adding the legacy SNIa to the homogeneous DES sample shifts the inferred cosmological parameters in a manner that would not be expected from the latter (Figure 4 ). This might be due to systematics with the legacy SNIa. We test this possibility by adding an offset parameter Δ ​ M legacy ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( − 1 , 1 ) \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}\sim\mathcal{U}\left(-1,1\right) mag to the absolute magnitude of the legacy SNIa, which therefore becomes as follows: M legacy = M DES + Δ ​ M legacy . \displaystyle M_{\mathrm{legacy}}~=~M_{\mathrm{DES}}+\Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}\,. (22) A higher Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} corresponds to intrinsically fainter legacy SNIa, which for fixed apparent magnitude implies that they must be closer to us. Since the redshifts are spectroscopically confirmed, this would lead to a higher H 0 H_{0} . Our results for Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} are shown in Figure 6 for the four considered cases discussed in Section 3.5 , namely cosmography, cosmography + AP, Λ \Lambda CDM, and Λ \Lambda CDM + AP. We consistently infer an offset of Δ ​ M legacy = + 0.05 \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}=+0.05 to + 0.07 +0.07 mag, with the detection significance ranging from 1.2 ​ σ 1.2\sigma for the more flexible cosmographic expansion, to 2.9 ​ σ 2.9\sigma for the less flexible Λ \Lambda CDM parametrisation with the AP consistency requirement. All four analyses agree on the magnitude of the offset, but differences in the uncertainty create differences in how confident each analysis can be that Δ ​ M legacy > 0 \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}>0 . In our baseline analysis where we use a cosmographic IDL and infer Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} alongside the other parameters, we find that Δ ​ M legacy = + 0.0646 ± 0.0391 \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}=+0.0646\pm 0.0391 mag, a 1.65 ​ σ 1.65\sigma offset (cf. Figure 5 ). Figure 6: The relative offset Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} (Eq. 22 ) of the legacy SNIa from the DES-Dovekie relation extrapolated to z → 0 z\to 0 , for the four analyses described in Section 3.5 . The vertical grey band shows the ≈ 0.04 \approx 0.04 mag offset independently reported by Efstathiou (2025) . To gain further insight into how a calibration offset might have arisen, we split the legacy SNIa into two subsamples and infer a separate Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} for each. Our aim is to find if any particular subset of the legacy SNIa has a calibration offset Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} that differs from the offset Δ ​ M legacy rest \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}^{\mathrm{rest}} that we obtain for the remaining legacy SNIa. Figure 7 shows Δ ​ M legacy − Δ ​ M legacy rest \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}-\Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}^{\mathrm{rest}} for a few possible splits. The legacy SNIa largely come from Foundation or from CfA. The former have a positive Δ ​ M legacy − Δ ​ M legacy rest \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}-\Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}^{\mathrm{rest}} . Since ‘rest’ in this context largely means CfA, this behaviour is mirrored in that case, explaining why the CfA SNIa have a negative Δ ​ M legacy − Δ ​ M legacy rest \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}-\Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}^{\mathrm{rest}} by almost the same amount and with a similar uncertainty. If the offset is survey-specific, the underlying issue may be the completeness correction for each survey or the conversion between different photometric filter systems, rather than any problem with the legacy SNIa observations in their original passband. Figure 7: Test of whether the legacy offset depends on which subset of the legacy SNIa we consider, based on splitting the legacy SNIa into two subsamples according to the distinguishing feature indicated at the left (e.g., the first row splits off the Foundation SNIa from the remaining legacy SNIa). The values show Δ ​ M legacy − Δ ​ M legacy rest \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}-\Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}^{\mathrm{rest}} , the inferred offset for the subsample of interest and the rest of the legacy SNIa, respectively. We jointly infer both offset parameters. Note this does not test whether the legacy SNIa are offset from the main DES sample (which is shown in Figure 6 ), but rather whether the offset depends on subsample within the legacy set. We also check for any redshift-dependent trend in Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} by splitting the legacy SNIa in redshift. A trend here might arise due to the greater importance of peculiar velocity at low redshift, while survey incompleteness may be an issue towards the high-redshift end of the z = 0.025 z=0.025 –0.087 range covered by the legacy SNIa. We therefore split the legacy SNIa into subsamples below and above a redshift threshold of 0.05 or 0.073, the lowest redshift SNIa in the main DES sample. Figure 7 shows that in both cases, Δ ​ M legacy − Δ ​ M legacy rest \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}-\Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}^{\mathrm{rest}} is very consistent with 0. We therefore conclude that the difference between the main DES sample and the legacy SNIa is not driven by any particular redshift bin. Figure 8: Top : H 0 H_{0} inferred from the IDL. Circles show results from our cosmographic analysis with k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 (Eq. 7 ). Squares show results using flat Λ \Lambda CDM (Eq. 9 ). The vertical shaded bands show H 0 SPA H_{0}^{\mathrm{SPA}} ( SPT-3G Collaboration, 2026 ) and H 0 SH0ES H_{0}^{\mathrm{SH0ES}} ( Breuval et al., 2024 ) , as indicated in the legend. The top row excludes legacy SNIa, while the middle row includes them without correction ( Δ ​ M legacy = 0 \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}=0 ). The bottom row includes the legacy SNIa allowing free Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} . Bottom : Our inferred Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} when we sample it jointly with r d r_{\rm d} and M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} , assuming our cosmographic IDL. The vertical grey band shows the range reported by Efstathiou (2025) . Both panels adopt the 100 prior on r d r_{\rm d} . The legacy SNIa calibration offset is directly related to H 0 H_{0} because intrinsically fainter SNIa must be closer to have the same apparent magnitude, leading to a higher H 0 H_{0} . We explore what impact this might have on the IDL using the approach described in Section 3.5 . The results are presented in Figure 8 and summarised in Table 5 . For our cosmographic expansion, allowing Δ ​ M legacy ≠ 0 \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}\neq 0 increases H 0 H_{0} from 67.98 ± 0.69 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 67.98\pm 0.69\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} to 71.03 ± 1.99 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 71.03\pm 1.99\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , which is now only 0.99 ​ σ 0.99\sigma below SH0ES. Allowing the Foundation and CfA/CSP legacy SNIa to have different offsets leaves this result almost unchanged, with H 0 = 70.91 ± 2.00 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=70.91\pm 2.00\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} . This shows that while the shape suggests a 1 ​ σ 1\sigma calibration difference between these legacy datasets, a flexible cosmographic expansion along with a single legacy offset parameter absorbs nearly all the difference with H 0 SPA H_{0}^{\mathrm{SPA}} . The full IDL thus gains little from allowing separate offset parameters for Foundation and CfA/CSP. H 0 H_{0} [km s -1 Mpc -1 ] using … Case cosmography Λ \Lambda CDM Legacy excluded (DES only) 76.25 ± 2.87 76.25\pm 2.87 68.98 ± 0.48 68.98\pm 0.48 Legacy included uncorrected 67.98 ± 0.69 67.98\pm 0.69 68.60 ± 0.46 68.60\pm 0.46 Legacy zero-point sampled 71.03 ± 1.99 71.03\pm 1.99 69.02 ± 0.48 69.02\pm 0.48 Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} [mag] + 0.0646 ± 0.0391 +0.0646\pm 0.0391 + 0.0377 ± 0.0129 +0.0377\pm 0.0129 Table 5: Inferred H 0 H_{0} in our baseline analysis (SNIa + DESI DR2 BAO + 100 r d r_{\rm d} ) with the legacy SNIa excluded, included without correction, or included after correction by Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} to align them with the DES relation extrapolated to z → 0 z\to 0 . The final row shows Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} . The preference for H 0 > H 0 SPA H_{0}>H_{0}^{\mathrm{SPA}} is still discernible in flat Λ \Lambda CDM, but it is far weaker due to the less flexible expansion history (Eq. 9 ). In this case, H 0 H_{0} rises from 68.60 ± 0.46 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 68.60\pm 0.46\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} without Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} to 69.02 ± 0.48 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 69.02\pm 0.48\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} with free Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} . The very small difference arises because fixing both the shape of the expansion history and its normalisation assuming Λ \Lambda CDM necessarily implies a Planck -like H 0 H_{0} regardless of whether the legacy SNIa can be recalibrated. However, assuming Λ \Lambda CDM at late times automatically excludes the possibility of solving the Hubble tension at late times. The fact that H 0 > H 0 SPA H_{0}>H_{0}^{\mathrm{SPA}} even in this case may be hinting at a late-time solution. Our results suggest that a calibration offset with the legacy SNIa contributes ≈ 3 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 \approx 3\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} to the H 0 H_{0} gap between local anchors and the IDL including legacy SNIa. Allowing these to be recalibrated relative to the homogeneous DES sample relaxes the tension with SH0ES from 4.69 ​ σ 4.69\sigma to just 0.99 ​ σ 0.99\sigma given the uncertainty in Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} . Averaging over the truncation order rather than selecting k max = 4 k_{\mathrm{max}}=4 raises this to 1.43 ​ σ 1.43\sigma (Appendix B.2 ). Remarkably, the H 0 H_{0} value recovered by the IDL using DES without legacy SNIa is very similar to the standard distance ladder result obtained by anchoring the DESI Fundamental Plane using the distance to the Coma Cluster ( Scolnic et al., 2025 ) or with a broader range of anchors ( Carr et al., 2026 ) . This agreement survives and in the latter case even improves upon averaging over the cosmographic order k max k_{\max} , which gives H 0 = 74.77 ± 4.83 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=74.77\pm 4.83\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} (Table 7 ). In this case the Bayesian evidence assigns 20% of the probability to k max = 5 k_{\max}=5 , which gives a lower and more uncertain result for H 0 H_{0} , as discussed next.

sections.heading: 4.8 Robustness tests
sections.text: The most striking feature of the results in Table 2 is the substantial difference between the H 0 H_{0} predictions of our cosmographic IDL constrained by DES and by DES + legacy, which we denote H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} and H 0 DES + legacy H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES+legacy}} , respectively. The poorer low-redshift coverage with DES alone forces our cosmographic expansion to extrapolate across the z ≲ 0.2 z\la 0.2 regime, though it has SNIa down to z = 0.073 z=0.073 . Since our cosmographic expansion does not exactly match the true H ⁡ ( 1 − a ) H(1-a) for any finite k max k_{\max} , it inevitably introduces some systematic error into the predicted H 0 H_{0} , even in the absence of measurement errors. This can be investigated using mock data. The size of the effect depends on the unknown true expansion history; for illustration we quantify it in the flat Λ \Lambda CDM cosmology that best fits the CMB ( SPT-3G Collaboration, 2026 ) . We set up 10 4 10^{4} mock datasets assuming this SPA cosmology, with the mock SNIa having the same redshift distribution and magnitude uncertainties as the real SNIa in DES or DES + legacy (further details are provided in Appendix D ). The difference Δ ​ H 0 ≡ H 0 DES − H 0 DES + legacy \Delta H_{0}\equiv H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}}-H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES+legacy}} exceeds the observed 8.27 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 8.27\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} in only 1.24% of the mocks (Figure 15 ). This corresponds to a Gaussian-equivalent significance of 2.24 ​ σ 2.24\sigma for a one-tailed test, which is appropriate because the sign of the Hubble tension is well known, so the ‘alternative hypothesis’ to Λ \Lambda CDM would be that Δ ​ H 0 ≈ 6 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 \Delta H_{0}\approx 6\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} and the legacy SNIa are subject to systematics. The observed Δ ​ H 0 \Delta H_{0} is therefore unlikely to arise from random fluctuations in a Λ \Lambda CDM cosmology coupled with extrapolation error due to the limited DES coverage at z ≲ 0.2 z\la 0.2 . However, our mocks suggest that these issues can provide a partial explanation given their tendency to find Δ ​ H 0 > 0 \Delta H_{0}>0 . This bias is related to a generic overestimation of H 0 H_{0} by ≈ 1 ​ σ \approx 1\sigma , even if the DES coverage at low redshift is further limited by a redshift floor (Figure 16 ). As shown by our noise-free mock, the bias is a truncation error arising from differences between the assumed Λ \Lambda CDM expansion history and our fourth-order cosmographic expansion. We do not know how accurately this can represent the real cosmological model, especially as a late-time solution to the Hubble tension must by definition differ from Λ \Lambda CDM. Even so, our mocks quantify the effect. The scatter of H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} across them ( 2.86 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 2.86\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} ) matches our stated uncertainty ( 2.87 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 2.87\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} ), so the error bar captures the statistical uncertainty. However, their mean exceeds the input H 0 H_{0} by 2.76 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 2.76\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , so the ± 1 ​ σ \pm 1\sigma ( ± 2 ​ σ \pm 2\sigma ) interval contains the true value in only 49 (85)% of the mocks. Calibrated on the mocks, our H 0 DES = 76.25 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}}=76.25\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} is reached in 133 of the 10 4 10^{4} realisations, i.e. 2.22 ​ σ 2.22\sigma for a one-tailed test, rather than the 3.13 ​ σ 3.13\sigma implied by the formal uncertainty. If we subtract the bias, H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} becomes 73.49 ± 2.87 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 73.49\pm 2.87\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} . This is 2.18 ​ σ 2.18\sigma above SPA and in excellent agreement with SH0ES ( 0.11 ​ σ 0.11\sigma ). We note that this correction assumes the SPA cosmology, so it illustrates the size of the bias rather than correcting for it in general. Figure 9: Polynomial order sweep for our cosmographic IDL in configuration A, using DES (black), DES + legacy (red), and DES + legacy with the legacy zero point Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} free (blue). Top : Bayesian evidence relative to the most probable order of each sample, Δ ​ ln ⁡ Z ≡ ln ⁡ Z − ln ⁡ Z max \Delta\ln Z\equiv\ln Z-\ln Z_{\max} . The grey band marks | Δ ​ ln ⁡ Z | < 1 \lvert\Delta\ln Z\rvert<1 , inside which two orders are not distinguished ( Trotta, 2008 ) . Stars and the vertical dotted line mark our baseline choice of k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 . Bottom : The posterior on H 0 H_{0} at each order, with the Bayesian model average over k max = 2 k_{\max}=2 –6 shown as diamonds in the column labelled “BMA” (Appendix B.2 ). The horizontal green and orange bands show H 0 SH0ES H_{0}^{\mathrm{SH0ES}} ( Breuval et al., 2024 ) and H 0 SPA H_{0}^{\mathrm{SPA}} ( SPT-3G Collaboration, 2026 ) , respectively. The truncation error can be reduced with a higher-order expansion, but this makes the model more flexible, which inflates the uncertainties and can lower the Bayesian evidence. We therefore test how our results depend on the order by repeating the analysis for k max = 2 k_{\max}=2 –6. The results are shown in Figure 9 , with further details in Appendix B . Although H 0 H_{0} changes significantly between orders, k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 is the lowest order that provides an adequate fit to the data. In fact, k max = 2 k_{\max}=2 and 3 raise χ min 2 \chi^{2}_{\min} by 210 and 30 for DES because they cannot describe the shape of the Hubble diagram across the DES redshift range. With k max = 5 k_{\max}=5 , we instead obtain H 0 = 68.52 ± 4.99 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=68.52\pm 4.99\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} for DES and H 0 = 66.14 ± 0.90 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=66.14\pm 0.90\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} for DES + legacy. This means that DES with k max = 5 k_{\max}=5 or 6 gives results that are consistent with both SH0ES and SPA because of their larger uncertainties, whereas k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 is consistent only with SH0ES. Even so, the higher orders remain consistent with the k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 result within the 1.58 ​ σ 1.58\sigma C.L. for DES and the 1.61 ​ σ 1.61\sigma C.L. for DES + legacy. The fifth-order results emphasise that without the legacy SNIa, the IDL is plausibly consistent with a late-time solution to the Hubble tension. They also highlight that the lack of effective DES coverage at low redshift makes it difficult to be sure what H 0 H_{0} to expect from the IDL, so the high H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} with k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 does not clearly confirm the Hubble tension. The Bayesian evidence of each order (Eq. 10 ) quantifies how strongly the data support our baseline. The first result to highlight is that k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 is the most probable order for DES, carrying 80% of the posterior probability in configuration A and 83% in configuration B. The evidence at this order exceeds that at k max = 2 k_{\max}=2 and 3 by 97 and 10 nats, respectively. Beyond k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 , the Bayesian evidence falls again, by 1.4 at k max = 5 k_{\max}=5 and by 4.8 at k max = 6 k_{\max}=6 . This is because the fifth coefficient improves χ min 2 \chi^{2}_{\min} by only 2.4, which does not compensate for the extra volume prior. This is different for DES + legacy, where k max = 5 k_{\max}=5 improves χ min 2 \chi^{2}_{\min} by 9.3 and is preferred over k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 by Δ ​ ln ⁡ Z = 1.1 \Delta\ln Z=1.1 , but even this preference is only weak evidence on the Jeffreys scale ( Trotta, 2008 ) . Once Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} is free, the two orders are indistinguishable, with Δ ​ ln ⁡ Z = 0.1 \Delta\ln Z=0.1 . Thus, the data support our baseline for DES, and they do not significantly disfavour it for DES + legacy regardless of whether we allow recalibration of the legacy SNIa, allowing us to keep the two samples on an equal footing. However, the evidence assigns 20% of the probability to the higher orders for DES, while for DES + legacy it slightly prefers k max = 5 k_{\max}=5 , so we cannot treat the fourth order as certain in either case. One way to deal with the uncertain polynomial order k max k_{\max} is to combine the results at different orders by averaging over the considered k max = 2 k_{\max}=2 –6 range with weights given by their posterior probabilities (Eq. 10 ). We present the BMA in Appendix B.2 . For DES alone, it gives H 0 = 74.77 ± 4.83 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=74.77\pm 4.83\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , compared with 76.43 ± 3.01 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 76.43\pm 3.01\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} at k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 from the same nested sampling. The central value moves little because k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 carries 80% of the probability. However, the uncertainty grows 1.6 × 1.6\times because the average includes the spread between orders, which in this case includes the 7.9 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 7.9\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} lower H 0 H_{0} at k max = 5 k_{\max}=5 . As a result, the tension with SPA falls from 3.13 ​ σ 3.13\sigma to 1.56 ​ σ 1.56\sigma . Once we include the legacy SNIa, k max = 5 k_{\max}=5 carries 73% of the probability and the BMA gives H 0 = 66.61 ± 1.18 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=66.61\pm 1.18\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} . This is 1.37 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 1.37\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} below our k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 result, but it remains 4.50 ​ σ 4.50\sigma below SH0ES, so our conclusions on the legacy SNIa remain unchanged. After recalibrating the legacy SNIa, the BMA gives H 0 = 69.50 ± 2.43 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=69.50\pm 2.43\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , which is only 1.43 ​ σ 1.43\sigma below SH0ES. Our fiducial results focus on the same polynomial order (4 th ) for all SNIa configurations to help isolate the effect of including the legacy sample without simultaneously changing the flexibility of the reconstruction, as would occur if we had used the BMA. It is also important to consider how our results are affected by the prior, which could matter for the DES-alone case because DES does not constrain the expansion history below z = 0.073 z=0.073 . Our prior bounds only the expansion history itself (Eq. 8 ), with no posterior approaching the prior limits (Section 3.1 ). In particular, the best-fitting expansion history for DES stays at least 0.92 in E E from both limits, so prior truncation effects should be negligible. We can also check the effect of the prior by using the least-squares method instead of NUTS, approximating that χ 2 \chi^{2} near its minimum varies quadratically with the model parameters. Applying the least-squares method to DES in terms of the C k C_{k} rather than E E at the control points gives H 0 = 76.70 ± 2.97 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=76.70\pm 2.97\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , while DES + legacy gives instead 68.00 ± 0.71 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 68.00\pm 0.71\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} . Both results are fully consistent with our NUTS inference, which we treat as our baseline because it relaxes the locally quadratic assumption. The similar results when using least squares with the C k C_{k} instead of NUTS with uniform priors on E E at the control points indicate that the parametrisation used has little impact on the results. Although our prior is uniform in the C k C_{k} over the allowed region, the envelope of Eq. 8 couples the different orders, making the marginal prior on each C k C_{k} bounded and unimodal rather than uniform. However, it is very broad, with σ C 1 = σ q 0 = 17.3 \sigma_{C_{1}}=\sigma_{q_{0}}=17.3 , σ C 2 = 148 \sigma_{C_{2}}=148 , σ C 3 = 378 \sigma_{C_{3}}=378 , and σ C 4 = 293 \sigma_{C_{4}}=293 , where σ x \sigma_{x} is the standard deviation of the prior on x x . This is 24 24 – 73 × 73\times the width of the corresponding posterior in all four of our cosmographic analyses (DES and DES + legacy in configurations A and B). As a result, the marginal prior density changes by less than 4% across the ± 2 ​ σ \pm 2\sigma range of any posterior. This is because every posterior sample stays at least 0.8 in E E from both limits of Eq. 8 . Thus, our prior neither truncates the posteriors nor appreciably shapes them. In fact, we obtain virtually the same results with other priors. In configuration A, independent uniform priors on the dimensional coefficients H 0 ​ C k H_{0}C_{k} , over ranges much wider than the posteriors, give H 0 = 76.83 ± 2.88 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=76.83\pm 2.88\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} for DES and 68.02 ± 0.70 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 68.02\pm 0.70\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} for DES + legacy, against 76.25 ± 2.87 76.25\pm 2.87 and 67.98 ± 0.69 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 67.98\pm 0.69\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , respectively, with our baseline prior. Moreover, a least-squares fit in the standard cosmographic parameters q 0 q_{0} , j 0 j_{0} , s 0 s_{0} , and l 0 l_{0} (which places no limits on them) returns H 0 = 76.70 ± 2.97 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=76.70\pm 2.97\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} and 68.00 ± 0.71 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 68.00\pm 0.71\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} for DES and DES + legacy, respectively, which is essentially identical to the above least-squares fit in the C k C_{k} . Even so, we adopt the envelope because it is simpler to implement and its edges are known in advance, since they are set by the expansion history itself rather than by a separate range on each C k C_{k} that would have to be tuned for every k max k_{\max} and then checked against the posteriors. This is important for the Bayesian evidence, since the Occam penalty at each order depends on the prior volume. With separate ranges on the C k C_{k} , this volume would depend on how we tune the ranges at each k max k_{\max} , whereas the envelope applies the same physical bounds at every order, so the comparison between orders (Appendix B.2 ) does not involve any order-by-order tuning.

sections.heading: 5.1 Cosmological implications
sections.text: Our IDL result for the absolute SNIa magnitude ( M DES = − 19.380 ± 0.012 M_{\mathrm{DES}}=-19.380\pm 0.012 ) is in tension with the SH0ES result using Cepheid distances to SNIa host galaxies ( Riess et al., 2022 , M B = − 19.253 ± 0.027 M_{B}=-19.253\pm 0.027 ;) . This could be viewed as merely a manifestation of the Hubble tension, given the opposite starting points of the two approaches. We argue instead for an alternative interpretation, recognising that the DES and SH0ES catalogues operate in different passbands. SH0ES standardises SNIa into a rest-frame Johnson B B -band ( Riess et al., 2022 ; Scolnic et al., 2022 ) , often calibrating their results using ground-based optical filters and HST WFC3 filters like F160W, F555W, and F814W (the numbers indicate central wavelengths in nm). By contrast, DES-Dovekie operates natively in Dark Energy Camera (DECam) passbands ( Flaugher et al., 2015 ; Burke et al., 2018 , g , r , i , z g,r,i,z ;) . Converting DECam light curves into a standardised B B -band magnitude requires spectral energy distribution (SED) template fitting (e.g., via SALT2 or SALT3) and colour conversions ( Guy et al., 2007 ; Kenworthy et al., 2021 ) . Unrecognised systematic shifts in filter transmission curves or colour-term corrections routinely introduce 𝒪 ⁡ ( 0.01 ) \mathcal{O}(0.01) mag shifts ( Stubbs and Tonry, 2006 ; Brout et al., 2022 ) . Furthermore, zero-point standards (e.g., AB vs. Vega definitions, CALSPEC white dwarf flux standards) across different telescopes (DECam at Cerro Tololo vs. ground-based legacy instruments or HST) carry non-negligible cross-calibration uncertainties ( Oke and Gunn, 1983 ; Bohlin et al., 2014 ) . Another complication is that white dwarfs are quite different from SNIa in terms of colour and especially in terms of brightness, with nearby white dwarfs and other standard stars perhaps causing saturation effects that would not arise with a more distant SNIa near the limit of a legacy survey. Given that Pantheon+ comprises a wide array of legacy surveys, it is difficult to be sure of the correct relative calibration between them ( Scolnic et al., 2015 ; Brout et al., 2022 ) . DES-Dovekie has the major advantage of being a uniform dataset based on a single survey, provided we exclude the legacy SNIa ( Popovic et al., 2026 ) . This is the main reason we treat the DES-only case as our baseline and DES + legacy as an extension. Building our IDL using only SNIa from the homogeneous DES catalogue predicts H 0 DES = 76.25 ± 2.87 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}}=76.25\pm 2.87\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , which is 1.03 ​ σ 1.03\sigma above the local SH0ES value ( Breuval et al., 2024 , H 0 SH0ES = 73.17 ± 0.86 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}^{\mathrm{SH0ES}}=73.17\pm 0.86\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} ;) . This result can be interpreted as a rediscovery of the Hubble tension using the IDL to derive H 0 H_{0} instead of the usual approach based on the standard distance ladder, though without the latter, we obtain a smaller significance of 3.04 ​ σ 3.04\sigma relative to 100 ( 3.13 ​ σ 3.13\sigma relative to H 0 SPA H_{0}^{\mathrm{SPA}} , or 2.22 ​ σ 2.22\sigma once calibrated on our Λ \Lambda CDM mocks). This holds for our baseline k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 , which is the order with the highest Bayesian evidence for DES (80% of the posterior probability). Using instead the BMA over k max = 2 k_{\max}=2 –6 reduces the tension with SPA to 1.56 ​ σ 1.56\sigma (Section 4.8 ). Importantly, this is not the usual Hubble tension between low- and high-redshift measurements because H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} inherits its absolute scale from the CMB through the 100 prior on r d r_{\rm d} . Thus, the tension between H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} and H 0 SPA H_{0}^{\mathrm{SPA}} compares two CMB-calibrated predictions that differ only in whether Λ \Lambda CDM holds after recombination. This makes it a measure of departures from the Λ \Lambda CDM expansion history at late times, not merely of a discrepancy between the local and early Universe. However, we stress that H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} requires extrapolation below the DES redshift floor of 0.073. Reducing the redshift floor to 0.025 by adding the legacy SNIa decreases the predicted H 0 H_{0} to H 0 DES + legacy = 67.98 ± 0.69 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES+legacy}}=67.98\pm 0.69\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , which is now 4.69 ​ σ 4.69\sigma below H 0 SH0ES H_{0}^{\mathrm{SH0ES}} . The 197 legacy SNIa are therefore central to the question of whether the IDL is consistent with SH0ES. The observed 8.27 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 8.27\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} difference between H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} and H 0 DES + legacy H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES+legacy}} might arise due to the inaccuracy of extrapolating our cosmographic expansion to z → 0 z\to 0 to handle the lack of effective DES coverage at z ≲ 0.2 z\la 0.2 . We test this possibility by constructing mock datasets assuming flat Λ \Lambda CDM with the SPA parameters ( SPT-3G Collaboration, 2026 ) . Our results in Appendix D show that such a large value for Δ ​ H 0 ≡ H 0 DES − H 0 DES + legacy \Delta H_{0}\equiv H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}}-H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES+legacy}} arises in only 1.24% of 10 4 10^{4} mock datasets in which the SNIa have the same redshift distribution and magnitude uncertainties as DES or DES + legacy. The progressive loss of low-redshift SNIa does lead to a slight bias in the recovered H 0 H_{0} due to our cosmographic expansion not being a perfect representation of Λ \Lambda CDM, but our redshift-floor sweep with mock data indicates that the lack of low-redshift coverage only biases our results upwards by 1 ​ σ 1\sigma (Figure 16 ). The sharp rise in H 0 H_{0} with z floor z_{\mathrm{floor}} evident in the real data (Figure 5 ) is thus unlikely to arise in Λ \Lambda CDM due to random scatter and extrapolation error. We suggest instead that it is due to systematics with the legacy SNIa, as discussed in Section 5.2 . Our results are based on a convergent cosmographic expansion over the relevant redshift range (Eq. 7 ). This leaves the possibility of biases in the inferred H 0 H_{0} coming from the choice of polynomial order (Appendix B ). Using a higher order than our baseline of k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 and restricting to SNIa from DES gives a lower H 0 H_{0} compatible with H 0 SPA H_{0}^{\mathrm{SPA}} , albeit with a lower evidence and a larger uncertainty that also admits consistency with SH0ES. We stress that k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 is the order preferred by the Bayesian evidence for DES (Eq. 10 ), whereas for DES + legacy the evidence cannot distinguish it from k max = 5 k_{\max}=5 , so we use k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 throughout for consistency. We can avoid the choice of order altogether by averaging over the orders with their posterior probabilities (see Appendix B.2 ). This BMA approach gives H 0 = 74.77 ± 4.83 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=74.77\pm 4.83\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} for DES, which is in 1.56 ​ σ 1.56\sigma tension with SPA, down from 3.13 ​ σ 3.13\sigma for k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 . The high H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} therefore depends on the order of the expansion. Once we propagate its uncertainty through to H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} , we find that DES alone does not determine H 0 H_{0} precisely enough to rediscover the Hubble tension, even though the central BMA value lies much closer to SH0ES than to SPA. Our Bayesian model comparison shows that the data do not strongly favour or disfavour a phenomenological late-time solution to the Hubble tension (Eq. 12 ) if we do not consider any local H 0 H_{0} anchor (see Table 3 ). The exp model becomes strongly preferred only if we add the SH0ES anchor on H 0 H_{0} and either exclude the legacy SNIa altogether or include them only with an arbitrary recalibration relative to the DES SNIa. For the DES + legacy case without recalibration, the legacy data taken at face value resist a high H 0 H_{0} consistent with SH0ES. A late-time solution to the Hubble tension is highly unlikely only insofar as the legacy SNIa are accurately calibrated relative to DES SNIa. The phenomenological exp model converges to Λ \Lambda CDM rapidly due to its very low z 1 z_{1} parameter (Eq. 12 ). This raises a fine-tuning issue concerning why the expansion history should closely follow Λ \Lambda CDM for many Gyr and only recently start to appreciably deviate from it. One possibility is that the Hubble tension might instead be solved through outflow from a local underdensity or void ( Haslbauer, Banik and Kroupa, 2020 ; Banik and Kalaitzidis, 2025 ; Banik, Nájera and Desmond, 2026c ) . This scenario requires enhanced structure growth on ≳ 100 \ga 100 Mpc scales to form a sufficiently large and deep void ( Banik et al., 2026a , for a review, see) . In this context, faster convergence to Λ \Lambda CDM would indicate a smaller void, which if anything poses a less serious fine-tuning argument because the required adjustment to Λ \Lambda CDM structure growth would be more modest. We explore this possibility by using a log-uniform prior on z 1 z_{1} , which in the context of a void model is related to the void size (Section 4.5.1 ). Since this is not known a priori, a scale-invariant prior may be more appropriate. The results do not change much, with the DES + SH0ES case preferring z 1 ≈ 0.03 z_{1}\approx 0.03 and A ≈ 8 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 A\approx 8\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} regardless of whether we use a uniform prior on z 1 z_{1} or ln ⁡ z 1 \ln z_{1} . Even so, our prior on A A bounds both values (Section 4.5.1 ), so z 1 ≈ 0.03 z_{1}\approx 0.03 cannot be read as a measurement of the size of a void. The different tests presented in this work paint a coherent picture: combining DES SNIa with DESI DR2 BAO assuming the Planck r d r_{\rm d} does not disfavour a late-time solution to the Hubble tension. This conclusion is not as robust as one would like given the limited coverage of DES at low redshift, requiring an extrapolation to reach the present epoch and thus predict H 0 H_{0} . This can in principle be overcome by including legacy SNIa, which reach down to z = 0.025 z=0.025 , largely eliminating the extrapolation uncertainty. This completely changes the picture, now strongly disfavouring a late-time solution. If the legacy SNIa are accurate, the Hubble tension is unlikely to be solved at late times. However, we present several empirical arguments for systematics with the legacy SNIa -- at least when recalibrated onto the DECam passbands, which they were not originally observed in. 1 1 1 In principle, the lack of low-redshift DES coverage and difficulties combining photometric systems can both be avoided if we take the opposite approach of considering only the SNIa in a legacy survey. The problem then becomes the rather shallow survey limit, which precludes calibration via the IDL. This prevents a definitive assessment of whether the Hubble tension should be solved at early or late times.

sections.heading: 5.2 Systematics with the legacy SNIa
sections.text: The results in Section 4.7 suggest that the legacy SNIa are offset from the homogeneous DES sample by Δ ​ M legacy = 0.0646 ± 0.0391 \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}=0.0646\pm 0.0391 mag, a 1.65 ​ σ 1.65\sigma offset that shows no dependence on redshift and at most a weak dependence on which legacy survey the SNIa come from. Importantly, the legacy SNIa already pull the predicted H 0 H_{0} downwards when we include only the 10 that overlap in redshift with DES ( z = 0.073 z=0.073 –0.087; see Section 4.4 ). Since SNIa at the same redshift must trace the same expansion history, a late-time departure from Λ \Lambda CDM would not be expected to make them disagree, whereas a difference in calibration would. This is why we consider the more plausible explanation to be a systematic in the legacy SNIa, in particular with how they were recalibrated onto the DECam passbands or in their selection functions. We now discuss how such an offset could arise. Since SNIa are transients, legacy SNIa cannot be observed on a modern filter system, making it difficult to prove how bright the legacy SNIa would have appeared to a modern instrument that is sensitive enough to reach high enough redshift to allow calibration via the IDL. Although white dwarfs and other standard stars were observed on both filter systems, the relative calibration for SNIa may be different due to the very different SED. In particular, there can be an interplay between the filter transmission curve and SNIa spectral features, but this would not occur in the relatively featureless spectrum of a white dwarf. As a result, nm-scale shifts in the wavelength centring of each filter might conceivably matter more for SNIa than for white dwarfs. There can also be saturation effects when a modern instrument like DECam is used to observe standard stars that were easily observable on a typically less sensitive legacy instrument. This can be mitigated by reducing the DES exposure time, but that can create its own uncertainties with shutter timing. Moreover, there can be non-linearities in the response of a charge-coupled device (CCD) to incident light. While not as common a concern today, non-linear CCD response might be more of an issue with legacy surveys. Since the calibration standards are typically brighter than legacy SNIa at z > 0.025 z>0.025 , a calibration valid for the former may not be valid for the latter at < 0.1 <0.1 mag accuracy. Another important concern is how the host galaxy contribution is subtracted from the SNIa light curve. For results to be comparable between two surveys, the host galaxy subtraction should be done similarly, but procedures can change over the decades and legacy instruments typically had a poorer angular resolution. Since SNIa often occur in relatively crowded parts of a galaxy, angular resolution can affect the estimated background light at the SNIa sky position. Differences in the background subtraction strategy can alter the SNIa colour and light curve shape, which would then affect its standardised magnitude via the Tripp formula ( Tripp, 1998 ) . We note that systematics with recalibrating legacy SNIa onto the DECam filters would have little impact on the Hubble tension. While this relies on SNIa at z < 0.15 z<0.15 which do mostly come from legacy surveys, recalibration onto DECam filters is not required. Instead, the same legacy surveys were in many cases able to find SNIa in a sufficiently nearby host galaxy that its distance can be measured using Cepheids, TRGB, SBF, or other well-established techniques. This allows a measurement of the absolute SNIa magnitude on the relevant photometric system, from which one can derive H 0 H_{0} ( Riess et al., 2022 ) . We demonstrate this with a short reanalysis of SH0ES where we refit their public SH0ES data vector and covariance with a separate absolute magnitude M s M_{s} for each SNIa survey s s instead of assuming a common M s ​ ∀ s M_{s}\forall s . Two surveys (SDSS and PS1MD) contain no SNIa in a Cepheid host and share no SNIa with any calibrated survey, so their M s M_{s} is unconstrained. We therefore remove their 57 Hubble-flow light curves. Since the SH0ES model is linear in its parameters, a generalised least-squares fit gives the exact posterior. Applying this to SNIa from the remaining surveys changes H 0 H_{0} from the published 73.04 ± 1.04 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 73.04\pm 1.04\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} to 72.85 ± 1.04 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 72.85\pm 1.04\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , which is still 5.1 ​ σ 5.1\sigma above H 0 SPA H_{0}^{\mathrm{SPA}} . Moreover, the data show no preference for survey-specific offsets. The 13 remaining surveys need at least one absolute magnitude, so a separate M s M_{s} per survey adds a further 12 parameters. Across the 297 remaining light curves (77 in Cepheid hosts and 220 in the Hubble flow), these extra M s M_{s} parameters improve χ 2 \chi^{2} by just 7.5, which is less than the improvement of about 12 expected from fitting noise alone. This confirms that even if we apply our baseline methodology of doubting cross-calibrations between different filters, the Hubble tension stays virtually unchanged. Our results therefore lend credence to a late-time solution to the Hubble tension without providing any reason to doubt its significance. On the contrary, we avoid the local distance ladder altogether and still obtain a high H 0 H_{0} that lies > 3 ​ σ >3\sigma above the CMB-derived Λ \Lambda CDM prediction for our baseline k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 ( 1.56 ​ σ 1.56\sigma for the BMA), yet is in good agreement with SH0ES and other local H 0 H_{0} anchors (Section 3.3 ). While there could be deficiencies in the standard distance ladder and/or our implementation of the homogeneous DES IDL, the good agreement between the H 0 H_{0} values from these quite distinct approaches lends support to the idea that a modification to the late-time expansion history (or redshift gradient) is responsible for both techniques showing an excess over H 0 SPA H_{0}^{\mathrm{SPA}} . The above results are in our configuration A, which depends on the tight 100 prior on r d r_{\rm d} . This relies on the validity of Λ \Lambda CDM prior to recombination. We relax this assumption in configuration B, which therefore does not assume a late-time solution to the Hubble tension and does not use the CMB or other high-redshift data. Instead, r d r_{\rm d} is calibrated using cosmology-independent CC datasets, which could in principle lead to a low r d r_{\rm d} characteristic of an early-time solution. Using DES SNIa and assuming Λ \Lambda CDM at late times, this approach yields r d = 148.48 ± 8.39 r_{\rm d}=148.48\pm 8.39 cMpc and H 0 = 69.0 − 4.6 + 3.4 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=69.0^{+3.4}_{-4.6}\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} (Table 2 ). The H 0 H_{0} constraint is only 1.2 ​ σ 1.2\sigma below SH0ES ( Breuval et al., 2024 ) . We note that an early-time solution by definition preserves Λ \Lambda CDM behaviour at late times, so it must reproduce the BAO constraint on H 0 ​ r d = 10154 ± 73 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}r_{\rm d}=10154\pm 73\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} ( DESI Collaboration, 2025 ) . The SH0ES value of H 0 H_{0} ( Breuval et al., 2024 ) then requires r d = 138.8 ± 1.9 r_{\rm d}=138.8\pm 1.9 cMpc. Our result is 1.1 ​ σ 1.1\sigma above this, mirroring the behaviour in H 0 H_{0} . This is to be expected given the tight BAO constraint on H 0 ​ r d H_{0}r_{\rm d} . Including the legacy SNIa has little impact on this result. While our configuration B results for H 0 H_{0} and r d r_{\rm d} lie closer to the 100 values than to those required by an early-time solution, such a scenario is still in good agreement with SNIa + BAO + CC. This is mainly due to the weak constraining power of CC. However, early-time solutions face other difficulties, as discussed in Section 1 .

sections.heading: 5.3 Comparison with the literature
sections.text: The IDL has a record of giving a low H 0 H_{0} similar to 100 . Anchoring the BAO scale to a standard early-Universe sound horizon and constraining H 0 H_{0} from the expansion history shape mapped by SNIa to reach low redshift, Aubourg et al. (2015) first obtained a low H 0 H_{0} from the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (BOSS) BAO, while Macaulay et al. (2019) predicted H 0 = 67.8 ± 1.3 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=67.8\pm 1.3\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} with an IDL based on SNIa in DES-SN3YR. The more recent analyses of Camilleri et al. (2025) and Ling et al. (2025) , which combine DES-SN5YR with DESI DR1 and DR2 BAO, respectively, return a comparably low H 0 H_{0} . Across three generations of SNIa samples and two BAO surveys, the IDL gives H 0 ≈ 67 H_{0}\approx 67 – 68 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 68\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} . This is near the 100 value, but well below the local value from SH0ES ( Breuval et al., 2024 ) . Our DES + legacy result is very much in line with these previous results. Sabogal et al. (2026) recently formalised this obstacle as a “shape wall”. If pre-recombination physics is standard, the sound horizon and the angular acoustic scale are fixed, so a late-time solution can raise H 0 H_{0} only by changing the shape of the expansion history E ⁡ ( z ) E(z) . Relative SNIa distances combined with BAO constrain this shape tightly enough to restrict any such increase in H 0 H_{0} to only a few percent, well short of the ≈ 9 % \approx 9\% needed to reach H 0 SH0ES H_{0}^{\mathrm{SH0ES}} . This makes the IDL a challenge for late-time solutions to the Hubble tension. The closest analysis to ours in both data and method is that of Popovic and Sullivan (2026) , who run a cosmographic IDL on the same DES-Dovekie catalogue ( Popovic et al., 2026 ) , calibrating the SNIa using DESI DR2 and a standard CMB sound horizon. Those authors conclude that the IDL leaves little room for a late-time resolution. There is a methodological difference with our approach in that their cosmographic expansion is a polynomial in z z ( Visser, 2004 , following) , whereas we expand in a ~ ≡ z / ( 1 + z ) \widetilde{a}\equiv z/(1+z) ( Cattoën and Visser, 2007 ) , which can be thought of as the lookback scale factor 1 − a 1-a (Eq. 7 ). This matters at high redshift because a series expansion in z z has a radius of convergence of | z | < 1 \lvert z\rvert<1 . This is insufficient to handle DES given it has SNIa out to z ≈ 1.14 z\approx 1.14 , while DESI DR2 BAO measurements go out to z = 2.33 z=2.33 . An expansion in z z is therefore not a model-independent cosmographic expansion, but rather a polynomial model for H ⁡ ( z ) H(z) , with asymptotic behaviour set by k max k_{\max} . Eq. 5 of Popovic and Sullivan (2026) shows that those authors use k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 , implying an asymptotic H ∝ z 4 H\propto z^{4} behaviour – far steeper than the z 3 / 2 z^{3/2} behaviour predicted by Λ \Lambda CDM (Eq. 9 ). Their recovered H 0 H_{0} is thus tied to this specific polynomial ansatz for H ⁡ ( z ) H(z) rather than providing a model-independent estimate of H 0 H_{0} . Our parametrisation has a ~ < 1 ​ ∀ z \widetilde{a}<1\>\forall\>z , keeping the expansion convergent throughout. Another problem with the Popovic and Sullivan (2026) analysis is their use of different polynomials for H ⁡ ( z ) H(z) and D L ​ ( z ) D_{\rm L}(z) , making the analysis internally inconsistent since c / H ⁡ ( z ) c/H(z) must be integrated to obtain D M ​ ( z ) D_{\rm M}(z) and thus D L ​ ( z ) D_{\rm L}(z) . While using two separate polynomials is a good approximation at low redshift, it is not accurate given the DES and DESI range of redshifts (up to z = 2.33 z=2.33 ). Leaving aside these problems with a cosmographic expansion in z z , once we adopt the same methodology as Popovic and Sullivan (2026) and use the same data, the results agree: by using the same likelihood, we recover their results within ≈ 1 ​ σ \approx 1\sigma . Those authors report a nominal H 0 = 66.82 ± 0.74 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=66.82\pm 0.74\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} from a sample that includes the low-redshift legacy SNIa. This corresponds to our DES + legacy configuration, for which we obtain H 0 = 67.98 ± 0.69 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=67.98\pm 0.69\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} . These results are consistent at the 1.15 ​ σ 1.15\sigma C.L. and disfavour a late-time solution. Popovic and Sullivan (2026) argue that moving the inferred H 0 H_{0} from 67 to 73 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 73\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} demands a magnitude gradient d ​ M DES / d ​ z ≈ 0.2 \mathrm{d}M_{\mathrm{DES}}/\mathrm{d}z\approx 0.2 mag, with a flat Λ \Lambda CDM fit after such a shift returning Ω m ≈ 0.23 \Omega_{\rm m}\approx 0.23 , a value that is 10 ​ σ 10\sigma discrepant with other probes. However, this argument presupposes the validity of Λ \Lambda CDM, so any departure from its predicted shape for the expansion history must be absorbed by Ω m \Omega_{\mathrm{m}} . Since a late-time solution requires a different shape, assuming the validity of Λ \Lambda CDM at late times produces a circular argument. A late-time solution is by definition a departure from the Λ \Lambda CDM background, so inferring a non-standard effective Ω m \Omega_{\mathrm{m}} under an imposed Λ \Lambda CDM fit is the expected signature of that departure rather than a falsification of it. Moreover, the probes against which a late-time solution was judged themselves assume a Λ \Lambda CDM background, whose adequacy is precisely the question at issue. Most importantly, their nominal sample relies on the legacy SNIa, so their exclusion of late-time solutions holds only if the legacy SNIa are accurate. The legacy “rung” has been contested in the literature, with several convergent lines of evidence pointing to a bias here. Within the DES-Dovekie compilation including the legacy SNIa, we measure a relative offset of Δ ​ M legacy = 0.0646 ± 0.0391 \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}=0.0646\pm 0.0391 mag between the legacy SNIa and DES (Section 4.7 ). This reproduces the offset first reported by Efstathiou (2025) from an independent comparison between Pantheon+ and DES. Watkins et al. (2026) reach the same conclusion from yet another angle, finding the high-redshift DES SNIa are well described by flat Λ \Lambda CDM, but the low-redshift sample is systematically offset by ≈ 0.05 \approx 0.05 mag. They attribute this to unresolved systematics in the low-redshift sample rather than to new physics. The interpretation of the offset is contested: Vincenzi et al. (2025) reproduce the difference with Pantheon+ but attribute about 43% of it to improvements made to the DES-SN5YR analysis of intrinsic scatter and host galaxy properties. Since each DES release also reanalysed the legacy SNIa, improvements to the pipeline can have a non-negligible impact on the legacy SNIa, which after all can only be used alongside DES once they are recalibrated onto the DECam passbands and appropriate corrections are made for survey selection and other effects. The revision to host galaxy masses is larger for the legacy SNIa than for DES hosts, so these improvements mainly affect the former. Vincenzi et al. (2025) attribute a further ≈ 38 % \approx 38\% of the difference with Pantheon+ to different selection functions for the DES subsets entering the two compilations, causing different bias corrections and thereby making a direct object-to-object comparison misleading ( Efstathiou, 2025 ) . We find an offset in the same direction. The cause is not important for our purposes as the impact on H 0 H_{0} is the same regardless. Our analysis in Section 4.7 suggests that around 3 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 3\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} of the gap between H 0 SH0ES H_{0}^{\mathrm{SH0ES}} and H 0 DES + legacy H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES+legacy}} is caused by an offset of Δ ​ M legacy = 0.0646 ± 0.0391 \Delta M_{\rm legacy}=0.0646\pm 0.0391 mag in the legacy SNIa (Eq. 22 ). Further support for a systematic offset with the legacy SNIa is that such an offset would most plausibly come from conversion between photometric systems, in which case we might expect the offset to be survey-specific. Given the legacy SNIa largely come from two sources (Foundation and CfA/CSP), we can infer separate offsets for these. Our results in Figure 7 show only weak ( 1.0 ​ σ 1.0\sigma ) evidence for a difference between these two components of the legacy rung. Furthermore, when we sample all the cosmological parameters together with two legacy magnitude offsets, the posterior on H 0 H_{0} remains virtually unchanged compared to having only one global offset for all the legacy SNIa. This shows that even if SNIa from Foundation and CfA/CSP require separate offsets, there is minimal impact on the predicted H 0 H_{0} . The legacy SNIa also explain why our conclusions differ from those of Bansal and Huterer (2026) . Those authors ask whether a modification to only the late-time expansion history can simultaneously fit H 0 SH0ES H_{0}^{\mathrm{SH0ES}} , the DESI BAO data, and relative SNIa distances, finding that this requires a sharp step in M SNIa M_{\mathrm{SNIa}} at z ≲ 0.01 z\la 0.01 (Section 1 ). Their analysis rests on Pantheon+, which contains the same low-redshift legacy surveys as our DES + legacy configuration. In that configuration, we reach the same verdict: H 0 DES + legacy H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES+legacy}} lies 4.69 ​ σ 4.69\sigma below H 0 SH0ES H_{0}^{\mathrm{SH0ES}} . However, we reach a different verdict with the homogeneous DES sample, in which a single survey, filter set, and selection function remove the need to cross-calibrate between surveys. In this case, H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} lies only 1.03 ​ σ 1.03\sigma above H 0 SH0ES H_{0}^{\mathrm{SH0ES}} , while allowing the legacy SNIa to be recalibrated by Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} leaves H 0 H_{0} only 0.99 ​ σ 0.99\sigma below H 0 SH0ES H_{0}^{\mathrm{SH0ES}} . The answer to the question posed by Bansal and Huterer (2026) therefore hinges on the legacy SNIa, whose conversion onto the DECam passbands is precisely where a low-redshift step in M SNIa M_{\mathrm{SNIa}} could arise without any new physics. Even so, our DES-only result is not completely free of the legacy SNIa. We caution that although we have removed the legacy SNIa from our main analysis, they are still used to train the algorithm used to fit DES light curves and extract the most relevant parameters. To our knowledge, no analysis of DES has yet hidden the legacy magnitude–redshift relation from this training, so the size of the effect is currently unknown. This makes it important to reanalyse DES events using an algorithm trained without the use of legacy SNIa apparent magnitudes, perhaps restricting to only the light curve shape to help with event classification. Such a reanalysis would give the cleanest answer to the question posed by Bansal and Huterer (2026) using only existing data. The issue of possible systematics with the legacy SNIa can be addressed through reanalyses like that described above, but the best way is probably through a homogeneous SNIa compilation that reaches a lower redshift than DES, which has little sensitivity at z ≲ 0.2 z\la 0.2 (though the closest SNIa it contains is at z = 0.073 z=0.073 ). The crucial evidence will come from ongoing campaigns like the Dark Energy Bedrock All-Sky Supernova (DEBASS) program ( Sherman et al., 2026 ) , the Asteroid Terrestrial-impact Last Alert System ( Marlin et al., 2026 , ATLAS; see the TITAN sample of) , the Young Supernova Experiment ( Jones et al., 2021 ; Aleo et al., 2023 , YSE;) , and the Zwicky Transient Facility ( Rigault et al., 2025 , ZTF;) . Of particular importance is DEBASS given it uses DECam, the same instrument used for DES. This will simplify the treatment of any relative calibration offset, though selection effects for DEBASS differ from DES and must be handled with care.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusions
sections.text: We constructed the IDL using the homogeneous DES-Dovekie catalogue of uncalibrated SNIa ( Popovic et al., 2026 ) and DESI DR2 BAO ( DESI Collaboration, 2025 ) . We used a cosmographic expansion in the lookback scale factor a ~ ≡ z / ( 1 + z ) = 1 − a \widetilde{a}\equiv z/(1+z)=1-a . We adopted a polynomial order of k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 , the order preferred by the Bayesian evidence for DES, and checked our results against the BMA over k max = 2 k_{\max}=2 –6. Our baseline analysis uses SNIa from DES alone ( z ∈ [ 0.073 , 1.14 ] z\in[0.073,1.14] ). This excludes legacy SNIa that are normally included in the catalogue. Our main analyses calibrate the BAO assuming Λ \Lambda CDM at early times through a Planck prior on r d r_{\rm d} ( 100 ) . The calibrated BAO results then allow a calibration of SNIa via the Etherington relation. We also conducted analyses where we relaxed the r d r_{\rm d} prior and instead constrained it using CC ( Moresco et al., 2022 ) . In both configurations, we included the historical legacy SNIa as an optional extension ( z ∈ [ 0.025 , 0.087 ] z\in[0.025,0.087] ). This allows us to assess their impact on the IDL and test them for possible systematics. Our baseline result with the Planck prior on r d r_{\rm d} is H 0 = 76.25 ± 2.87 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=76.25\pm 2.87\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , which is fully consistent with SH0ES ( Breuval et al., 2024 ) but in 3.04 ​ σ 3.04\sigma tension with 100 and 3.13 ​ σ 3.13\sigma tension with SPT-3G Collaboration (2026) . This tension is specific to our baseline order. Averaging over k max = 2 k_{\max}=2 –6 with weights given by the Bayesian evidence gives H 0 = 74.77 ± 4.83 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=74.77\pm 4.83\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , which reduces the tension with H 0 SPA H_{0}^{\mathrm{SPA}} to 1.56 ​ σ 1.56\sigma because the fifth order predicts a lower H 0 H_{0} with a larger uncertainty. Excluding DES SNIa at low redshifts does not much affect the predicted H 0 H_{0} , which for k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 remains stable at a value far above H 0 SPA H_{0}^{\mathrm{SPA}} out to the highest considered z floor z_{\mathrm{floor}} of 0.3 (Figure 5 ). Adding the legacy SNIa reduces H 0 H_{0} to 67.98 ± 0.69 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 67.98\pm 0.69\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , only mildly above Planck and H 0 SPA H_{0}^{\mathrm{SPA}} but 4.69 ​ σ 4.69\sigma below SH0ES ( Breuval et al., 2024 ) . Using the BMA instead changes H 0 H_{0} to 66.61 ± 1.18 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 66.61\pm 1.18\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} and the tension with SH0ES to 4.50 ​ σ 4.50\sigma . The accuracy of the legacy SNIa is therefore central to assessing whether the IDL is compatible with a high H 0 H_{0} , and thus whether the Hubble tension can be solved at late times. Replacing the 100 constraint on r d r_{\rm d} with CC data increases the uncertainty due to the much weaker constraints on r d r_{\rm d} , giving H 0 = 75.7 ± 5.3 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=75.7\pm 5.3\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} with DES and 67.6 ± 3.6 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 67.6\pm 3.6\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} with DES + legacy ( 74.1 ± 6.3 74.1\pm 6.3 and 66.2 ± 4.0 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 66.2\pm 4.0\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} for the BMA). The central values are similar to the corresponding analyses with the Planck r d r_{\rm d} prior, but the results are far less precise. We therefore focus only on results with the Planck r d r_{\rm d} prior in what follows. To see if the Δ ​ H 0 = 8.27 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 \Delta H_{0}=8.27\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} gap between our results with DES and DES + legacy can arise in Λ \Lambda CDM, we set up mocks where we generated simulated Dovekie and DESI DR2 catalogues sampled from Λ \Lambda CDM with the SPA parameters that best fit the CMB ( SPT-3G Collaboration, 2026 ) . Only 1.24% of our 10 4 10^{4} mocks exceed the observed value for Δ ​ H 0 ≡ H 0 DES − H 0 DES + legacy = 8.27 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 \Delta H_{0}\equiv H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}}-H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES+legacy}}=8.27\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} (Appendix D ). The BMA gives a similar gap of 8.16 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 8.16\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , although our mocks are analysed only at k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 . Assuming the expansion history has a shape similar to that in Λ \Lambda CDM, the high observed Δ ​ H 0 \Delta H_{0} is thus unlikely to arise from random errors and systematic uncertainties in extrapolating our cosmographic expansion from the DES range ( z = 0.073 z=0.073 –1.14) down to z → 0 z\to 0 . We suggest instead that the unusually high Δ ​ H 0 \Delta H_{0} is driven by systematics with the legacy SNIa, as discussed below. We find a consistent calibration of M DES ≈ − 19.38 M_{\mathrm{DES}}\approx-19.38 for all polynomial orders with appreciable posterior weight ( k max ≥ 4 k_{\max}\geq 4 ), regardless of the r d r_{\rm d} prior. With the Planck prior on r d r_{\rm d} , this is in 4.2 4.2 – 4.3 ​ σ 4.3\sigma tension with the SH0ES Cepheid-based calibration of M B = − 19.253 ± 0.027 M_{B}=-19.253\pm 0.027 ( Riess et al., 2022 ) . However, we must bear in mind that SH0ES standardises SNIa into the rest-frame Johnson B B -band, whereas DES operates in DECam passbands. Furthermore, Pantheon+ ( Scolnic et al., 2022 ) combines different surveys with their own zero-points, which might have systematic offsets between them. We therefore argue that the tension between M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} from the IDL and M B M_{B} from Cepheid calibration does not necessarily represent the well-known Hubble tension. Instead, it could in principle be explained by differences in the passbands and relative calibration offsets. We test the feasibility of a late-time solution to the Hubble tension using the phenomenological exp model (Eq. 12 ). This provides a flexible description of a late-time solution to the Hubble tension through an extra contribution to H ⁡ ( z ) H(z) that enhances the late-time acceleration ( Nájera et al., 2026 ) . We found that the data are agnostic as to whether this model is preferred over Λ \Lambda CDM based on the Bayesian evidence. Since our results prefer a high H 0 H_{0} despite assuming the Planck prior on r d r_{\rm d} , we can include local H 0 H_{0} anchors into our analysis. If we add three H 0 H_{0} anchors that are not based on SNIa ( Mukherjee et al., 2021 ; Jensen et al., 2025 ; Vogl et al., 2025 ) , we find that the Hubble tension cannot realistically be solved for the DES + legacy case as H 0 = 67.66 ± 1.01 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=67.66\pm 1.01\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} . This changes when restricting to DES SNIa, since now H 0 = 70.00 − 0.98 + 4.78 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=70.00^{+4.78}_{-0.98}\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , which would substantially reduce the Hubble tension at late times and is preferred over Λ \Lambda CDM by the Bayesian evidence (Table 3 ). We note that SH0ES would measure only H 0 win = 70.23 ± 0.99 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}^{\rm win}=70.23\pm 0.99\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} in this model, 2.25 ​ σ 2.25\sigma below the published value, because much of the excess expansion rate lies below the SH0ES Hubble-flow window. The preference reaches around 11 nats if we use instead the strong SH0ES anchor on the local H 0 H_{0} and exclude the legacy SNIa. It is therefore possible to solve, or at least significantly ameliorate, the Hubble tension at late times given DES, but such a scenario is highly disfavoured by DES + legacy, while including the legacy SNIa with arbitrary recalibration gives an intermediate result. Without the legacy SNIa, a successful solution has A ≈ 5 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 A\approx 5\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} ( H 0 ≈ 72.5 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}\approx 72.5\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} ) and z 1 < 0.086 z_{1}<0.086 at the 1 ​ σ 1\sigma C.L. when using the non-SNIa distance ladder anchors on H 0 H_{0} . Upon using the SH0ES anchor instead, this changes to A ≈ 8 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 A\approx 8\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} ( H 0 ≈ 75.5 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}\approx 75.5\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , or H 0 win ≈ 71.9 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}^{\rm win}\approx 71.9\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} ) and z 1 ≈ 0.03 z_{1}\approx 0.03 , though our prior on A A bounds both values. We also found that the Hubble tension cannot be solved with CPL, which always gives a low H 0 H_{0} value that cannot be combined with the local anchors. Neglecting them, we found that CPL is preferred over Λ \Lambda CDM only if the legacy SNIa are included at face value, but disfavoured by 1.79 nats if we exclude the legacy SNIa. These mixed results for the CPL model are a separate issue from whether there are deviations from Λ \Lambda CDM, as the data seem to suggest even without considering SNIa at all ( Banik et al., 2026c ) . A similar deviation is apparent in DES SNIa (Figure 2 ), though the underlying reason need not be evolving dark energy. Our baseline is to use only SNIa from the homogeneous DES catalogue, avoiding the need to convert between filter systems. To test if the legacy SNIa might be subject to systematics in either the original observations or in how they have been recalibrated onto the DES photometric system, we predict the legacy SNIa apparent magnitudes based on DES SNIa. Our results suggest a systematic offset of Δ ​ M legacy = 0.0646 ± 0.0391 \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}=0.0646\pm 0.0391 mag ( 1.65 ​ σ 1.65\sigma ) in the legacy SNIa ( 0.053 ± 0.040 0.053\pm 0.040 mag for the BMA), making them intrinsically fainter and thus closer to home. This is consistent with several previous studies ( Efstathiou, 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Ormondroyd et al., 2026 ; Watkins et al., 2026 ) . Applying this correction to align the legacy SNIa with the main DES sample, the inferred H 0 H_{0} rises to 71.03 ± 1.99 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 71.03\pm 1.99\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , only 0.99 ​ σ 0.99\sigma below SH0ES ( 69.50 ± 2.43 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 69.50\pm 2.43\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} and 1.43 ​ σ 1.43\sigma for the BMA). Since the legacy SNIa largely come from Foundation and CfA/CSP, we applied separate offsets to legacy SNIa depending on their source. This revealed weak evidence for the offset being survey-specific, but a similar approach showed no evidence that the offset depends on redshift (Figure 7 ). Intra-data systematics might therefore undermine the conventional conclusion that SNIa strongly disfavour a late-time solution to the Hubble tension. Ongoing homogeneous surveys like DEBASS ( Sherman et al., 2026 ) will provide a new low-redshift calibration using the same instrument as DES, which should resolve this issue. Preliminary DEBASS DR0.5 distances do not show the ≈ 0.05 \approx 0.05 mag offset reported here and by other authors between the legacy low-redshift sample as given in the Dovekie catalogue and the extrapolated DES distance–redshift relation ( Watkins et al., 2026 ) . Their study tentatively suggests that the legacy offset arises from systematics in the legacy SNIa or how they were analysed, but this needs to be checked with a larger sample of SNIa and careful treatment of selection effects in the underlying discovery surveys. Until then, we cannot confidently assert that the IDL rules out a late-time solution to the Hubble tension.
