sections.heading: Appendix A Alcock–Paczynski consistency
sections.text: The AP test is an internal consistency test that is independent of both r d r_{\rm d} and M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} (Section 3.4 ). In this test, we compute the AP ratio F AP ≡ D M / D H F_{\mathrm{AP}}\equiv D_{\mathrm{M}}/D_{\mathrm{H}} from the SNIa shape and compare it to the BAO results to check for mutual consistency. We implement this assuming only smoothness of the SNIa distance–redshift relation. We then compare the F AP F_{\mathrm{AP}} SNIa predictions to DESI DR2 BAO observations at three redshifts where there is a good overlap between the datasets. In particular, DESI DR2 measurements at effective redshifts of z = 0.510 z=0.510 , 0.706, and 0.934 lie within the range covered by the DES catalogue. We lack BAO measurements of F AP F_{\mathrm{AP}} at lower redshift, while the DES catalogue of SNIa runs out at higher redshift. Reaching the next DESI DR2 BAO measurement at z = 1.32 z=1.32 would entail an extrapolation beyond the highest redshift DES SNIa at z = 1.14 z=1.14 . This leads to much larger uncertainties, so we do not report the result.

sections.heading: A.1 Methodology
sections.text: Our predictions for F AP F_{\mathrm{AP}} are based on the same cosmographic expansion as used throughout this work (Eq. 7 ). Both distances follow directly from it in a flat metric: D M ​ ( z ) = c ​ ∫ 0 z d ​ z ~ H ⁡ ( z ~ ) , D H ​ ( z ) = c H ⁡ ( z ) . \displaystyle D_{\rm M}\left(z\right)~=~c\int_{0}^{z}\frac{\mathrm{d}\tilde{z}}{H(\tilde{z})}\,,\qquad D_{\rm H}\left(z\right)~=~\frac{c}{H\left(z\right)}\,. (23) This implies D H = D M ′ D_{\rm H}=D_{\rm M}^{\prime} , where a prime denotes differentiation with respect to z z . In other words, the Hubble distance reported by DESI (based on the redshift depth of the BAO ruler) is exactly the derivative of the comoving distance (based on the angular scale of the BAO ruler). The SNIa reconstruction tells us the shape of D M ​ ( z ) D_{\rm M}(z) , which we can differentiate to obtain D H D_{\rm H} and thus F AP F_{\mathrm{AP}} . Cancelling out the speed of light, we obtain that F AP ​ ( z ) ≡ D M ​ ( z ) D H ​ ( z ) = H ⁡ ( z ) ​ ∫ 0 z d ​ z ~ H ⁡ ( z ~ ) . \displaystyle F_{\rm AP}(z)~\equiv~\frac{D_{\rm M}(z)}{D_{\rm H}(z)}~=~H(z)\int_{0}^{z}\frac{\mathrm{d}\tilde{z}}{H(\tilde{z})}\,. (24) To relate these results to our cosmographic expansion (Eq. 7 ), we recall that H ⁡ ( z ) = H 0 ​ E ​ ( z ) H(z)=H_{0}\,E(z) , where E ⁡ ( z ) = 1 + ∑ k = 1 k max C k ​ ( 1 − a ) k , E ⁡ ( 0 ) = 1 . \displaystyle E(z)~=~1+\sum_{k=1}^{k_{\max}}C_{k}\left(1-a\right)^{k}\,,\qquad E(0)~=~1. (25) E ⁡ ( z ) E(z) carries the shape of the expansion history, while H 0 H_{0} carries its normalisation. Substituting into Eq. 24 , we obtain the following: F AP ​ ( z ) = H 0 ​ E ​ ( z ) ​ ∫ 0 z d ​ z ~ H 0 ​ E ​ ( z ~ ) = E ⁡ ( z ) ​ ∫ 0 z d ​ z ~ E ⁡ ( z ~ ) . \displaystyle F_{\rm AP}(z)~=~H_{0}\,E(z)\int_{0}^{z}\frac{\mathrm{d}\tilde{z}}{H_{0}\,E(\tilde{z})}~=~E(z)\int_{0}^{z}\frac{\mathrm{d}\tilde{z}}{E(\tilde{z})}\,. (26) This is the central equation for the AP test. Notice that since H 0 H_{0} cancels out identically, F AP F_{\mathrm{AP}} is a function only of the shape coefficients C k C_{k} . The SNIa absolute magnitude cancels for the same reason. SNIa constrain the apparent magnitude m ⁡ ( z ) = M DES + 5 ​ log 10 ​ [ ( 1 + z ) ​ D M ​ ( z ) / Mpc ] + 25 m(z)=M_{\mathrm{DES}}+5\log_{10}[(1+z)D_{\rm M}(z)/\rm{Mpc}]+25 . Since D M ∝ 1 / H 0 D_{\rm M}\propto 1/H_{0} at fixed shape, SNIa alone measure only the shape coefficients together with the single degenerate combination M DES − 5 ​ log 10 ​ H 0 M_{\mathrm{DES}}-5\log_{10}H_{0} , never M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} or H 0 H_{0} separately. Holding M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} fixed in the fit is therefore a gauge choice that leaves F AP F_{\rm AP} untouched, so the calibration does not enter the prediction. A similar cancellation occurs on the BAO side, since a BAO survey measures D M / r d D_{\rm M}/r_{\rm d} and D H / r d D_{\rm H}/r_{\rm d} , so forming the ratio F AP = ( D M / r d ) / ( D H / r d ) F_{\rm AP}=(D_{\rm M}/r_{\rm d})/(D_{\rm H}/r_{\rm d}) causes r d r_{\rm d} to divide out identically. This cancellation is also what makes the AP test precise despite the SNIa sample being uncalibrated. The large M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} uncertainty is entirely common-mode between the numerator and denominator in the AP ratio. This leaves only the error in the shape of the expansion history, which is constrained quite well by SNIa given their large number and wide redshift range. To predict BAO measurements of F AP F_{\mathrm{AP}} , we must by definition not consider the BAO data we are trying to predict. We therefore fit the cosmographic parameters using only SNIa, assuming some fixed M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} . Since the SNIa only reach z = 1.144 z=1.144 ( a ~ = 0.534 \widetilde{a}=0.534 ), we impose the prior envelope of Eq. 8 up to a ~ max = 0.534 \widetilde{a}_{\max}=0.534 rather than a ~ max = 0.70 \widetilde{a}_{\max}=0.70 in this fit, so that the prior constrains only the range with available data. We then evaluate Eq. 26 by numerical quadrature on the actual posterior draws returned by the sampler. Every draw therefore carries the full covariance of the C k C_{k} through to F AP F_{\mathrm{AP}} .

Assuming only that the SNIa distance–redshift relation is smooth, we fit H ⁡ ( z ) H(z) to the SNIa alone and predict F AP ≡ D M / D H F_{\rm AP}\equiv D_{\rm M}/D_{\rm H} at the three DESI BAO redshifts, all of which lie inside the SNIa range. The test carries no absolute calibration and no sound horizon assumption. Errors are evaluated on the actual posterior draws of the full SNIa catalogue. Table 6 lists the SNIa-predicted and DESI-measured F AP F_{\rm AP} at the three redshifts suitable for a comparison. We find that the SNIa constraint on the shape of the expansion history predicts AP ratios that are in good agreement with BAO measurements, as quantified by χ 2 = 6.33 \chi^{2}=6.33 for DES and 6.13 for DES + legacy. The corresponding p p -values of a higher χ 2 \chi^{2} are 9.7% and 10.5%, respectively. These mild levels of tension indicate that SNIa and BAO give consistent results for the shape of the expansion history. This agreement cannot be manufactured by a shared calibration, making it a genuine predictive success of the SNIa-derived shape. Despite the overall agreement, the SNIa prediction at z = 0.510 z=0.510 falls below DESI, with a pull from the latter of − 1.91 ​ σ -1.91\sigma for DES and − 1.98 ​ σ -1.98\sigma for DES + legacy. This feature is robust as it carries the same sign and size in both samples. It is also stable against the polynomial order and whether we bin the SNIa in redshift. Although a 2 ​ σ 2\sigma tension is not significant on its own, there is also a similar tension of the opposite sign at z = 0.934 z=0.934 , where the pull is + 2.03 ​ σ +2.03\sigma for DES and + 1.78 ​ σ +1.78\sigma for DES + legacy. However, there is negligible pull at z = 0.706 z=0.706 . The tension is further mitigated by correlations between F AP F_{\mathrm{AP}} predictions at different redshifts, which we account for when calculating the total χ 2 \chi^{2} . Figure 10: The shaded bands show the SNIa-shape mean prediction and 1 ​ σ 1\sigma uncertainty for the AP ratio F AP ≡ D M / D H F_{\rm AP}\equiv D_{\rm M}/D_{\rm H} using either DES (black) or DES + legacy (red). The dark blue squares with error bars show DESI DR2 measurements of F AP F_{\rm AP} . The F AP F_{\rm AP} values shown here are relative to the predicted value at that redshift in the SPA cosmology ( SPT-3G Collaboration, 2026 , Ω m = 0.3175 \Omega_{\rm m}=0.3175 ;) . Figure 10 shows the results relative to the fiducial SPA Λ \Lambda CDM prediction. Given that BAO measurements are in reasonable agreement with the SPA cosmology ( Banik et al., 2026c ) , the AP consistency between SNIa and BAO at z = 0.706 z=0.706 also indicates consistency here with the CMB-derived expectation in Λ \Lambda CDM. However, the BAO measurements of F AP F_{\mathrm{AP}} are not exactly in line with the CMB-calibrated Λ \Lambda CDM expectation (cf. figure 3 of Banik and Kalaitzidis, 2025 , which uses the Planck cosmology) . This causes the SNIa-derived predictions to be in less tension with the SPA cosmology than they are with DESI DR2 BAO – though even here the tension is modest. This justifies our approach of combining SNIa and BAO datasets using the Etherington relation. Despite the good overall agreement, SNIa and BAO appear to follow opposite trends in the ratio F AP / F AP Λ ​ CDM , SPA F_{\mathrm{AP}}/F^{\Lambda\rm{CDM,SPA}}_{\rm AP} , which decreases with redshift when using BAO but increases with redshift when using SNIa. However, this is not too significant, especially given that the SNIa prediction becomes rather uncertain at z > 0.8 z>0.8 , reducing the discrepancy with Λ \Lambda CDM. Since the tension is largely in the slope rather than the normalisation, we can try to quantify this by fitting F S ​ N / F B ​ A ​ O = α + β ⁡ ( z − z p ) F_{SN}/F_{BAO}=\alpha+\beta(z-z_{\rm p}) over the three DESI redshifts, where z p = 0.614 z_{\rm p}=0.614 is a suitable pivot redshift. This approach yields α − 1 = − 0.019 ± 0.021 \alpha-1=-0.019\pm 0.021 and β = 0.41 ± 0.18 \beta=0.41\pm 0.18 for DES, while α − 1 = − 0.023 ± 0.021 \alpha-1=-0.023\pm 0.021 and β = 0.38 ± 0.17 \beta=0.38\pm 0.17 for DES + legacy. The level is consistent with unity, but the shape tilt is around 2.2 ​ σ 2.2\sigma in both samples. This does not amount to a significant shape discrepancy because the three residuals give a total χ 2 = 6.33 \chi^{2}=6.33 for DES and 6.13 for DES + legacy, which means the tension cannot exceed 2.52 ​ σ 2.52\sigma even if it could be collapsed onto one parameter.

sections.heading: B.1 Results at a fixed order
sections.text: The results of our polynomial order sweep are shown in Tables 7 and 8 for configurations A and B, respectively. When using DES alone, the orders that give a high H 0 H_{0} are k max = 2 k_{\max}=2 and 4, but a second-order expansion does not fit the data: its evidence is 97 nats lower. By contrast, a fourth-order expansion fits the data well and is the most probable order. Even so, we cannot confidently say that the homogeneous DES IDL confirms the Hubble tension. This is because k max = 5 k_{\max}=5 gives H 0 = 68.52 ± 4.99 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=68.52\pm 4.99\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , which is compatible with both SPA and SH0ES. Importantly, it is also consistent with k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 at the 1.36 ​ σ 1.36\sigma C.L. The k max = 6 k_{\max}=6 result continues the trend towards lower and less precise H 0 H_{0} , which is now 63.30 ± 7.75 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 63.30\pm 7.75\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} . Increasing the polynomial order makes the model more flexible, so the uncertainty grows rapidly. The evidence weighs this flexibility against the improvement in the fit, thereby assigning 20% of the probability to k max = 5 k_{\max}=5 and < 1 <1 % to k max = 6 k_{\max}=6 . This means that the fifth order cannot be dismissed, which is why we average over the orders in Appendix B.2 . We note that while the specific weights assigned to k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 and 5 in the crucial DES-only case depend on the specific priors that we adopt (Table 1 ), χ min 2 \chi^{2}_{\min} improves by only 2.44 when going from the former to the latter. This is a very modest reduction given there are 1555 data points without the legacy SNIa, suggesting that any reasonable way of quantifying the Occam penalty would prefer k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 when using DES alone. The situation is less clear when using DES + legacy because then the improvement in χ min 2 \chi^{2}_{\min} is 9.26. Fortunately, the much better coverage of the legacy SNIa at low redshifts makes the choice of polynomial order far less relevant to the inferred cosmological parameters than for DES alone. k max If we replace our model-independent cosmographic expansion with flat Λ \Lambda CDM, the resulting χ min 2 \chi^{2}_{\min} is only 2.3 (1.3) above that at k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 for DES (DES + legacy). Since Λ \Lambda CDM has three fewer shape parameters than a quartic, this might suggest that Λ \Lambda CDM is the preferred description of the data. However, it is important to stress that the cosmographic expansion should not be seen as a rival model to Λ \Lambda CDM, but rather as a Taylor series which can describe any expansion history over a given redshift range. For this reason, we do not include Λ \Lambda CDM in the average over orders, none of which can exactly match Λ \Lambda CDM for finite k max k_{\max} . We instead compare Λ \Lambda CDM to specific alternatives using the Bayesian evidence in Section 4.5 . An important caveat to our results is that the intrinsic scatter term in the SNIa covariance is calibrated so that Λ \Lambda CDM provides an acceptable fit to the Hubble diagram, since the intrinsic scatter is difficult to obtain any other way. This means a reduced χ 2 \chi^{2} close to unity is not necessarily a success of the Λ \Lambda CDM model, justifying our focus on relative rather than absolute likelihoods.

sections.heading: B.2 Bayesian model average over the polynomial order
sections.text: Unless stated otherwise, values quoted in the main text use our baseline order of k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 . However, Appendix B.1 shows that we cannot confidently confirm the Hubble tension with the DES IDL because the predicted H 0 H_{0} depends on the order. Rather than selecting one order, we therefore treat k max k_{\max} as a discrete parameter and marginalise over it. The posterior of any quantity θ \theta is then the Bayesian model average P ⁡ ( θ | D ) = ∑ k max = 2 6 w ⁡ ( k max ) ​ P ​ ( θ | D , k max ) , \displaystyle P\left(\theta\,|\,D\right)~=~\sum_{k_{\max}=2}^{6}w\left(k_{\max}\right)\,P\left(\theta\,|\,D,k_{\max}\right), (27) where P ⁡ ( θ | D , k max ) P(\theta\,|\,D,k_{\max}) is the posterior at order k max k_{\max} and w ⁡ ( k max ) w(k_{\max}) is the weighted posterior probability of that order (Eq. 10 ). We quote the mean and standard deviation of Eq. 27 in the BMA rows in Tables 7 and 8 . Its variance is the probability-weighted average of the variances at each order plus the variance of their central values, so the average carries the uncertainty in the order as well as the uncertainty at each order. The only exception is q 0 q_{0} for DES + legacy, whose posterior is bimodal because k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 and 5 place it on opposite sides of zero. For these cases, we report the two intervals that together comprise the 1 ​ σ 1\sigma highest posterior density region. The first result to highlight is that the BMA is dominated by k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 and 5 in every case. The lower orders are excluded by at least 7.9 nats, while k max = 6 k_{\max}=6 never carries more than 2.1% of the probability. For DES, k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 carries 79.5% of the probability and k max = 5 k_{\max}=5 carries 19.8%. The weighted average gives H 0 = 74.77 ± 4.83 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=74.77\pm 4.83\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , compared with 76.43 ± 3.01 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 76.43\pm 3.01\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} for k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 . The central value hardly moves, but the uncertainty grows 1.6 × 1.6\times because the k max = 5 k_{\max}=5 posterior is centred 7.9 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 7.9\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} lower. When allowing recalibration of the legacy SNIa, k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 and 5 carry 45.7% and 52.3% of the probability, respectively, so their weighted average gives H 0 = 69.50 ± 2.43 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=69.50\pm 2.43\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} and Δ ​ M legacy = + 0.053 ± 0.040 \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}=+0.053\pm 0.040 mag. Configuration B ranks the orders in the same way, with k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 preferred for DES and k max = 5 k_{\max}=5 marginally preferred for DES + legacy (Table 8 ). The BMA changes the interpretation of the DES result more than that of any other sample. For DES alone, the H 0 H_{0} tension with SPA falls from 3.13 ​ σ 3.13\sigma at k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 to 1.56 ​ σ 1.56\sigma , though the result remains consistent with SH0ES at the 0.33 ​ σ 0.33\sigma C.L. This means that once we propagate the uncertainty in the order, DES alone does not determine H 0 H_{0} precisely enough to discriminate between SH0ES and SPA, even though its central value lies much closer to SH0ES. On the other hand, the conclusions on the legacy SNIa are robust. The averaged H 0 H_{0} for DES + legacy is 4.50 ​ σ 4.50\sigma below SH0ES, compared with 4.69 ​ σ 4.69\sigma at k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 , the small reduction arising from the larger uncertainty. Once the legacy SNIa are recalibrated, the average is consistent with SPA at the 0.94 ​ σ 0.94\sigma C.L. and with SH0ES at the 1.43 ​ σ 1.43\sigma C.L., which is only slightly worse than the 0.99 ​ σ 0.99\sigma tension with SH0ES for k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 . The recalibration also raises the averaged H 0 H_{0} by 2.9 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 2.9\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , which is similar to the ≈ 3 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 \approx 3\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} shift at k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 (Section 4.7 ). Thus, the averaged results confirm that a late-time solution to the Hubble tension remains possible insofar as we exclude or recalibrate the legacy SNIa. Unlike a least-squares fit, the evidence depends on the prior, so it is important to check how much the weights rely on it. Our prior is uniform over all expansion histories with 0 ≤ E ⁡ ( a ~ ) ≤ 2 + 7 ​ a ~ 0\leq E(\widetilde{a})\leq 2+7\widetilde{a} (Section 3.1 ). Halving the width of this band about the line E = 1 + 3.5 ​ a ~ E=1+3.5\widetilde{a} is a linear contraction in the C k C_{k} , so it divides the prior volume at order k k by exactly 2 k 2^{k} . Provided the posterior lies inside the narrower band, ln ⁡ Z \ln Z then rises by k ​ ln ⁡ 2 k\ln 2 , so the evidence ratio between consecutive orders shifts by ln ⁡ 2 ≈ 0.69 \ln 2\approx 0.69 in favour of the higher order (the Occam penalty is lower due to the narrower prior range). We find that at least 99% of the posterior lies inside the halved width band for every sample at k max ≥ 3 k_{\max}\geq 3 , so this shift applies almost exactly. Halving the band moves the DES weights at k max = 4 k_{\max}=4 and 5 from 0.80 and 0.20 to 0.65 and 0.33, respectively, while the DES + legacy weights shift from 0.25 and 0.73 to 0.14 and 0.82. However, the averaged H 0 H_{0} moves by at most 1.2 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 1.2\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} and is now 73.56 ± 5.60 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 73.56\pm 5.60\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} for DES, 66.41 ± 1.10 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 66.41\pm 1.10\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} for DES + legacy, and 69.05 ± 2.38 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 69.05\pm 2.38\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} with the legacy SNIa recalibrated. These lie 1.13 ​ σ 1.13\sigma above SPA, 4.85 ​ σ 4.85\sigma below SH0ES, and 1.63 ​ σ 1.63\sigma below SH0ES, respectively, so our conclusions are not driven by the width of the prior. This highlights the advantage of a prior on the normalised expansion history itself over independent priors on each C k C_{k} , whose widths are difficult to set but would nonetheless set the Occam penalty of every order separately.

The dotted orange lines mark H 0 H_{0} and q 0 q_{0} in flat Λ \Lambda CDM with the SPA parameters, whose small uncertainties are neglected here ( SPT-3G Collaboration, 2026 ) . If we include the legacy SNIa but allow them to be recalibrated relative to the main DES sample by Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} , we obtain results intermediate between the DES-only and DES + legacy cases. The bottom right panel shows that this is driven by a preference for Δ ​ M legacy > 0 \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}>0 , though it is probably ≲ 0.1 \la 0.1 mag. sections.heading: C.1 Late-time solutions
sections.text: In Section 4.5 , we tested whether two proposed phenomenological adjustments to Λ \Lambda CDM can alleviate the Hubble tension, bearing in mind their greater model flexibility. In what follows, we only consider the exp model (Eq. 12 ) because the CPL model predicts a low H 0 H_{0} and thus cannot be combined with local H 0 H_{0} anchors (Table 3 ). We first show the triangle plots for the analyses unconstrained by any local H 0 H_{0} anchor (Figure 13 ). As might be expected without any local anchor, the amplitude term A A is consistent with zero in all cases, though there is an interesting 1.3 ​ σ 1.3\sigma preference for A < 0 A<0 using DES + legacy. This is associated with a preference for lower H 0 H_{0} , making it even more difficult to solve the Hubble tension. If we allow recalibration of the legacy SNIa, the result is very similar to that using DES alone. Given the lack of preference for any excess H 0 H_{0} at all, the redshift scale of the excess ( z 1 z_{1} ) is largely unconstrained. Figure 13: Triangle plot for the exp model (Eq. 12 ), proposed as a late-time solution to the Hubble tension. Results are shown using SNIa from DES (black), DES + legacy (red), and DES + legacy with free Δ ​ M legacy \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}} (blue). No H 0 H_{0} anchors are considered here. As a result, the excess amplitude A A is consistent with zero and the redshift scale z 1 z_{1} is unconstrained. The dotted orange lines mark Ω m \Omega_{\rm m} and H 0 H_{0} in flat Λ \Lambda CDM with the SPA parameters, whose small uncertainties we neglect ( SPT-3G Collaboration, 2026 ) . We next show the triangle plots when adding a local H 0 H_{0} anchor (Figure 14 ). The top panel considers three anchors that do not involve SNIa, while the bottom panel uses the SH0ES anchor ( Breuval et al., 2024 ) . These anchors are in principle independent but are consistent with each other, allowing us to combine all four anchors. We refrain from doing so because the statistical power would be dominated by SH0ES. Our results show that z 1 z_{1} is not well constrained if we include the legacy SNIa, even if we allow them to be recalibrated. Excluding them leads to a tight upper limit on z 1 z_{1} . With the non-SNIa anchors, the z 1 z_{1} posterior is truncated at low values only by our prior floor of 0.001. However, when using DES + SH0ES without the legacy SNIa, the z 1 z_{1} posterior becomes sharply peaked and is not truncated by the prior on z 1 z_{1} . This peak does not measure z 1 z_{1} on its own, however. The SH0ES anchor constrains the product A ​ z 1 Az_{1} , and the peak sits where this ridge meets the upper edge of our prior on A A (Section 4.5.1 ). We therefore do not interpret z 1 ≈ 0.03 z_{1}\approx 0.03 as a property of a local void. Figure 14: Similar to Figure 13 , but including a local H 0 H_{0} anchor (Section 3.3.3 ). The top panel jointly uses the three anchors not including SNIa ( Jensen et al., 2025 ; Vogl et al., 2025 ; Mukherjee et al., 2021 ) . The bottom panel uses the SH0ES anchor ( Breuval et al., 2024 ) .

sections.heading: Appendix D Redshift-floor sweep in Λ \Lambda CDM mocks
sections.text: A central result of this paper is the difference in H 0 H_{0} and q 0 q_{0} depending on whether we consider DES or DES + legacy (Figure 4 ). Our result for H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} involves extrapolating over the poorly covered regime at z ≲ 0.2 z\la 0.2 to reach z → 0 z\to 0 . The resulting extrapolation uncertainty can be mitigated by adding legacy SNIa, which reach down to z = 0.025 z=0.025 and thereby yield a far more precise H 0 DES + legacy H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES+legacy}} . However, the result differs from H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} . To determine how plausible it is that H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} exceeds H 0 DES + legacy H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES+legacy}} by the observed Δ ​ H 0 = 8.27 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 \Delta H_{0}=8.27\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , we set up mock datasets assuming flat Λ \Lambda CDM with the SPA parameters based on the latest CMB observations ( SPT-3G Collaboration, 2026 , H 0 = 67.19 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=67.19\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} and Ω m = 0.3175 \Omega_{\rm m}=0.3175 ;) and the 100 sound horizon of r d = 147.05 r_{\rm d}=147.05 cMpc. We neglect uncertainties in these parameters because we expect larger uncertainties from the SNIa, especially for DES alone due to the need to extrapolate to the present epoch. We generate mock BAO and SNIa data at the same redshifts as the real data, ensuring that every mock realisation of Λ \Lambda CDM with the SPA parameters has the same redshift coverage as the real data. We calculate ‘true’ SNIa apparent magnitudes in the assumed cosmology as follows: m SNIa Λ ​ CDM = M DES + 5 ​ log 10 ​ [ ( 1 + z hel ) ​ D M , Λ ​ CDM ​ ( z HD ) ] + 25 , \displaystyle m_{\rm SNIa}^{\Lambda\mathrm{CDM}}=M_{\mathrm{DES}}+5\log_{10}\left[\left(1+z_{\rm hel}\right)\,D_{\mathrm{M},\Lambda{\rm CDM}}(z_{\rm HD})\right]+25, (28) where Λ \Lambda CDM superscripts indicate that the quantity does not include observational errors, the redshifts are the same as observed, and D M D_{\mathrm{M}} is the comoving distance to z HD z_{\rm HD} in the SPA cosmology. Since the absolute calibration of the SNIa is irrelevant to the inferred cosmological parameters, we adopt M DES = − 19.40 M_{\mathrm{DES}}=-19.40 and do not report M DES M_{\mathrm{DES}} results from our mocks. We then add observational scatter based on the total covariance matrix C SNIa \textbf{{C}}_{\rm SNIa} of the real data in the DES-Dovekie catalogue ( Popovic et al., 2026 ) . The apparent magnitude is therefore as follows: m SNIa ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( m Λ ​ CDM , C SNIa ) . \displaystyle m_{\rm SNIa}~\sim~\mathcal{N}\left(m_{\Lambda\mathrm{CDM}},~\textbf{{C}}_{\rm SNIa}\right). (29) We follow a similar approach with the BAO. We generate mock BAO data at the same redshifts as those with real data from DESI DR2 BAO, propagating errors using their published covariance matrix C BAO \textbf{{C}}_{\rm BAO} at each redshift ( DESI Collaboration, 2025 , except at the lowest redshift where only D V D_{\rm V} is available; see) . The mock BAO measurements of D H , M , V / r d D_{\rm H,M,V}/r_{\rm d} are therefore as follows: D M , H , V r d ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( D M , H , V Λ ​ CDM r d , C BAO ) . \displaystyle\frac{D_{\rm M,H,V}}{r_{\rm d}}~\sim~\mathcal{N}\left(\frac{D_{\rm M,H,V}^{\Lambda\mathrm{CDM}}}{r_{\rm d}},~\textbf{{C}}_{\rm BAO}\right). (30) For both the SNIa and BAO, we set up a single noiseless mock in which we do not add observational errors, so m SNIa = m SNIa Λ ​ CDM m_{\rm SNIa}=m_{\rm SNIa}^{\Lambda\mathrm{CDM}} and D M , H , V BAO / r d = D M , H , V Λ ​ CDM / r d D_{\rm M,H,V}^{\rm BAO}/r_{\rm d}=D_{\rm M,H,V}^{\Lambda\mathrm{CDM}}/r_{\rm d} . We use the noiseless mock to separate the impact of observational errors and deficiencies in our fourth-order cosmographic expansion. We conduct 10 4 10^{4} realisations of the above setup. In each case, we extract H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} and H 0 DES + legacy H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES+legacy}} using the least-squares approach to reduce computational costs. The top panel of Figure 15 shows the joint distribution of these two H 0 H_{0} estimates as a scatter plot, with the 1 ​ σ 1\sigma and 2 ​ σ 2\sigma contours overlaid due to the large number of points in the central region. The solid red star shows the result for the real data using NUTS, corresponding to the main part of this paper. The open blue diamond shows the result using instead the least-squares method, which gives an almost identical result but is much faster to evaluate. The observed combination of H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} and H 0 DES + legacy H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES+legacy}} is quite unlikely in the SPA cosmology, for which the true H 0 H_{0} is shown using the solid lines. The dashed grey line shows the line of equality, from which the dotted red line is offset upwards by the observed Δ ​ H 0 \Delta H_{0} . It is immediately apparent that in our mocks, both recovered H 0 H_{0} values are somewhat higher than the truth. This remains the case even in our noiseless mock, which we indicate using a green plus symbol. The bias is thus an inherent property of our cosmographic IDL, though it is small compared to the random scatter caused by observational errors. In particular, ⟨ H 0 DES ⟩ \langle H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}}\rangle is biased by + 2.76 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 +2.76\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} compared to the true value, but the standard deviation of the best-fitting H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} between different mocks is 2.86 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 2.86\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} . H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} is thus biased upwards by only + 0.96 ​ σ +0.96\sigma . Due to the better redshift coverage of DES + legacy, it achieves a smaller bias: ⟨ H 0 DES + legacy ⟩ \langle H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES+legacy}}\rangle exceeds the true value by only + 0.57 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 +0.57\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} . Since the standard deviation of the best-fitting H 0 DES + legacy H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES+legacy}} values is 0.69 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 0.69\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , this represents a bias of + 0.82 ​ σ +0.82\sigma . The results also show a weak positive correlation between H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} and H 0 DES + legacy H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES+legacy}} , with a correlation coefficient of + 0.25 +0.25 . Higher H 0 DES + legacy H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES+legacy}} is thus generally associated with a correspondingly higher H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} (the regression of H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} on H 0 DES + legacy H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES+legacy}} has a slope of 1.04), albeit with large scatter. This correlation mitigates the impact on Δ ​ H 0 \Delta H_{0} . Figure 15: Top : Joint distribution of H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} and H 0 DES + legacy H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES+legacy}} , inferred from applying our fourth-order cosmographic IDL analysis to 10 4 10^{4} mock datasets assuming Λ \Lambda CDM with the SPA parameters ( SPT-3G Collaboration, 2026 ) . The true H 0 H_{0} is indicated using solid lines. The contours show the 1 ​ σ 1\sigma and 2 ​ σ 2\sigma regions, outside which individual points are shown with higher opacity. The dashed grey line is the line of equality. The dotted red line is offset upwards by the observed Δ ​ H 0 = 8.27 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 \Delta H_{0}=8.27\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} so it intersects the observed point, shown here as the red star. This is obtained using NUTS, but the open blue diamond shows that the corresponding least-squares result (labelled ‘LS’) is almost identical, so we use least-squares for the mocks. The green plus shows the result of our noiseless mock. Bottom : The distribution of Δ ​ H 0 = H 0 DES − H 0 DES + legacy \Delta H_{0}=H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}}-H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES+legacy}} from the same mocks. The solid black line shows the mean result, while the dotted black line shows the result in the noiseless mock. The solid red line shows the observed Δ ​ H 0 \Delta H_{0} using NUTS, while the dotted red line shows the almost identical result using least-squares. The red shading at the right shows the region where Δ ​ H 0 \Delta H_{0} exceeds the observed value. The bottom panel of Figure 15 shows the distribution of Δ ​ H 0 \Delta H_{0} . The dotted black line shows the result of our noiseless mock. This sits near the mean of the distribution from our 10 4 10^{4} mocks including noise, which we show as a solid black line. These results indicate a small positive bias of around + 2.2 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 +2.2\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} . The solid red line shows the result for the real data using NUTS. This is very similar to the corresponding least-squares result, which is shown as a dotted red line. Since the mocks are fitted by least squares, the like-for-like statistic is the least-squares Δ ​ H 0 = 8.70 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 \Delta H_{0}=8.70\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} of the real data, which only 85 of the 10 4 10^{4} mocks exceed (0.85%, 2.39 ​ σ 2.39\sigma for a one-tailed test). The NUTS value that we quote is therefore the more conservative of the two. We shade the region in which Δ ​ H 0 \Delta H_{0} exceeds the observed 8.27 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 8.27\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} . This occurs in just 124 of our 10 4 10^{4} mocks. The P P -value of 1.24% corresponds to 2.24 ​ σ 2.24\sigma for a one-tailed test, which is appropriate given the known sign of the Hubble tension (Section 4.8 ). It is therefore clear that the high observed Δ ​ H 0 \Delta H_{0} is indeed unlikely in mock datasets where the underlying cosmology is Λ \Lambda CDM with the SPA parameters. Part of this signal is the inaccuracy of our cosmographic expansion at finite k max k_{\max} , which biases H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} upwards by 2.76 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 2.76\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} in our mocks, i.e. by 0.96 times its formal uncertainty. The formal uncertainty matches the scatter between mocks, but it does not absorb this bias, so the ± 1 ​ σ \pm 1\sigma interval contains the input H 0 H_{0} in only 49% of the mocks. These results indicate that H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} cannot easily be reconciled with the SPA cosmology, despite assuming standard pre-recombination physics to set r d r_{\rm d} and not using the standard distance ladder. Our mocks show that the recovered H 0 H_{0} becomes less precise and less accurate (more biased) if we remove the legacy SNIa due to the loss of coverage at low redshifts. To better understand this process, we repeat the redshift-floor sweep of Section 4.4 in the Λ \Lambda CDM mock datasets mentioned above. The results are shown in Figure 16 , with the left panel showing H 0 H_{0} and the right panel showing q 0 q_{0} in every 20 th mock, so that the same 500 realisations appear in both panels. The thick solid line without points shows the median value at each redshift across the 10 4 10^{4} mocks. The thin solid (dotted) lines on either side show the 1 ​ σ 1\sigma ( 2 ​ σ 2\sigma ) uncertainty using Gaussian equivalent percentiles. The curves with points show results with the real data. The dotted horizontal line in each panel shows the true value in the mocks. The recovered H 0 H_{0} and q 0 q_{0} are not much biased at low z floor z_{\mathrm{floor}} values due to the minimal extrapolation required to reach the present epoch. As we increase z floor z_{\mathrm{floor}} , the recovered H 0 H_{0} is systematically biased high, while the opposite occurs for q 0 q_{0} . However, this bias is not sufficient to explain the high observed H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} within the SPA cosmology. Indeed, very few mocks have a curve that rises steeply to match the observed H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} at its redshift floor of 0.073. Figure 16: Top : The results of our redshift-floor sweep for H 0 H_{0} ( left panels ) and q 0 q_{0} ( right panels ) in our Λ \Lambda CDM mocks where the SNIa redshift distribution matches DES (black) and DES + legacy (red). The true values are shown using horizontal dotted orange lines in the top panels. The thin lines show 500 of the mocks in each sample’s own colour, using a fixed stride through the ensemble. The median of all 10 4 10^{4} mocks is shown as a thick solid line without points. The thin solid lines around it in the same colour show the 1 ​ σ 1\sigma range using Gaussian equivalent percentiles, while the dotted lines show the 2 ​ σ 2\sigma range. The result with the real data, obtained by least squares as for the mocks, is shown using a thick solid line with points. The inset focuses on the region covered by the legacy SNIa. Their redshift floor is shown with a vertical dotted red line, while the DES redshift floor is shown with a vertical dotted black line. We do not show the DES + legacy results beyond the redshift range of the legacy SNIa, as only DES SNIa are available there. Bottom : The uncertainty is shown in two ways, both plotted as ± σ \pm\sigma error bars around a central value of zero. The vertical scale is the same as the top panels. For clarity, the redshift is dithered symmetrically relative to the actually adopted z floor z_{\mathrm{floor}} . The dotted bars show half the 16th–84th percentile range of the best-fitting value between mocks. The solid bars show the median value across the mocks of the uncertainty returned by our analysis from each mock. Since not all mocks yield the same uncertainty, we use shaded rectangles in the colour of each sample to show the 1 ​ σ 1\sigma Gaussian equivalent range in the uncertainty returned by each mock. These are only visible at high z floor z_{\mathrm{floor}} because different mocks give results with a very similar precision. The bottom panels of Figure 16 show that the bias of our analysis is largely within its statistical uncertainty. The uncertainty our analysis returns for a single mock closely matches the scatter of the best-fitting values between mocks, both of which grow steadily with z floor z_{\mathrm{floor}} . Across a broad range of redshift floors, including that of DES, the true H 0 H_{0} lies close to the 1 ​ σ 1\sigma lower limit of the median H 0 DES H_{0}^{\mathrm{DES}} from the mocks, while the true q 0 q_{0} lies close to the 1 ​ σ 1\sigma upper limit. The two mirror each other because a lower q 0 q_{0} implies a faster late-time acceleration, and hence a higher H 0 H_{0} . Our mocks cannot tell us the truncation error for the real cosmology, but in a Λ \Lambda CDM-like one it is comparable to our reported uncertainty, even if DES had no SNIa below z = 0.3 z=0.3 . Since DES reaches z = 0.073 z=0.073 and has good coverage down to z ≈ 0.2 z\approx 0.2 , we expect our cosmographic expansion to perform well on the real data. We caution that in a redshift-floor sweep, the different points are all strongly correlated because every point uses a dataset that is strictly a subset of the data used at the preceding point. Even so, it is interesting that the DES-only result remains quite stable to the progressive addition of SNIa at low redshifts by decreasing z floor z_{\mathrm{floor}} . This suggests a lack of redshift-dependent internal tension within DES, making it all the more surprising that adding the legacy SNIa causes such a sharp change in behaviour for both H 0 H_{0} and q 0 q_{0} . The change is so sharp that in the narrow redshift range where DES and legacy samples overlap, there is a visible discrepancy between the results using DES and DES + legacy. This is especially evident in the insets to the top panels of Figure 16 at z ≈ 0.08 z\approx 0.08 . The result of the redshift-floor sweep using the real DES + legacy data is therefore not expected from our Λ \Lambda CDM mocks. The smoother behaviour in the DES alone case is much more in line with what we might expect, but in this case the values of H 0 H_{0} and q 0 q_{0} differ from those in the SPA cosmology despite assuming a standard r d r_{\rm d} . This issue could presumably be rectified if H 0 ​ r d H_{0}r_{\rm d} and q 0 q_{0} had values different from those in the SPA cosmology. However, the sharp feature in the DES + legacy case at precisely the redshift where legacy SNIa start being included seems unlikely to arise in any realistic cosmology. This coincidence is better understood as a systematic problem with the legacy SNIa measurements, at least when recalibrated onto the DES filter system.

A model-independent test using DES-Dovekie supernovae and DESI DR2 BAO 2026 Does the inverse distance ladder rule out late-time solutions to the Hubble tension? A model-independent test using DES-Dovekie supernovae and DESI DR2 BAO – D José Antonio Nájera † † thanks: E-mail: antonio.najera@port.ac.uk Affiliation: Institute of Cosmology & Gravitation, University of Portsmouth, Dennis Sciama Building, Burnaby Road, Portsmouth PO1 3FX, UK Indranil Banik † † thanks: E-mail: indranilbanik1992@gmail.com Affiliation: Institute of Cosmology & Gravitation, University of Portsmouth, Dennis Sciama Building, Burnaby Road, Portsmouth PO1 3FX, UK Harry Desmond † † thanks: E-mail: harry.desmond@port.ac.uk Affiliation: Institute of Cosmology & Gravitation, University of Portsmouth, Dennis Sciama Building, Burnaby Road, Portsmouth PO1 3FX, UK Accepted XXX. Received YYY; in original form ZZZ Abstract It has been argued that the inverse distance ladder disfavours late-time solutions to the Hubble tension. We test this with a cosmographic expansion where H H is a fourth-order polynomial in 1 − a 1-a . We combine the uncalibrated DES-Dovekie SNIa with DESI DR2 BAO, assuming a standard sound horizon r d = 147.05 ± 0.30 r_{\rm d}=147.05\pm 0.30 Mpc. Using only DES SNIa yields H 0 = 76.25 ± 2.87 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=76.25\pm 2.87\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , which is 3.1 ​ σ 3.1\sigma above the CMB-calibrated Λ \Lambda CDM prediction but consistent with SH0ES ( 1.0 ​ σ 1.0\sigma ). Adding the legacy SNIa decreases H 0 H_{0} to 67.98 ± 0.69 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 67.98\pm 0.69\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} , 4.7 ​ σ 4.7\sigma below SH0ES. The 8.27 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 8.27\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} drop in H 0 H_{0} upon including the legacy SNIa cannot be attributed to expected sample variance: under a fiducial Λ ​ CDM \Lambda\text{CDM} model, only 1.24 % 1.24\% of 10 4 10^{4} mock realisations exhibit such a large H 0 H_{0} shift due to the changed redshift sampling. This points to a systematic tension between DES and legacy SNIa datasets. We next add local H 0 H_{0} anchors (the bright siren, SNII, TRGB + SBF) and test a parametrisation where the Λ \Lambda CDM H ⁡ ( z ) H(z) is enhanced by Δ H ( z ) = A exp ( − z / z 1 ) \Delta H(z)=A\exp(-z/z_{1}) . We recover H 0 = 70.00 − 0.98 + 4.78 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=70.00^{+4.78}_{-0.98}\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} and z 1 < 0.086 z_{1}<0.086 at 1 ​ σ 1\sigma confidence using DES SNIa, but H 0 = 67.66 ± 1.01 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}=67.66\pm 1.01\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} and z 1 z_{1} is unconstrained using DES + legacy. Late-time solutions are thus viable with the homogeneous DES catalogue, but not with the legacy SNIa as published. Allowing them to be arbitrarily recalibrated relative to the main DES sample yields an inferred offset of Δ ​ M legacy = 0.0646 ± 0.0391 \Delta M_{\mathrm{legacy}}=0.0646\pm 0.0391 mag, raising the predicted H 0 H_{0} to 71.03 ± 1.99 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 71.03\pm 1.99\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} . Ongoing SNIa surveys like DEBASS will provide a homogeneous sample of SNIa down to redshifts accessible via the distance ladder, assessing the validity of the current legacy samples and hence the feasibility of late-time solutions to the Hubble tension. Keywords: cosmology: theory – cosmology: observations – cosmological parameters – supernovae: general – distance scale – methods: statistical 1 Introduction One of the most challenging problems in modern cosmology is the tension between different estimates of the present expansion rate H 0 H_{0} . This Hubble tension describes the discrepancy between the expansion rate of the Universe inferred through local distance measurements ( Breuval et al., 2024 , e.g. H 0 SH0ES = 73.17 ± 0.86 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}^{\mathrm{SH0ES}}=73.17\pm 0.86\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} from SH0ES;) and the predicted expansion rate based on calibrating the parameters of the Lambda cold dark matter ( Λ \Lambda CDM) standard cosmological paradigm ( Efstathiou, Sutherland and Maddox, 1990 ; Ostriker and Steinhardt, 1995 ) using the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB), which gives a far lower value ( SPT-3G Collaboration, 2026 , e.g. SPT-3G + ACT DR6 + Planck obtained that H 0 SPA = 67.19 ± 0.38 ​ km ​ s − 1 ​ Mpc − 1 H_{0}^{\mathrm{SPA}}=67.19\pm 0.38\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} ;) . These results are in 6.4 ​ σ 6.4\sigma tension with each other. An even higher tension has recently been claimed by the Local Distance Network based on combining several popular local determinations and taking into account their covariance ( H0DN Collaboration, 2026 ) . However, this does not properly model selection effects or distance priors ( Desmond et al., 2026 ; Stiskalek et al., 2026 ) . The three possible explanations for the tension are unaccounted-for systematics in the distance ladder, statistical inadequacy of the inferences ( Becker et al., 2015 ; Feeney et al., 2018 ; Desmond et al., 2026 ; Percival, 2026 ; Stiskalek et al., 2026 ; Stiskalek and Desmond, 2026 , e.g.) , and new physics beyond the standard Λ \Lambda CDM model (e.g. Di Valentino et al., 2025 , and references therein) . New physics could primarily affect the Universe prior to recombination or have little impact until more recent epochs, leading to a distinction between early-time and late-time solutions. A useful expansion probe is provided by supernovae (SNe) of Type Ia (SNIa). These thermonuclear explosions occur when a carbon–oxygen white dwarf in a binary system reaches a mass close to 1.2 ​ M ⊙ 1.2\,M_{\odot} , as predicted by models like the dynamically driven double-degenerate double-detonation ( D 6 ) \left(\mathrm{D}^{6}\right) scenario ( Shen et al., 2018b ; Shen et al., 2018a ; Bauer et al., 2021 ) . Since SNIa occur at nearly the same mass, they are good standardisable candles, i.e., the peak absolute magnitude M B M_{B} in the B B band can be estimated independently of the redshift z z ( Phillips, 1993 ; Tripp, 1998 ; Phillips et al., 1999 ) . Due to the known H 0 H_{0} – M B M_{B} degeneracy ( Cai and Wang, 2026 ; Wang and Wang, 2026 ) , SNIa require an absolute calibration to measure H 0 H_{0} . Since SNIa are very luminous ( M B ≈ − 19.3 M_{B}\approx-19.3 ), they can be detected out to z ≈ 2 z\approx 2 ( Scolnic et al., 2022 ) . However, it is difficult to access all of this redshift range using just one survey. Modern SNIa catalogues like Pantheon+ ( Scolnic et al., 2022 ) , Union3 ( Rubin et al., 2025 ) , and Unite ( Camilleri et al., 2026 ) typically combine different surveys. This may create problems due to the use of different filters, selection functions, and relative calibration offsets ( Betoule et al., 2014 ; Scolnic et al., 2014 ; Scolnic et al., 2015 ; Efstathiou, 2025 ) . A homogeneous catalogue with only one survey and one selection function would be far preferable for cosmological inference. This is provided by the Dark Energy Survey ( DES Collaboration, 2016 , DES;) through its Dovekie catalogue ( Popovic et al., 2026 ) . This single-instrument dataset with a single filter system is typically complemented by legacy SNIa from older surveys to improve the leverage on the shape of the expansion history at z ≲ 0.2 z\la 0.2 , where there are very few SNIa in DES ( DES Collaboration, 2024 , though it has SNIa down to z = 0.073 z=0.073 ;) . However, including the legacy SNIa risks the aforementioned problems with combining surveys, and assessing this legacy sample relative to the DES sample is a main aim of this paper. Our baseline analysis involves only SNIa in the DES data, which we label simply DES. We also consider an extension including the legacy SNIa (DES + legacy), which corresponds to what other authors typically mean by “DES” ( DESI Collaboration, 2025 , e.g.) . This distinguishes our work from similar studies ( Popovic and Sullivan, 2026 , most notably) , which generally do not distinguish between legacy and DES SNIa. Our main motivation is the presently open discussion on whether the legacy SNIa have been correctly recalibrated onto the DES photometric filter system, something which cannot be directly verified through further observations given the transient nature of SNIa ( Efstathiou, 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Ormondroyd et al., 2026 ) . Since the legacy SNIa lie in z ∈ [ 0.025 , 0.087 ] z\in[0.025,0.087] , they provide a critical lever on the value of H 0 H_{0} , making it crucial that they be unbiased. This motivates further analyses where we calculate the possible offset between the legacy SNIa and the main DES sample. This is also a crucial issue for the evidence for evolving dark energy, which is largely driven by the legacy SNIa; allowing an offset provides a better fit to the data in a Bayesian sense than allowing a time-variation in the equation of state of dark energy ( Ormondroyd et al., 2026 ) . In Section 4.5 , we explore the extent to which the legacy SNIa affect the evidence for evolving dark energy. There are two main routes to determine the absolute SNIa magnitude M SNIa M_{\rm SNIa} . The first route is through the cosmic distance ladder, usually with three rungs. The first rung involves geometry to calibrate distance indicators like Cepheid variable stars ( Leavitt and Pickering, 1912 ; Riess et al., 2022 ; Breuval et al., 2024 ) , the tip of the red giant branch ( Lee et al., 1993 ; Madore and Freedman, 1995 ; Freedman et al., 2019 ; Hoyt et al., 2024 , TRGB;) , or the J-region Asymptotic Giant Branch ( Madore and Freedman, 2020 ; Lee et al., 2025 , JAGB;) . The second rung is where the M B M_{B} calibration happens using SNIa host galaxies near enough to contain a first rung indicator. The third rung contains SNIa in the Hubble flow at z ≳ 0.023 z\ga 0.023 , where peculiar velocities are not important in Λ \Lambda CDM, allowing a determination of H 0 H_{0} from the slope of the Hubble diagram. Using this approach, the SH0ES collaboration derived a value of M B = − 19.253 ± 0.027 M_{B}=-19.253\pm 0.027 ( Riess et al., 2022 ; Scolnic et al., 2022 ) . The second route to M SNIa M_{\rm SNIa} is through the inverse distance ladder (IDL). This involves anchoring M SNIa M_{\rm SNIa} using our understanding of the early Universe to set the baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) comoving sound horizon r d r_{\rm d} at the end of the baryon drag epoch ( Hu and Sugiyama, 1996 ; Eisenstein and Hu, 1998 , z d ≈ 1060 z_{\rm d}\approx 1060 ;) and then propagating this to intermediate redshifts using the BAO evident from galaxy clustering, which nowadays is typically obtained from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Data Release 2 ( DESI Collaboration, 2025 , DR2;) . One common assumption which we follow is to adopt the Planck constraint of r d = 147.05 ± 0.30 r_{\rm d}=147.05\pm 0.30 comoving Mpc (cMpc) from Planck Collaboration VI 2020 (hereafter 100 ). This explicitly adopts Λ \Lambda CDM at early times, so the IDL approach implicitly assumes that the Hubble tension, if due to new physics, must be solved at late times. Under this assumption, M SNIa ≈ − 19.30 M_{\rm SNIa}\approx-19.30 to − 19.40 -19.40 ( Camilleri et al., 2025 ; Popovic and Sullivan, 2026 ) , which is significantly lower than suggested by the local distance ladder. This is because a lower H 0 H_{0} value requires SNIa to be more distant at given z z , which for given apparent magnitude requires the SNIa to be brighter. The discrepancy with the locally determined M B M_{B} leads to the usual conclusion that a successful solution to the Hubble tension requires a smaller r d r_{\rm d} , which is possible only through new pre-recombination physics ( Cai and Wang, 2026 ; Sabogal et al., 2026 ; Tiwari et al., 2026 ) . Although the expansion history is nowadays mainly probed through the distance–redshift relation, it is possible to bypass distances altogether by instead focusing on the lookback time. The elapsed time between any two redshifts can be found using the cosmic chronometer (CC) technique, which involves comparing massive passive elliptical galaxies at those redshifts to determine the relative age ( Jimenez and Loeb, 2002 ; Moresco et al., 2012 ; Moresco, 2015 ; Moresco et al., 2016 ; Moresco et al., 2022 ; Moresco, 2024 ) . Since we can relate distance and lookback time using the speed of light c c , we can use CC datasets to calibrate M B M_{B} without assuming any value for r d r_{\rm d} , thereby obtaining an estimate for H 0 H_{0} ( Cogato et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . Early-time solutions to the Hubble tension seek to resolve it by decreasing r d r_{\rm d} , which requires modifying the redshift dependence of the sound horizon and/or the redshift of recombination ( Mirpoorian et al., 2025 ) . Since BAO measurements are most sensitive to the product H 0 ​ r d H_{0}r_{\rm d} , reducing r d r_{\rm d} allows for an increased H 0 H_{0} . However, these solutions face at least seven problems ( Vagnozzi, 2023 ) . One of these is that they would imply a significantly reduced age of the Universe ( Vagnozzi et al., 2022 ) . This prediction is in significant tension with the observed ages of the oldest Galactic stars and globular clusters ( Montalbán et al., 2021 ; Valcin et al., 2020 ; Valcin et al., 2021 ; Cimatti and Moresco, 2023 ; Souza et al., 2024 ; Valcin et al., 2025 ; Valcin et al., 2026 ; Banik et al., 2026b ) . These features cannot be explained through a simple change to r d r_{\rm d} . Moreover, currently known early-time solutions struggle with Big Bang nucleosynthesis (BBN) due to their need for a generically higher baryon density to match the CMB anisotropies, which affects primordial light element abundances ( Giovanetti, 2026 ; Launders et al., 2026 ; Poulin et al., 2026 ) . More generally, the success of Λ \Lambda CDM in fitting the CMB anisotropies by now limits the scope for substantial modifications prior to recombination ( Calabrese et al., 2025 ; SPT-3G Collaboration, 2026 , 100 ;) , including in models where electron density fluctuations cause inhomogeneous recombination ( Lynch et al., 2026 ) . Late-time solutions to the Hubble tension avoid these problems by assuming standard pre-recombination physics, but such models have their own problems at z ≲ 1 z\la 1 ( Krishnan et al., 2021a ) . In particular, Bansal and Huterer (2026) find that a model modifying only the late-time expansion history cannot simultaneously fit H 0 SH0ES H_{0}^{\mathrm{SH0ES}} , the DESI BAO data, and relative SNIa distances. A fit is possible only if M SNIa M_{\mathrm{SNIa}} takes a sharp step at very low redshift ( z ≲ 0.01 z\la 0.01 ) or the distance-duality relation is broken. Both escapes are trivial since they decouple the calibrated SNIa from the remaining data. Importantly, their analysis rests on the Pantheon+ catalogue. A step in M B M_{B} at low redshift is degenerate with precisely the relative calibration offsets between surveys described above, given the difficulty of covering a very wide redshift range using the same survey. Their most successful late-time magnitude step model has a transition in the redshift range where a heterogeneous compilation is least able to separate new physics from filter-related changes to the zero point. This motivates the test we present here. We note that astrophysically it is difficult to understand why SNIa might abruptly change in intrinsic brightness, with terrestrial data placing strong constraints on models with a sharp change in G G in the geologically recent past ( Banik, Desmond and Samaras, 2025 ) . Such models also face difficulties with the mass–radius relation of red dwarf stars due to their long thermal timescales ( Sakstein and Desmond, 2026 ) . Our main goal is to assess if the IDL can accommodate a late-time solution to the Hubble tension, i.e., if the assumption of standard pre-recombination physics is compatible with the high H 0 H_{0} required to match various local constraints ( Di Valentino et al., 2025 ; H0DN Collaboration, 2026 ) . The observational data we use for this purpose are described in Section 2 . We then explain the IDL, our Bayesian model comparison of late-time solutions to the Hubble tension, and consistency tests (Section 3 ). We go on to present our results (Section 4 ) and discuss their implications (Section 5 ). We conclude in Section 6 . In Appendix A , we present the Alcock–Paczynski (AP) consistency test between DESI DR2 BAO and DES-Dovekie SNIa. Appendix B reports how the inferred cosmological parameters depend on the polynomial order. Appendix C contains all the posteriors from our analyses. In Appendix D , we use Λ \Lambda CDM mocks to better understand how our analysis is affected by the limited DES coverage at low redshift. 2 Observational data 2.1 DES-Dovekie SNIa The DES-Dovekie compilation of SNe provides 1820 spectroscopically and photometrically classified events with their full statistical plus systematic covariance ( Popovic et al., 2026 ) . The intrinsic scatter contribution to this covariance is calibrated so that Λ \Lambda CDM yields an acceptable fit to the Hubble diagram. This is because we currently lack sufficiently large samples of SNIa with redshift-independent distances from which the intrinsic scatter can be inferred, as is usually done with other indicators like Cepheids. The total SNIa uncertainties are therefore scaled to a reference cosmology, which means that an acceptable χ 2 \chi^{2} under Λ \Lambda CDM in SNIa-dominated analyses like ours does not by itself demonstrate that Λ \Lambda CDM is an adequate description of the data. Some studies report a descending trend in H 0 H_{0} with the redshift of the data used to measure it ( Krishnan et al., 2020 ; Krishnan et al., 2021b ; Lopez-Hernandez and De-Santiago, 2025 ; Jia et al., 2025 ; Jia et al., 2026 ) . Unlike those studies which infer H 0 H_{0} from data in a narrow redshift range centred on z z and thereby obtain a curve of H 0 ​ ( z ) H_{0}(z) , our approach uses a redshift floor, so we denote the results as H 0 ​ ( z floor ) H_{0}(z_{\mathrm{floor}}) . A clear trend in H 0 ​ ( z floor ) H_{0}(z_{\mathrm{floor}}) which becomes asymptotically flat would indicate that the lowest redshift SNIa carry the cosmological parameters away from the more robust result from higher redshift SNIa. On the other hand, a flat trend in H 0 ​ ( z floor ) H_{0}(z_{\mathrm{floor}}) at the low-redshift end would indicate that different SNIa subsets prefer much the same present expansion rate, though error bars should widen at high z floor z_{\mathrm{floor}} as more data is excluded. 3.3 Bayesian evidence for a late-time solution to the Hubble tension 3.3.1 Alternative models To assess if the data prefers a late-time solution to the Hubble tension over Λ \Lambda CDM, we consider the following phenomenological expansion history ( Nájera, Banik, Desmond and Kalaitzidis, 2026 ) : H ⁡ ( z ) = H 0 , Λ ​ CDM ​ Ω m ​ ( 1 + z ) 3 + ( 1 − Ω m ) + Δ ​ H ​ ( z , A , z 1
